In 2023, 216 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Bangladesh, Kenya, Mexico, the Netherlands), international and multilateral organizations (EU, UN, World Bank), political parties and media outlets put FGG’s policy and practice recommendations on their agendas. Trade & Investment • In 2023, the Dutch government has set their agenda for implementation of the Feminist Foreign Policy and how to include trade, investment and tax issues. The paper was presented at the Dutch government shaping feminist foreign policy event. (g) • In 2023, the Dutch MoFA selected FGG’s session on Reimagining Feminist Trade for the Ministries conference. Recognizing our expertise on gender and trade, on in the panel to address a feminist energy transition and the impact of mining on women. (g) • Throughout 2023, different media channels (Politico , EurActiv) reported on the EU and Mercosur deal as a result of FGG’s lobby and advocacy activities. FGG published academic briefings that exposed that the EU additional declaration did not include any enforceable measures that would address concerns of deforestation, increased climate impacts and human rights violations. • In June 2023, twelve opinion articles were published in national newspapers in Uganda and Ghana on the gendered impacts of fossil fuels, call for a halt in the expansion of oil and gas activities and highlighting the dangers of oil and gas expansion. These articles significantly contributed to the mounting pressure exerted by local communities on AfreximBank, compelling the institution to reconsider its support for oil and gas projects in Uganda and Africa. (g + x) • In 2023, WTO acknowledged the need to include rules on gender rights under trade negotiations during the public forum of 2023 and as part of panel discussions after a meeting with FGG. (g) • Throughout 2023, in different debates and meetings with the new Brazil parliament, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs the General Secretariat of the Presidency, President Lula’s office, Ministry of Industry and Trade, Agrarian Development and Women’s affairs topics like trade and gender rights as well as environmental consequences to sustainable development of trade agreements were on the agenda of these new key political actors. (g + x) • The Ugandan Parliament and department of Finance, Planning and Economic Development, Ministry of Trade and the Uganda Investment Authority and Uganda Free Zones Authorities are reviewing investment policies in relation to investment protection and the consequences of trade agreements. FGG supported partners with technical knowledge on trade agreements in order for them to lobby at these key actors in Uganda. • In March 2023, The office of the US trade representative (USTR) and the US Department of Commerce discussed the positions of Indonesian civil society regarding the US Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (IPEF) during a CSO stakeholder engagement meeting during the 2nd negotiation round in Bali, Indonesia in. FGG and partners participated in the stakeholder meeting and made direct interventions on the issue of mineral supply chains under the 2nd pillar of the framework pertaining to supply chains. • The Permanent Mission of Indonesia to the WTO discussed Indonesian civil society concerns regarding the WTO, ongoing trade negotiations, and EU’s enforcement regulation for the WTO lawsuit against Indonesia on the nickel ban. FGG and partners have been engaged in several lobby meetings with the government. • In October 2023, the UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights and the Environment prepared and presented a report to the General Assembly on ISDS being an obstacle to the urgent actions needed to address the planetary environmental and human rights crises. FGG advised the UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights and the Environment and provided input for the report during a meeting in June. Climate and environmental policies • In May 2023, the risks of digital monopolies were on the agenda of the ‘beyond growth’ conference organized by the EU parliament. A member of FGG was invited as a speaker for the panel called ‘Building a fair, social, green, autonomous digital future for a post-growth economy’, to share our work on digital monopolies at the conference. • In 2023, media gave renewed attention to the Netherlands still being the biggest conduit tax haven in the world. The Tax Justice Network , hosted by FGG, published a report that showed that the Netherlands still facilitates the existence of large tax conduit structures, causing other countries to lose revenues. • In 2023, the Nigerian government and an oil regulator agreed to consider the National Principles on Responsible Divestment in the Oil industry , a tool developed by Nigerian CSOs and findings of a research mission to the Niger delta. FGG facilitated the research mission, did research that fed into the development of the principles and supported and participated in strategic discussions. Implementation of the principles would help ensure a transparent process to assess the capacity of the incoming companies, with meaningful consultation throughout, address environmental pollution and deteriorating and abandoned infrastructure. • In 2023, a multi-stakeholder platform with key actors in climate disaster risk management (such as humanitarian workers, community representatives and government actors) in Malawi , as a result of the Caravan of Hope movement (which was organized by youth groups trained by FGG) talked about the issues they raise such as Malawi’s state for preparedness and responsiveness to climate induced disasters. • In 2023, the Dutch delegation to the COP invited FGG to hold a learning session about gender and climate during a delegation meeting 2 weeks ahead of the COP. FGG co-coordinated the sessions and provided concrete recommendations for gender-responsive and accessible climate finance. • In 2023, the Dutch minister for Climate , just before COP28 received participants of the Feminist Climate Academy and discussed recommendations to ensure a gender-just outcome of COP28. FGG took part in organizing the academy and trained youth on climate action and lobby. • In 2023, the Dutch minister of Finance discussed with FGG and CSOs the role of the Coalition of Finance Ministers for Climate Action in relation to climate finance issues. She agreed the coalitions needs to work more on gender as a current gap. FGG lobbied for a moment in her busy schedule at COP28 to discuss gender and climate. (g) • In 2023, the Dutch national media reported on developments regarding the Loss and Damage fund. FGG was approached as climate and gender expert to provide information and quotes. (g) • In 2023, the state minister for the Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resources in Bangladesh stated that signing additional energy agreements or treaties is not necessary to attract further investment. FGG and partners undertook various awareness raising and campaigning activities to advocate against Bangladesh’s accession to ECTs. • In 2023, the European Commission and the European Parliament put pressure on the new EU Climate Commissioner for strong commitments on climate issues. FGG was part of a broader coalition voicing critical opinions about the Commissioners connections with the fossil fuel industry and his role in undermining Dutch environmental policies. As a result of this media attention and a petition signed by over a 100.000 people the public pressure that was exerted on him led to these commitment. • In November 2023, the coalition Kick Big Polluters Out, received massive media attention worldwide on fossil fuel lobbyists which have been granted access to the COP28 summit. Their research highlighted that it was nearly four times more than last year and decision makers and media ere informed about the corporate capture of climate negotiations. • In 2023, different media outlets (including Al Jazeera, Financial Times, France 24, El Diario and Reuters) reported on the climate case involving the residents of of a community in Indonesia versus a multinational cement company seeking reduction of the company’s CO2 emissions and compensation for climate damages suffered. FGG provided communication and strategic support to raise international awareness for the legal case. • In 2023, different media outlets (including the NY Times) reported on the importance of climate litigation as a result of FGG’s outreach to media resulting in quotes from FGG spokes people on the importance of climate litigation. • In 2023, at least 7 different media outlets (including the BBC news) reported on the demand for international negotiations for a UN Global Plastics Treaty that seeks to end plastic pollution by dramatically reducing plastic production, consumption and trade and scaling up system change solutions. FGG developed messaging and carried out communications outreach on the treaty. • During the third negotiating session, in November 2023 in Nairobi, the Chair of the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC) to develop an international legally binding instrument on plastic pollution including in the marine environment incorporated positions advocated by FGG and its partners into article 1 and article 10 of the agreement. FGG provided coordination, communication and strategic support to this lobby on the treaty process, as a contribution to the broader movement working on the agreement. • In 2023, various media (including CNN) reported on the IPCC AR6 synthesis report. FGG actively reached out to the media responding to the IPCC AR6 report emphasizing the accelerating climate impacts. • In 2023, the supervisory body of the UNFCCC and the parties to the UNFCCC mentioned the influence of strong civil society engagement in the process of several occasions. No Article 6.2 and 6.4 decisions were approved by the parties to the UNFCCC COP 28 and they are being sent back to the Subsidiary Body to be picked up at the Bonn intersessional in 2024 and to the Supervisory Body before returning to COP29 for a decision. FGG supported many CSOs in the run up and during the UNFCCC intersessional in Bonn and the COP28 to show a front against false solutions and article 6.4. including through trainings, webinars, development of materials, coordinated actions on the topic, and hosting joint press conference on false solutions. • In 2023, over 400 media outlets reported on the Bonn climate talks and the COP28 on topics advocated for by FGG and partners. FGG prepared and campaigned by developing positions, joint campaigns, press statements and social media coverage. Topics covered included: carbon markets and offsets, just and equitable energy transition, climate finance / means of implementation, calls to kick big polluters out of the COP28 policy spaces, civil society access demands, historical responsibility, nuclear energy, fossil fuel phase out, false solutions (CCS/CCUS, hydrogen, nuclear, and carbon removal technologies such as geoengineering, or nature-based). (x) • In 2023, media reported on the environmental impacts of the Gaza war. FGG amplified the voices of a CSO in the media, which led to interest by a journalist developing a podcast featuring the CSO. • In 2023, 1 government environmental authority from Argentina invited a CSO to participate at a public hearing. FGG financially supported the CSO to advocate for a wetlands law, engaging with government at different levels as part of work on an ongoing campaign (together with a network of 50 organisations) for the enactment of a National Wetlands Law (Law on Minimum Standards of Environmental Protection for the wise and sustainable use of wetlands). • In 2023, many English-language, Arabic, French, Spanish and Portuguese media outlets have published reviews, articles, op eds, extracts or interviews on green colonialism and climate justice in the Arab region . FGG and partner CSOs have undertaken research and published longreads and a book critically interrogating the present reality and future prospects for a just transition in North Africa which were used by partners as the basis for national and regional advocacy. • In 2023, French and Arabic media outlets popularised a case study on Green Hydrogen in Morocco , highlighting green hydrogen as a false solution. FGG and partners undertook research and published the case study. Tenure policies • In 2023, the Payra port authority in Bangladesh planned to use an alternative road through an embankment after the protest of the Eatbaria village community to stop use village roads for carrying construction materials by heavy vehicles. The alternative road plan through the embankment is causing the displacement of 136 landless families who have been living on beside the embankment for years. FGG and partners are supporting the communities with training and joint strategising. • In 2023, the President of Uganda sent a team to the Kiryandongo district to do a situational analysis and assess allegations of human rights violations and land grab committed by multinational corporations investing in plantations in the area and forceful evictions of 2 communities from the land. This happened in response to a campaign set up by the community in the area affected by the land grabs, FGG supported these communities with this campaign. • In 2023, the Ministry of Land, Housing and Urban development in Uganda invited FGG and other actors to review and provide proposals for the Land Amendment Bill 2023, including in relation to community and women’s land rights and on citizen’s participation in decision making on land rights and the incorporation of the principle of FPIC for communities affected by investments. FGG advocated for strengthening the Uganda land rights legal framework and implementations for years. (g+x) • In 2023, a County Government of a county in Southern Kenya stated the importance of women's rights, especially widow’s rights to inheritance, property and land rights. This resulted from FGG’s sustained advocacy with the county. (g) • In 2023, a local radio station in Southern Kenya allocated a weekly programme for a widow’s association to discuss widow’s rights to land and property. This was a result of the launch of a widow’s association for the county supported by FGG. • In 2023, the Municipal Environment and Natural Resources (MENRO) Officer of Opol Local Government Unit in the Philippines reiterated the support of the Opol Local Government Unit and cited their efforts in the crafting of their forest land use plan in which all related environmental plans and projects will be addressed accordingly by the implementing agencies. (x) • In 2023, the Jambi Province DRPD in Indonesia established a special committee for the human rights issues faced by Orang Rimba IPs and served as a starting point and opportunity for advocating the rights of Orang Rimba IPs. FGG supported the CSO through small grants and technical support to continue its advocacy collaboration with various government agencies (x). • In 2023, after developing an advocacy strategy in which a collective movement with different stakeholders was formed, the Ministry of Interior, Land Management and Agriculture in Cambodia accepted the meeting requested by the Indigenous Peoples Alliance. • In 2023, a plantation company has started the formal process of acquiring a land concession for their project which is a result of the pressures from communities and CSOs on the company. FGG supported the local communities to apply pressure on the company to organise their land so they can be held accountable. Public financial institutions • In 2023, a Dutch development bank and a Ugandan tree planting company co-funded by the bank asked FGG and partners to jointly review a Compliance Advisor Ombudsman (CAO) mediation process from 2010 to review procedural gaps to be addressed by the bank and the company as a way of auditing the land acquisition process and to identify community members that were not compensated and establish remedy for them. FGG participated in a fact finding mission to assess the community’s complaints and compiled a missing report and a meeting with the bank and the company to present the findings. • In 2023, NL Atradius was planning to provide an Export Credit Insurance to SBM Offshore for the amount of 300 million euros for a Floating Production Storage and Offloading facility for the exploration of oil and gas in the Mero-field in Brazil. Public pressure from FGG and partner CSOs resulted in questions from Dutch parliamentarians about the ECI from the Dutch government. The Dutch government decided it would not approve 8 out of the 10 fossil projects for which export credit insurances were requested through Atradius. (4 billion was requested, only 322 million was approved). • FMO, MIGA and JCM power held consultations among affected communities by the Salima Solar project as a result of the claims and complaints from the community, FGG supported the communities financially and with knowledge on how to gain visibility. The consultation process commenced to discuss land acquisition complaints through a local grievances mechanism. It was a meaningful consultation sharing insights on intimidation and coercion as well as allegations of gender-based violence. (g) Rules for business and corporate conduct, cross-sector • In 2023, FGG was invited to share work on social economy in the age of digitization at the OECD Economy Summit in March 2023 in the company of influential representatives from the World Economic Forum, the Città Metropolitana di Bologna and Google among others. • In 2023, a member of parliament in Bangladesh joined Global Inter-parliamentary Network (GIN) on the LBI. This addition to his agenda is a result of his participation in the Asia Regional LBI forum. FGG supported his attendance to the forum and lobbied for his role in the GIN. • In 2023, a Representative of the House in Mozambique , attended the 2nd Africa BHR forum, with events about implications in the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and a Gender-Responsive Legally Binding Treaty on Transnational Corporations for Extractives, Women's Economic Justice, and Corporate Accountability in Africa. FGG and partners lobbied to engage the Mozambique government in the next LBI negotiations. (g) • The Ministry of Justice (Directory of external cooperation) in Mozambique sent a letter to the Minister of Justice requesting to coordinate the country's agenda and host a multi-stakeholder event to update the Government about the process and effectively engage them in discussions. Mozambique attended the negotiations in Geneva, after years of not attending. FGG organised a strategy meeting to inform, understand and influence the State’s position on the next LBI negotiations. (x) • A representative of the Mozambique parliament was part of the panel discussion on the LBI themed ‘the role of parliaments in promoting political change and a just economy in the Africa continent”, FGG lobbied to have a representative included in the discussions. • In 2023, the Ministry of Justice, Constitutional and Religious affairs in Mozambique hosted a strategy discussion on how to effectively engage and position the government towards the next round of UN Binding Treaty negotiations. Which is a result of FGG lobbying the ministry and government of Mozambique to actively engage in the process. • In 2023, 5 members of the African Missions (Cameroon, Nigeria, Kenya, Mozambique and Ethiopia) participated in an exchange and learning session in Geneva on Legally Binding Treaty on BHR. FGG and other members of Feminist for a Binding Treaty together with Lawyers for Human Rights, provided an overview of their gender-responsive recommendations on the treaty text. (g) • In 2023, the Asia Task Force put Feminist for a Binding Treaty demands on the agenda of the meeting during the Asia Regional LBI forum. The aim was to ensure Asian actors understand the political relevance of the LBI, the rights of victims, legal identity and liability of TNC's, prevention and state obligations and the gender perspective. (g) • In 2023, the Local Chiefs in Phalombe district in Malawi engaged in resource mobilisation for an evaluation centre on climate change, and learn from disasters and its impacts -such as the mismanagement in the aftermath of Cyclone Freddy, all with a gender focus. FGG trained and facilitated youth groups in the district to engage with these officers and mobilise them. (g) • In February 2023, six Dutch Parliamentarians (from CU, GL, PvdA, SP, D66 and VOLT) one Europarliamentarian from PvdA joint a CSO and private sector movement in public action “The Sweatshop” organized to raise awareness and public support on the need to adopt the Dutch initiative law for mandatory human rights legislation. FGG -through the MVO platform- lobbied for national legislation. • In 2023, the Dutch political parties GroenLinks and SP raised the need for extra unilateral measures against tax avoidance during a debate on policy coherence. FGG contributed to the Building Change Coalition which lobbied towards the parties. • In 2023, the Dutch government received and discussed the OESO DAC review and participated in the process. As part of the review as an NGO representative, FGG emphasized policy coherence risks of the Dutch government, including tax, IMVO and women’s rights. (g) • In 2023, the Dutch Parliament discussed a motion about UN global tax body to call on the Dutch government to recognize the UN as the forum where to develop global tax rules. FGG lobbied the Dutch political party SP to file a motion and provided input. • In 2023, the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs put Tax and the Global Tax body more often on the agenda which is strongly related to a push in previous meetings. FGG raised the issue during several meetings with the Ministry. • In 2023, The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MINEX and the Presidential Commission for Peace and Human Rights (COPADEH) of Guatamala , discussed the progress in construction of the National Action Plan and the position of the State in the UN negotiations on BHR. FGG lobbied the commission by presenting the framework on guiding principles on BHR and the discussions of the UMBT with recommendations focused on gender and indigenous rights. (g) • In January 2023, three Dutch political parties (VOLT, D66 and PvDD) posed questions on whether the gender perspective is sufficiently included in the Dutch initiative law for mandatory human rights legislation during the question round on this law, specifically asking about gender-responsive identification of risks, stakeholder engagement and if women are sufficiently protected by this law. FGG provided input through advocacy meetings, policy briefs and letters to parliaments. (g) • In 2023, 3 key actors from the Philippines, the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP), Philippine Commission on Women (PCW) and Commission on Human Rights (CHR) committed to more gender responsive laws and national action plans on business and human rights. This includes gender mainstreaming in government programs and openness to more dialogues during the WEHRD National Consultation organised by a CSO partner. (g) • In 2023, European MEPs and Philippines policymakers discussed strengthening human rights principles in the Philippines, including trade, business and human rights. FGG and partners co-organised several activities in the Philippines to build a renewed dialogue about the significance of the Binding Treaty, trade and investment and human rights among social movements, civil society organizations, trade unions and public officials. (x) • The G77 chair discussed multistakeholderism as the corporate capture of multilateral governance. FGG and partners are advising the G77 in the preparations for the Summit of the Future (SOTF). • In January, the Division Secretary for Energy and Mineral Resources in Bangladesh discussed a petition signed by 25,720 people urging the Energy Ministry not to sign the ECT on the grounds that it would negatively affect the public interest and the nation's energy sector. FGG provides financial and technical support to a partner in Bangladesh. • The risks of joining ECT were discussed with representatives of two committees of the East African Legislative Assembly (EALA), and the Ugandan and Tanzanian parliaments . FGG supported the partners with their lobby and advocacy towards the representatives as well as financially. Rules for business and corporate conduct, extractives sector • In 2023, the City Councillor of Tariquia in Bolivia put the recommendations of WHRDs to stop fracking in Taqiquia and protect nature and human rights on her agenda. They publicly supported the importance of the topic in the media and committed to addressing the matter in council . FGG conducted the research and organised meetings with the councillor.(g+x) • In 2023, the Dutch political party PvDD put parliamentary questions on the agenda of the Commission Debate about human and women's rights violations under the EU conflict minerals Regulation while implementing the Dutch Minerals Strategy. FGG provided the input for these questions based on exchanges with partners in Uganda, Zambia and DRC on impact of the EU legislation on women and their communities. GroenLinks , during the same debate, asked parliamentary questions on how the Dutch Government is going to ensure human rights are respected in the Dutch Minerals Strategy. (g) • In 2023, the IFC which is a financier of a palm oil company in Guatemala organized several meetings with FGG and partners to discuss and work on a complaint filed by the Pico de Oro community in relation to the violation of the right to free movement by the palm oil company. • In 2023, the Water Development Board Authority in Bangladesh temporarily halted initial construction works of the Super Dyke project, led by the Ministry of Water Development, that threatened to displace more than 700 families. This happened in response to massive demonstrations (in “human chains”) by members and leaders of the affected community, the local union parishad chairman, and political figures. It remains to be seen whether the work will simply resume again at a later stage. FGG supported with an awareness raising campaign done by local community groups. • In 2023, the County Governor of a county in Kenya has threatened not to renew the expired leases for salt firms as their operations have not benefited the locals over the years. FGG’s partner has consistently addressed the various adverse human rights and environmental impacts of the operations of salt firms and supported communities to speak out towards government and the firms. • In 2023, the parliament of Zimbabwe gazetted the Mines and Minerals Bill and public hearings were held in March 2023 by the Parliamentary Portfolio Committee on Mines and Minerals Development, but the Bill has not yet passed into law. FGG and partner have been instrumental in advocating for responsible mining practices and stakeholder inclusion within the mining sector. • In 2023, the Ministry of Mines and Mining development in Zimbabwe formally adopted the enhancing of women’s participation as a priority for 2024 in the policy provisions o a Minerals Development Policy which is under development. FGG and partner highlighted the significance of gender mainstreaming in mining policies to promote inclusivity and empower women in the sector. (g) • In 2023, various media groups in Zimbabwe reported on the Women in Gemstones Association. FGG has supported these women to form an association and provide training on how to establish a legal entity. • In 2023, the European Parliament approved a hearing on the role of the fossil fuel industry in Europe’s response to the energy crisis. FGG initiated a petition calling for the accountability of the fossil fuel industry and an end to their access to decision makers in the context of the energy crisis to the PETI committee of the European Parliament, which led to the commitment of the parliament to these hearings which will take place in February 2024. (g + x) • In 2034, 3 members of the European Parliament from different political parties supported Fossil Free Politics demands. MEPs from 4 political parties signed a call for a conflict of interest policy at EU level. FGG worked closely with the MEPs on the statements demanding the industry is no longer allowed to capture Europe's climate and energy policies for it own interests. • In 2023, the petition ‘end to the fossil fuel industry influence on politics, starting with the immediate removal of their lobbying badges’, which was the result of a collaboration between FGG and We-Move, gathered over 100.000 signatures within less than 3 weeks. • In 2023, different media outlets covered the campaign against the Bolivian government and their intentions to start exploitation of oil and gas wells in the Bolivian Amazon and the National Reserve of Tariquia. FGG supported the partner CSO with their research on the government and the campaign that followed throughout the year. • In 2023, different media outlets covered the campaign against new fossil projects (#Atlanticazo) and against the project to extend an oil pipeline that will have severe consequences on the coasts of the provinces of Rio Negro and Chubut. The anniversary of the movement was covered by media outlets such as La Nación (conservative), Revista Cítrica and ANRed. • In 2023, RSPO in Malaysia endorsed the Conflict Prevention Platform (CPP) as a key instrument to address mounting conflicts faced by RSPO plantation companies. FGG supported CSOs to lobby and free up funding for this topic at RSPO. • In 2023, the Dutch government responded in Dutch Parliament to questions asked and a joint NGO-letter addressing concerns raised by CSOs concerning Malaysian timber entering the Dutch market under the Dutch Timber Procurement policy. FGG supported CSOs with writing the letter, arranging legal assistance and information sharing. • In 2023, different national and local media outlets in Nigeria communicated about illegal logging as a result of lobbying by local FGG partners. They also successfully brought it as a topic of priority concern to the office of the Governor of Cross River State . • In 2023, the Dutch Ambassador of the Philippines visited a fishing community in Cavite, Manila Bay, who have been affected by offshore sand mining by Boskalis for the ADSB-backed New Manila International Airport (NMIA) project. FGG supported the partner with their skills to lobby at the Dutch Embassy. This resulted in a visit from the Ambassador which gives an important signal. • After the kidnapping of two WEHRDs in the Philippines, the Dutch embassy expressed their commitment to use silent diplomacy to support efforts of FGG partners to bring the two activists -kidnapped by the military- back in safety. (x) • In 2023. 2 partners of the Philippines together with FGG held a meeting with ING bank, one of the banks funding the NMIA project . During this meeting the staff present agreed to put pressure on the project owner San Miguel corporation to publicly disclose more information. • In 2023, Global Witness publishes their report ‘Runaway Risk’ on the subject of corporate due diligence in relation to the NMIA case. The report included detailed references to the role of the Dutch state and ADSB in this project. FGG lobby and advocacy resulted in a strong FGG perspective in this report. • In 2023, as a response to the Runaway Risk report, Dutch parliamentarians from the GroenLinks and PvdA parties submitted parliamentary questions requesting -among other things- an independent investigation into the role of the Netherlands in the NMIA case. • In February 2023, following the launch of the Frontlinie documentary on the NMIA case, Pakhuis de Zwijger organised a public debate that was attended by circa 200 people. During this debate the NMIA case was discussed in relation to the need for binding due diligence legislation in the Netherlands. There was also media attention and FGG was invited to discuss the documentary and the need for binding due diligence law in the Netherlands on the national radio. • In 2023, 1 partner in Malawi received access to a permanent round table to monitor, address and prevent incidences of gender based violence. FGG supported the partner in strengthening their network resulting in access to the round table. (g) • In 2023, different media outlets reported on a European CSO’s legal case against its government funding a liquefied natural gas project in Mozambique. FGG supported the CSOs by amplifying key messages about the legal case. • In 2023, different media outlets reported on a European CSO’s legal case against a crude oil pipeline project in Tanzania and Uganda. FGG supported these groups by amplifying key messages about the legal case. • In 2023, government representatives from Latin American and African countries at the WTO discussed the perspectives of the Global South with regards to critical minerals extraction. In 2024, 251 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Bangladesh, Kenya, Mexico, the Netherlands), international and multilateral organizations (EU, UN, World Bank), political parties and media outlets put FGG’s policy and practice recommendations on their agendas. Trade & Investment • In Kenya, Strathmore University, Kenyan National Assembly and the Law Society of Kenya (a leading national collective of lawyers and jurists) hosted a public lecture together with an FGG partner on the topic of the risks and harms of international investment treaties. This happened after FGG had started engaging this actor in various awareness raising and information sharing activities in regards to the Energy Charter Treaty. This is important because so far there is limited knowledge within Kenyan civil society or academia about the risks and harms of current international investment agreements, particularly in relation to investor protection at the detriment of rights and the environment in the host community. • In 2024, the WTO set the agenda on incorporating a development dimension into digital trade and electronic commerce. Additionally, UNCTAD and the UN-CSTD formed a Working Group on Data Governance to tackle equity in data flows and the distribution of data value for development. FGG’s submission advocated for transparent, evidence-based regulatory frameworks for effective competition oversight. • In 2024, the United Nations Summit of the Future examined the implications of digital technologies in the session "Inequalities and Leave No One Behind," where FGG cautioned against techno-determinism. FGG lobbied for inclusive digital innovation through strategic interventions. • In 2024, the South Centre highlighted data governance by inviting FGG to brief diplomats on the Global Digital Compact. FGG lobbied for equitable international data governance practices through capacity-building efforts. • In 2024, the UN SDG Action Campaign focused on the Pact for the Future with a virtual event inviting experts to reflect on its revised draft. FGG advocated for addressing power asymmetries in financial and global governance regimes through capacity-building initiatives. • In 2024, UNESCO set the agenda on contextual AI governance by inviting comments on their consultation paper “Regulatory Approaches for Artificial Intelligence.” FGG’s input reflected its advocacy for a holistic, rights-respecting approach to AI governance that fosters democracy, economic equity, and ecological sustainability. • In 2024, the Secretary-General's Envoy on Technology advanced the agenda on AI’s positive impact by inviting comments on the AI Opportunity Scan. FGG emphasized AI’s transformative potential while cautioning against structural barriers that prevent equitable access for many countries and communities. FGG supported this through knowledge sharing, awareness campaigns, and capacity building. • In 2024, the German Federal Ministry for Digital and Transport prioritized AI regulation with a focus on sustainability by organizing a panel discussion and inviting FGG to address aligning AI with environmental sustainability. FGG advocated for global cooperation to mitigate the extractivist nature of AI and emerging technologies through strategic interventions and capacity building. • In 2024, the OHCHR Committee on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights highlighted digitalization's impact on economic, social, and cultural rights by inviting FGG and its partners to present actionable recommendations. FGG advocated for recognizing the effects of digitalization on labor, indigenous knowledge, and development sovereignty while exploring commons-driven data ownership mechanisms through capacity-building initiatives. • In 2024, UNESCO and WCCES emphasized technology’s role in education by inviting FGG to present findings from the "Technology Integration for Inclusive Education" research project. FGG promoted strategies to include technology meaningfully in classrooms, addressing diverse learning needs, including those of students with mild learning difficulties, through capacity-building activities. • In 2024, the Government of India advanced efforts to bridge the gender digital divide by prioritizing capacity-building measures to enhance women's digital literacy. This aligned with FGG’s advocacy for gender-transformative digital policies addressing root causes of gender inequality. (g) • In 2024, the International Labour Organisation advanced global governance of decent work in the platform economy by releasing a white paper and inviting stakeholder responses to a questionnaire on a decent work agenda. This reflected FGG’s advocacy for algorithmic transparency and social security guarantees for workers. • In 2024, the Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence prioritized diversity and gender equality in global AI governance by inviting FGG to participate in a project titled "Towards Real Diversity and Gender Equality in Artificial Intelligence: Evidence-Based Promising Practices and Recommendations." FGG contributed to this initiative, emphasizing inclusive and equitable emerging technologies with a focus on gender justice. (g) • In 2024, the European Parliament and the Dutch government reached out to FGG for further information on issues concerning the influence of Big Tech companies in the health sector. They sought to discuss advocacy opportunities related to this topic. This engagement was prompted by FGG’s publication of a long read outlining the risks associated with the European Health Data Space (EHDS). An FGG member also led a coalition that issued a joint statement urging EU member states and the European Parliament to include safeguards in the final EHDS draft, addressing the use of patient data and digital health infrastructures. • In 2024, members of the European Parliament reached out to FGG to discuss policy recommendations from a CSO statement addressing concerns about the European Health Data Space proposal.Fair and green systems: agroecology • In 2024, FGG strengthened its strategy to denounce and resist multistakeholderism and corporate capture through advocacy aimed at CSOs and lobbying governments. These efforts raised awareness about the role of the UN Summit of the Future in legitimizing and legalizing multistakeholderism. Several organizations, including FGG, denounced the 2024 UN Civil Society Conference in Support of the Summit of the Future through an open letter, describing the conference as a "Corporate Multistakeholder Strategy in Civil Society Clothing." • In 2024, FGG and its partners jointly developed a proposal on the multilateralism they envision. Subsequently, FGG organized a large encounter titled “Stop Neoliberal Globalization, Corporate Capture & the Far-Right,” which united concerned popular sectors working towards substantive changes across the UN system. (x) • Ministry of Education, Culture, Research and Technology Indonesia, Attended a national workshop on Youth Food Systems Dialogue and movement organised by an academe partner and shared the importance of Indigenous Knowledge to Sustainable food systems, as a counterbalance to the overexploitation of natural resources and destruction of the environment. • The positions of African civil society were discussed during the ministerial meeting held in Morocco in April during FAO regional conference for Africa. Civil society met in February to undertake the necessary consultations to prepare the CSO declaration to be read at the conference. The declaration included recommendations from the African civil society assessment of the UNFSS, supported by FGG members and partners in 2023. (g) • In 2024, one CSO participated in a series of TV shows on NTV Uganda, discussing the need for the establishment of laws and policies around food and agriculture to regulate the sector. Additionally, the CSO took part in three radio talk shows focused on the legal and health implications of the ongoing national food and nutrition policy framework, reaching an estimated audience of 3 million people.Fair and green systems: energy, water, other public goods and services • The Department of Public Health and Engineering (DPHE) in a major coal power plant affected area in Southwest Bangladesh committed to providing water tanks at the beginning of 2025 to solve the water crisis for mega development project affected several dozen landless families affected by the project’s operations. • In 2024, consultants from the World Bank visited an FGG partner in the southwest coastal zone of Bangladesh to assess the potential financing of Tidal River Management (TRM) in the area. This visit involved key informant interviews with local civil society, institutional stakeholders, and communities, who shared their needs and demands for restoring drainage capacity and reviving tidal river basins. The visit followed years of FGG-supported movement building, advocacy, and research on TRM. • In 2024, during the CBA18 conference in Arusha, FGG members collaborated with partners to put the topic of “decolonizing climate finance” on the agenda. Together, they advocated for more accessible climate finance for local CSOs and communities supporting transformative practices. This session attracted significant attention from participants, including bilateral and multilateral financiers, policymakers, and practitioners, and was highlighted as a key topic in the conference report. • In 2024, at the "Waterproof" event organized by the Partners for Water programme of RVO, FGG participated as a main speaker during the plenary talk show to address the Dutch water sector, constructively confronting it with the lived realities of FGG partners and their communities due to non-inclusive approaches. Concrete suggestions were offered to the 150+ attendees on building their work around self-motivated local action and engaging local civil society early in their processes. • In 2024, during the International Conference on Water and Flood Management in Bangladesh, the Netherlands Embassy selected the “Youth Aspiration Paper” by the youth Paani Committee members for a poster presentation in the "Water and Delta Governance in Bangladesh" session. The youth highlighted their vision for locally-led water governance, emphasizing the need for inclusivity and local empowerment. • In 2024, the European Union set the agenda on agriculture and digitalisation by inviting FGG to a roundtable in Telangana. FGG has been lobbying and advocating for digital policies to align with the livelihood realities of women farmers and their producer collectives through knowledge and capacity building. • In 2024, following a petition initiated by FGG and its partners, the European Parliament organized a hearing to examine the role of the fossil fuel industry in Europe's response to the energy crisis. FGG was the initiator of this petition. • In 2024, FGG and its partners urged the EU and member states in five countries to exclude fossil fuel lobbyists from their delegations to the climate COP in November. The EU honoured this request and excluded such lobbyists from its delegation. FGG was the initiator of this demand. • Municipal Trial Court of Kidapawan Facilitated the event organised by a CSO partner on the issue of Charter Change where he challenged the organisations that there is a big moral and social obligations and emphasised that changing the charter is not the solution to the economic, and socio cultural problems of the country that seeing the motives behind Peoples initiatives satisfies the interest to dwell in power for those politicians who want to perpetuate their rule. (x) • In 2024, government ministries from Chile, Mexico, Brazil, and Colombia expressed support for public alternatives to public service delivery. Representatives from progressive administrations in these countries shared contemporary examples of public alternatives to "green structural adjustment" during the Latin America and Caribbean Regional Policy Meeting, held in Bogotá, Colombia, from May 6–9. The event brought together leaders from 23 trade unions, two global union federations, five allied research centres, and progressive government representatives across 14 countries in Latin America and the Caribbean. Participants exchanged experiences and explored strategies to promote a “public pathway” approach to a just energy transition. FGG and partners co-organised the meeting to strengthen policy proposals for the region. (g)

In 2025, FGG aims for 139 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Bangladesh, Kenya, Mexico), international and multilateral organizations (EU, UN, World Bank), political parties and media outlets to put FGG’s policy and practice recommendations on their agendas. FGG’s aim for 2025 is to set agendas on among other things, the following: Trade & Investment • Trade and investment treaties that harm people and the environment, an example is that key actors in Uganda (such as the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development) will discuss the implications of the Energy Charter Treaty. • The ratification of the UN Global Plastic Treaty among governments in Asia Pacific countries. • The necessity to review current Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs).Tenure policies • A Ugandan sugar factory will have a meeting with a community to respond to the allegations of unlawful evictions from their land. • Major gaps in policy and implementation with regard to large infrastructure projects and international standards and frameworks (OECD, KMBF) as a result of the findings of FGG’s dredging report are on the agenda of the Dutch water sector. • The government of West Kalimantan will facilitate dialogues with partners in including customary areas into the regional regulation concerning the 2024 – 2043 West Kalimantan Spatial Plan. Climate and environmental policies • The need for respecting human rights and women’s rights in minerals and metals supply chains, needed for the energy transition, is on the agenda of a Dutch government institution, the Dutch delegation to the COP and the commission for Climate and Green Growth. • The dangers of false solutions, ongoing reliance on fossil fuels and the urgent need to block carbon markets will gain significant media coverage both globally and nationally in the lead-up to COP30. Public financial institutions • Policies aimed at preventing the negative impacts of public finance for mining projects, including for women and marginalised communities are on the agenda of the Dutch government and EU parliament. Rules for business and corporate conduct, cross-sector • The need for a gender-responsive approach in the national transposition law of the CSDDD is on the agenda of political parties. • Policy-makers and businesses are aware of, and take actions to prevent, business practices that must be avoided during the implementation of the CSDDD such as irresponsible disengagement, shifting compliance costs and responsibilities to suppliers, over-reliance on unreliable audits and certifications. • In engagement with policy makers, corporate misconduct (particularly in relation to the OPT), unjust transition policies and related harmful corporate practices, and the role of auditors and certifiers will be on the agenda of meetings in at least 5 cases. Rules for business and corporate conduct, extractives sector • Human rights due diligence in mining will be on the agenda of the Kenyan Ministry of Mining and Department of Justice. • The negative impacts of the fossil industry will be covered by media in Latin America. • The risks of stranded assets being offloaded onto producer countries, and the associated financial, environmental and decommissioning risks, are priorities on the agenda of three oil producing countries and/or regional bodies (Ghana, Nigeria, Colombia).Rules for business and corporate conduct, garment sector • Garment brands are made to engage in a number of Urgent Appeal cases taken up by CCC and its partners, in our attempts to bring remedy to affected workers. This brand engagement includes (depending on the stage of the case) communication with the CCC partner and Urgent Appeal case coordinators, communication with their suppliers, reporting on the facts of the case (or at least their version of those facts), negotiating a course of remedy. • FGG campaign demands, statements, op-eds and research targeted at the garment sector are proactively featured in a number of mainstream (online) media outlets which reach beyond already existing support bases in terms of public outreach.Rules for business and corporate conduct, tech sector • Corporate accountability and digital trade rules as well as safeguarding workers’ rights in the digital economy are on the agenda at government bodies and multilateral fora. • Government bodies in India at national and state level are enhancing progressive platform, data and AI regulation.Fair and green systems: agroecology • The importance to provide support and resources to enhance the capacity of indigenous and local communities in the implementation of agroecological practices is on the agenda in the Philippines. • Stakeholders can engage in dialogue on agroecology through different platforms. Fair and green systems: energy, water, other public goods and services • As result of the Real Utopias awards program, co-coordinated by FGG, examples of national-local level transformation solutions will be on the agenda of the public and the media. • More inclusive financial mechanisms for transformative practices will be discussed by the GEF based on recommendations from Drynet and FGG.
