comment.narrative: In 2021, FGG aims for 42 instances in which key actors adopt and/or implement FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments increase democratic decision-making and protection of human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability in policies and practices affecting trade and value chains. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)

In 2021, in 28 instances key actors adopted and/or implemented FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments increase democratic decision-making and protection of human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability in policies and practices affecting trade and value chains.

In 2022, FGG aims for 26 instances in which key actors adopt and/or implement FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments increase democratic decision-making and protection of human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability in policies and practices affecting trade and value chains. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)

In 2022, in 53 instances key actors adopted and/or implemented FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments increase democratic decision-making and protection of human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability in policies and practices affecting trade and value chains.

In 2023, FGG aims for 6 instances in which key actors adopt and/or implement FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments increase democratic decision-making and protection of human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability in policies and practices affecting trade and value chains. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)

In 2023, FGG contributed to 31 policy and/or practice changes that are aimed at improved government policies in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: • In 2023, during the COP28 the Loss and Damage fund was agreed and adopted. FGG has been continuously campaigning and engaging with the Transnational Committee process, including providing recommendations to the Dutch representative in the committee, especially focused on women and communities being pushed deeper into poverty with every disaster that destroys their homes and flood their crops. (g) • In 2023, the Dutch Government pledged 15 million euros to setting up the Loss and Damage fund which is a result of years of campaigning by FGG and is a significant pledge to climate finance and ODA according to international agreements. • In 2023, local Upazila Nirbahi Officer-UNO (local government representative) of Kolapara has adopted stricter measures to monitor the processing of inheritance certificates. This is important for families displaced by mega projects in Kolapara in relation to their claims about lost land and other property. This happened after advocacy meetings with the local government administrators and other officials, by groups from affected areas and local CSOs supported by FGG. • In 2023, 3 local union parishads in Rampal and Kolapara , provided 80 families with landless certificates and included 15 marginalized women in safety net programmes. These were people from an area impacted by land grab, forced displacement, loss of livelihoods and environmental pollution as a result of the building of a large coal fired power plant. Landless certificates are official documents provided by Bangladesh government actors, highlighting the status of the person in question as landless, and entitles the certificate holder to access government safety net programmes and support services for people living in poverty and without sustainable livelihoods. FGG supported local CSOs to advocate at the Union Parsihad representatives for marginalized communities. • In 2023, the Upazila administration in a village near Khulna in Bangladesh, incorporated 38 landless families displaced by the Rampal Power Plant without proper compensation into a rehabilitation project providing each family with alternative housing and a plot of land. FGG supported the community to advocate with administrators for allocating housing. • In 2023, the president of Uganda reversed an eviction order given earlier by his prime minister, prescribing the forceful eviction of the Apaa group from their ancestral lands. FGG trained the community on peaceful resistance and campaigning tactics which led to the reversion. (x) • In 2023, the local government of a district in Western Uganda started conducting quarterly sensitization meetings with the communities on their rights, conducted radio talk shows to educate the communities on their rights, remedies and referral pathways and stated their intention to organize dialogue meetings between the communities and private investors and to make the district investment committee operational. FGG and partners have documented various human rights abuses and met with the local government to address these and call for an end to impunity for the corporates involved. • In 2023 , the judiciary, ward administrators, local administration and social services in a county in Western Kenya applied an alternative justice system to resolve land disputes of 2 widows who were being dispossessed and reinstatement of land to 1 widow after a meeting organised by FGG with the Nyarongi Paralegals Network as a mediation process among the parties. These were inheritance dispute cases where women’s rights had been violated (disinheriting of widows after their husbands deceased) • In 2023, County governments of 2 counties in Kenya in Southern Kenya registered 2 lands as community lands. FGG has trained the communities and local government representatives on the Community Land Act. • In 2023, the Zimbabwe School of Mines formally introduced a continued Gemmology Course particularly targeting women artisanal miners which happened after a recommendation by FGG and partners in which they introduced courses for the gemstone sector. • In December 2023, at the annual UN Climate Conference (COP28), the Netherlands launched a coalition of 12 countries to phase out fossil fuel subsidies . FGG engaged by putting pressure on the Dutch delegation before and during the COP28 and providing support during ongoing negotiations at the COP28. • In 2023, the Municipal Local Government Unit (MGLU) of Opol, Misamis Oriental in the Philippines, approved the creation of an IP standing committee and its budget which is a result of the lobbying efforts by the Municipal IPMR representing the Dulangan Unified Ancestral Domain in pushing for an IP standing committee. FGG provided capacity development and technical support to the municipal during IPMR and IPs reflection sessions. The IPMR was selected as a Chairperson of this committee and acquired eight other memberships in various committees within the municipality. (x) • In 2023, the Department of education (DepEd) and Sangguniang Bayan Board Member of MLGU Don Carlos in the Philippines issued a declaration of recognizing the Indigenous Peoples school as an extension elementary school in the area. This also led to the approval and support of a Sanggunian Bayan Board Member of the Municipal LGU. The declaration and recognition are a result of the IP community being proactive in submitting resolutions and attending a series of dialogues. FGG supported this community by accompanying them in their organizational strengthening processes. • In 2023, the District Parliament of Maybrat in Indonesia, issued a district regulation recognizing IP rights. The district regulation included indicative maps of four sub tribes which is a result of different workshops, field visits and hearing from the local government where leaders of the indigenous communities have carried out the mapping of their customary territories and submitted a draft regional regulation in 2022. FGG provided capacity development and technical support on the mapping of their territories. (x) • In 2023, the district Parliament of Manokwari in Indonesia issued a district regulation recognizing IP rights of five sub tribes and the list of their clans was approved and legalized , which is a result of facilitating the drafting of regional regulations composed of academic manuscripts for the recognition of Indigenous Peoples rights at the provincial level. FGG provided technical support to the CSO partner. (x) • The Tanzanian government cancelled the Bilateral Investment Treaty with Canada. BE supported local partners to study the BIT agreements and raise awareness in media on its harmful clauses to sustainable development, human rights and the environment. • The Forest Department of a government agency in Asia started implementing forest rights legislation resulting in formal recognition of various community land titles after these communities with the support of FGG successfully lobbied for the recognition of their land tenure titles. • A government agency in Asia, including the ministry of environment -governing coastal zones- adjusted their coastal zone policy after FGG partners continuously lobbied to start protecting these areas. • The National nodal government agency on food security of a country in Asia started implementing a joint collaborative programme on NTFPs allocating staff and resources. A formal MoU was agreed upon and with this a concrete implementation of national governmental policies concerning food security and biodiversity (under UNCBD). FGG provided counsel and fundraising support to ensure our partner was able to cover its part of the co-funding arrangement with the national agency. • The Mayor of the Municipality of Cabo de Santo Agostinho and the President of the legislative Chamber listened to affected communities of the proposal to change the status of a local park area to a commercial use of the Port of Suape. The Public Prosecutor’s Office called a meeting on 13 September to hear the communities’ grievances and proposal for the area. This resulted in the Port of Suape cancelling its plans to privatise the area and there ending in an important victory as a result of the community mobilisation. BE and local partners have engaged with (women) representatives to strengthened their lobby and advocacy capacity and be able to defend their community’s rights. (x) • In 2023, the RSPO adopted a Social Auditing Guidance and started the implementation of an 18 months pilot of the Guidance which will broaden the human rights, workers rights and the rights of female workers in the Palm Oil Sector. FGG and partner CSOs have lobbyed for this throughout the year. (x + g) • In 2023, the Committee on World Food Security - which serves as a forum in the United Nations System for review and follow up on food security policies - included a coordinating role (platform) in its Multi Year Program of Work 2024-2027 to leverage its convening power as the foremost inclusive international and intergovernmental platform to discuss food security and nutrition situation and coordinate collective action at all levels . This is significant in relation to defending civic space, as global food system governance is at risk of corporate capture. This outcome is the result of years of civil society advocacy for the CFS to take a leading role in coordinating global policy responses to the food crisis. Specifically, pressure from the Civil Society and Indigenous Peoples Mechanism (CSIPM) through on-the-ground mobilisation, in the form of two consultation processes in 2020 and 2022 and the “You do politics, We go Hungry” campaign. Since 2019, FGG has been an active member of the CSIPM working group on global food governance and the task team on global policy coordination on food crises. In 2023, FGG supported the work of the task team by contributing to the strategy and drafting documents for submission to governments. (x) • In July 2023, the EU-Indonesian FTA/CEPA did not make progress during negotiations . The last round of negotiations were stalled based on key positions of the Indonesian government. Throughout the year FGG and partners have lobbied the Indonesian and EU negotiators to take into account the concerns and recommendations of Indonesian civil society in the Indonesia-EU CEPA negotiations.

In 2024, FGG aims to contribute to 24 policy changes that are aimed at improved government policies in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: The UN Committee on World Food Security will adopt recommendations on structural reforms, such as including gender justice, to address the food crisis;Adoption by the CBD’s Subsidiary Body on Implementation of some recommendations put forward by FoEI for the development of the Action Plan on Biodiversity Mainstreaming;The Dutch government will adopt recommendations in the renewal of the Dutch Fund for Climate and Development, geared towards improving gender responsiveness;A strong EU CSDDD law is adopted, including strong provisions on liability and access to courts for victims and climate obligations for companies;The Parliament committee on energy demands the Kenyan Ministry of Energy to rescind the interest on ECT as an option for improving energy infrastructure;The government in India continues to opt out of the trade pillar of the final rounds of the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework for Prosperity and protect space for policy sovereignty.

In 2024, FGG contributed to 50 policy and/or practice changes that are aimed at improved government policies in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: • In 2024, the interim government of Bangladesh formed a five-member national committee to review deals made under the 'Quick Enhancement of Electricity and Energy (Special Provisions) Act (QEEES Act)'. This act bypassed public procurement requirements, undermining transparency and accountability, and leading to corruption. FGG has supported partners in their campaign for the repeal of the QEEES Act. (x) • In 2024, the High Court of Bangladesh declared Section 9 of the QEEES Act, which provided immunity provisions, as “illegal and unconstitutional”. Section 9 prevented court challenges, undermined citizens' rights, and shielded corrupt actors. Repealing this act and reviewing past deals are essential steps to restoring integrity in the energy sector. FGG has supported partners in their campaign for the repeal of the QEEES Act. (x) • In 2024, the Bangladesh Water Development Board of Bagerhat allocated a budget for the restoration of five sluice gates at Badokhali Beel to manage water flow and prevent waterlogging, as indicated in their 2025 budget file. Local FGG partners have been working with the local community of Badokhali Beel, its Conservation Committee and local CSOs. We campaigned and advocated. • In 2024, the Khulna City Corporation began cleaning up the Mayur River. This initiative improves waste disposal practices and water flow for Khulna city, which relies on this vital waterway for water resources and drainage. FGG partners supported Khulna Surokkha Moncho in mobilizing local CSOs in Khulna to address issues in the city's master plan concerning waste disposal and river water flow. • In 2024, the Water Development Board (WDB) of Cox’s Bazar provided 150 large geo-bags to prevent embankment erosion. This is a result after advocacy meetings organised by FGG partners which brought together the Cox’s Bazar Water Development board, local CSOs and community leaders. • In 2024, the Department of Youth Development (DYD) in Moheshkhali provided sewing skills training and certificates to 60 landless women affected by the Matarbari Coal Power Plant. These certifications enabled the women to apply for special small business loans with a one-year grace period, empowering them to generate income through tailoring and establish their own businesses. FGG partners held a meeting with the DYD during which this was promised. (g) • In 2024, the Department of Public Health and Engineering (DPHE) provided a deep tubewell to the Dilapara community near the Matarbari Coal Power Plant. This addressed a severe water crisis for 25 families, ensuring essential access to safe drinking and domestic water which is a result of advocacy by FGG partners and a local CSO platform. • In 2024, the Social Welfare Department of Moheshkhali Sub-district included 65 families in government safety net programs, providing 40 fishermen cards, 22 Open Market Sale (OMS) cards, and 3 widow allowance cards. The lists were made public on the government website and is a result of meetings with the Moheskhali Social Development Officer and FGG partners. • In 2024, the County Government of Kilifi invested in clean water provision for domestic use in Marereni by extending the water provision network to households and supplying free water meters to manage consumption. This initiative addressed contamination and compensated the community. • In 2024, Ndhiwa Law Court and the Ministry of Land and Physical Planning (MoLPP) (Kenya) collaborated with an FGG partner to actively resolve women’s land rights issues in Homabay villages, including handling 4 succession cases. (g) • In 2024, the Kenyan Ministry of Lands and Physical Planning and the National Land Commission formally recognised contested lands in 4 villages as community land during adjudication processes and initiated the titling process after years of sustained advocacy efforts by FGG and parters. This is significant as it ensures the community retains access to and control over land critical for their livelihoods. • In 2024, the Kilifi County Government Department of Lands and the Ministry of Lands secured community land certificates through a land adjudication process in Mkono wa Jongoo, Kapupuni, Pumwani, and Mnazi Mmoja villages. FGG and partners have been advocating for registration of community lands over the past years as part of the FGG programme in Kenya. • In 2024, Taasisi ya Madini (the Mining Institute linked to Taita Taveta University, Kenya) trained women and youth artisanal miners on value addition for gemstones in Taita Taveta. This was the institution’s first cohort of women trainees, marking a shift in practice due to engagements with FGG's partner highlighting the need to include women and youth in their programs. (g) • In 2024, FMO, the lead of DFCD, incorporated multiple recommendations from a FGG member’s multi-country DFCD report. These included a paragraph on gender equality and social inclusion in investment evaluations and expanding eligibility for smaller enterprises. This ensures DFCD funding benefits women and marginalised groups (g) • In 2024, the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs adopted FGG’s recommendations, as detailed in a letter dated 29 May 2024, responding to Parliamentary questions. The Minister emphasised intensifying efforts to reach women and marginalised groups in DFCD investments. A new paragraph on gender equality and social inclusion was added to the investment committee’s evaluation format, advancing climate finance benefits for women and marginalised communities. (g) • In 2024, CSW members, negotiation blocks, and alliances adopted policy by including debt and tax in the CSW68 agreed conclusions. This development acknowledged the connection between women’s rights and debt cancellation for the first time in UN texts, opening avenues for gender-responsive public services in the global south. FGG contributed as CSO representative in the Dutch delegation, selected based on expertise on women’s rights, tax and debt. A result of multiple conversations and negotiations with Dutch delegation (OCW, BZ and Permanent Vertegenwoording NL in NY), to stress the importance of the relation between the issues. (g) • In 2024, the Dutch Government formally exited the Energy Charter Treaty (ECT), following an earlier announcement in 2022 and subsequent internal approvals. This decision supports unhampered climate action by removing ECT constraints. FGG has supported the wider civil society calls upon the Dutch government to exit the treaty. • In 2024, Rampal Sub-district authorities added 15 additional families from the recommended 116 in Koigordashkathi village to the rehabilitation project for displaced landless families affected by the Rampal Coal-fired Power Plant. These families received new land and alternative houses to rebuild their lives and livelihoods. FGG contributed through its partners who continued to lobby with authority and enabled families to obtain landless certificated, access government services and participate in rehabilitation. • In 2024, the Federal Court of Pernambuco, Brazil, upheld the decision supporting the full reopening of the Tatuoca River, which had previously been blocked by the construction of a dam by the Port of Suape. The case faced a potential threat when the Port Complex attempted to remove the jurisdiction of the Federal Court from prosecuting it. However, appeals by FS and local communities successfully dismissed this action, allowing the case to proceed. On June 24, 2024, the Federal Court reaffirmed the lower court's decision, ensuring the reopening of the river remains legally valid. (x) • In 2024, a government agency in Asia formally implemented forest rights legislation, resulting in the official recognition of multiple community and forest land titles. This marked a significant step toward securing land tenure for Indigenous Peoples and local communities, reinforcing their rights and role in sustainable forest governance and was a result of lobbying by the local communities and FGG partners. • In 2024, after ongoing lobbying by FGG partners, a government agency in Asia implemented a joint collaborative programme on non-timber forest products (NTFPs), working in partnership with communities. As part of this initiative, the agency allocated dedicated staff and resources, demonstrating institutional commitment to the sustainable use and governance of NTFPs. • In June 2024, the WTO Joint Statement Initiative on E-commerce did not include harmful provisions related to liberalized cross-border data flows and prohibitions on source code disclosures, marking a shift in digital trade policy, particularly for the United States. FGG advocated for this change in the trade regime, focusing on opposing such provisions to promote socially just, inclusive, and environmentally sustainable development through knowledge-sharing, awareness campaigns, and capacity-building initiatives. • In 2024, the Inclusive Green Growth (IGG) department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs included one of FGG’s recommendations—to allocate 88% of total climate finance to initiatives promoting gender equality—in its annual plan for 2025. FGG and its partner published a report and discussed these recommendations during a lunch meeting with IGG civil servants. (g) • In 2024, the Dutch Parliament passed a motion urging the government to prioritize the development of a time-bound phase-out path for fossil fuel subsidies as a central issue in the EU’s position for COP29, and to take action on this within the EU context. FGG provided input for this parliamentary debate. • In July 2024, after extensive negotiations, the EU adopted the CSDDD. While the final proposal was weakened compared to earlier versions from the Commission and European Parliament—particularly in areas such as climate obligations, exclusion of the financial sector, and the value chain—it still incorporated key provisions. These included a due diligence obligation for companies, civil liability provisions enabling victims to bring companies to court, and an obligation for companies to implement climate transition plans. FGG had been campaigning for a robust CSDDD over the past four years. • In 2024, COP16 adopted a new Programme of Work on Article 8(j) and related provisions concerning Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (IPLCs). The decision established a permanent Subsidiary Body on Article 8(j), providing IPLCs with a platform to influence global biodiversity policies and replacing the temporary working group. This achievement marked a significant milestone in recognising IPLCs' contributions to biodiversity conservation. FGG played a pivotal role by advocating for years and preparing written submissions with proposals for the programme’s key elements, objectives, and structure (x). • In 2024, COP16 made strides toward policy coherence between climate and biodiversity, introducing a consultation process under the Rio Conventions (CBD, UNFCCC, UNCCD). Parties, observers, and stakeholders were invited to submit their views by May 2025 to explore enhanced collaboration through a potential joint work programme. FGG actively campaigned for this initiative through civil society statements and an organised event during COP16. (x) • In 2024, COP16 adopted a revised decision on biodiversity mainstreaming after rejecting a flawed action plan criticised for promoting corporate-led false solutions. Years of civil society advocacy led by FGG and partners contributed to this outcome. FGG drew attention to the issue with an open letter to all country focal points during COP16, published on the CBD Alliance website. While the harmful proposals were removed, the decision still fell short of fully integrating biodiversity across economic sectors as originally intended (x). • In 2024, the EU and the Dutch government formally initiated the process of withdrawal from the Energy Charter Treaty (ECT). This significant step was the result of years of advocacy, research, and movement building by FGG members. • In 2024, the OECD included OECD Watch’s recommendations in three guidance documents for National Contact Points (NCPs) on complaint handling. These improvements followed detailed submissions from OECD Watch, which is ran by FGG, advocating for changes to the guidance documents. • In 2024, seven governments—Argentina, Hungary, Iceland, Luxembourg, Peru, Poland, and the United States—established new NCP stakeholder advisory bodies. This progress aligns with OECD Watch's long-standing advocacy for creating multistakeholder advisory bodies, which was bolstered by the 2024 (re)Evaluation of NCPs. • In 2024, the NCIP En Banc Committee in the Philippines issued a Certificate of Recognition to a domain-wide Indigenous Peoples (IP) community for their Certificate of Ancestral Domain Title (CADT) application, marking a significant milestone in their ancestral domain claim. FGG had previously supported the community in 2021 by providing organisational strengthening and mobilisation assistance, leading to their lobbying efforts for this recognition. (x) • In 2024, the NCIP Regional Office in the Philippines awarded a Certificate of Recognition to an Indigenous community for their ancestral domain claim. This recognition is crucial for securing evidence of ownership, particularly amidst competing claims by private entities seeking to use the land for tourism development. FGG provided technical assistance during the CADT application process and grants for formulating the Ancestral Domain Sustainable Development and Protection Plan (ADSDPP). (x) • In 2024, the Legislative Body of the Province of Bukidnon in the Philippines approved the Bukidnon Indigenous Peoples Code. FGG supported the Provincial IPMR during the development of an Indigenous Peoples Agenda, engaging community leaders through workshops to gather their perspectives. (x) • In 2024, the Municipal LGU of Kadingilan, Bukidnon, allocated an annual budget to include Semayaan- a yearly cultural practice and tradition of the Menuvu Kirinteken Ilentungen community in their Municipal Development Plan. The BLGU also adopted an ordinance recognising sacred sites, protecting water systems, and promoting community traditions such as the yearly Semayaan cultural practice of the Menuvu - Kirinteken Ilentungen community. This progress resulted from advocacy by FGG and the IPMR for ordinances safeguarding cultural practices and local policies. • In 2024, the Sangguniang Bayan or Legislative Body of Don Carlos, Bukidnon in the Philippines approved a resolution adopting the NCIP National Advisory to ensure Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) for Indigenous Cultural Communities, as mandated by the Indigenous Peoples Rights Act (IPRA). FGG provided legal support and capacity-building assistance to the Municipal IPMR, who collaborated with a legal advocacy organisation to craft this resolution. (x) • In 2024, Indonesia’s Social Forestry Program was reaffirmed under the new administration for the 2024–2029 term. The program aims to cover 15 million hectares, with a dedicated task force to accelerate the recognition of Indigenous Peoples’ forests. The task force will streamline verification procedures for the five million hectares of IP forests allocated by the previous administration. (x) • The newly elected Indonesian Government integrated Agrarian Reform, including Social Forestry, into its long-term plans spanning 2025 to 2045. They established a multistakeholder task force to expedite the Agrarian Reform Program, fostering sustainable development and Indigenous forest management. • In 2024, Kenya and the Netherlands did not renew their Bilateral Investment Treaty (BIT). Although the BIT was set for automatic renewal, the Kenyan government informed the Netherlands of their decision not to proceed. Kenya follows Uganda, which terminated its BIT with the Netherlands in 2017. This decision is significant as it paves the way for exploring alternative BIT models, a concept previously explored by the Dutch government in 2019. FGG and partners contributed to this outcome by producing a report in May 2023 on 60 years of Dutch BITs. • In April 2024, 65% of Ecuadorian rejected an attempt to overturn Ecuador’s 2008 constitutional ban on international arbitration for investment disputes through a referendum. FGG contributed to this outcome by publishing a report on ISDS in Ecuador in March, mobilising funds for communications work, organising a public forum, hosting radio and online streaming interventions, developing a global declaration signed by over 100 organisations worldwide. • In April 2024, the European Parliament voted overwhelmingly in favour of the European Commission’s proposal for the EU and Euratom to exit the Energy Charter Treaty (ECT). This follows the European Parliament’s November 2022 resolution urging the EU’s withdrawal, an outcome of sustained campaigning by FGG and partners. • In 2024, the UK announced its decision to exit the ECT, becoming the first non-EU country to do so. Portugal also made a unilateral decision to exit the ECT, while the Spanish Congress voted for an official withdrawal. These developments strengthen the position of ECT expansion countries to withdraw or refuse to sign on. • In 2024, President Xiomara Castro announced Honduras will withdraw from the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID). FGG and partners have provided technical support to the CSO movement in Honduras and the government, drafting a declaration of support, which was presented to the Vice Chancellor for Foreign Policy.

In 2025, FGG aims to contribute to 18 policy changes that are aimed at improved government policies in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: • The Deputy from the SEMILLA party in Guatemala implements a methodology by structurally organising dialogue between national institutions and communities, affected by the expansion of palm oil in their territory. • The Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) implements FGG’s recommendations by opposing international agreements such as the Energy Charter Treaty, that undermine state sovereignty and protect corporate interests over public welfare in the energy sector. • The IPED framework (the trade pillar of which India continues to opt out of), bilateral FTA negotiations and the WTO implement fair e-commerce rules that support workers and small enterprises in countries in the Global South as well as just taxation of transnational tech corporations.

description.narrative: governments increasing democratic decision-making
# key actors who support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations

comment.narrative: In 2021, FGG aims for 74 key actors to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments increase democratic decision-making and protection of human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability in policies and practices affecting trade and value chains. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)

In 2021, 57 key actors supported and/or promoted FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments increase democratic decision-making and protection of human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability in policies and practices affecting trade and value chains.

In 2022, FGG aims for 60 key actors to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments increase democratic decision-making and protection of human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability in policies and practices affecting trade and value chains. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)

In 2022, 32 key actors supported and/or promoted FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments increase democratic decision-making and protection of human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability in policies and practices affecting trade and value chains.

In 2023, FGG aims for 60 key actors to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments increase democratic decision-making and protection of human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability in policies and practices affecting trade and value chains. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)

In 2023, 62 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Bangladesh, Brazil, Colombia, Mexico, Thailand), international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations supported and/or promoted FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved government policies (result area C). • In 2023, the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs -along with other European member states- expressed its concerns to the Bangladesh government regarding safety in the textile sector and condemned the violence through public statements. FGG, together with Mondiaal FNV sent a letter to the Ministry to address the critical situation in Bangladesh around the minimum wage struggle requesting to issue a statement directed to the government of Bangladesh. • UNCTAD’s 2023 issue Paper on Data for Development emphasises the neo-colonial dynamics of the data economy, its infrastructural and access challenges and the green transition. FGG contributed to this paper by preparing inputs that fed into this document. • In 2023, the Director of Department of Climate Change and Meteorological Services assured affected youth/women/communities to better provide information on disaster preparedness and drafted an action plan in response to the petition which was presented in a meeting with FGG and partners. The plan meets most of FGG’s recommendations, such as being inclusive to youth and women.(g) • In 2023, 3 Dutch political parties (PvdD, GL/PvdA, D66) included the Loss and Damage fund in their party programmes In the run up to the 2023 national elections which is a result for continued campaigning for a Loss and Damage Fund by FGG and partners. • In 2023, the DFCD consortium and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs actively engaged in a roundtable discussion about the findings of FGG’s research on how to ensure women and marginalized groups benefit from climate finance. The consortium provided valuable feedback to the report while indicating to make use of several recommendations in the second phase of DFCD. (x) • In 2023, the Dutch government published a letter confirming the importance of accountability and protection of civic space in the UNFCCC process. This was a response to the letter written by FGG and other NGOs on the COP28 presidency and the need to counter shrinking civic space in the UNFCCC. (x) • In 2023, the UN General Assembly voted unanimously to adopt Vanuatu’s resolution for an Advisory Opinion by the International Court of Justice regarding countries’ responsibilities to climate change and human rights. FGG has supported the World’s Youth for Climate Justice campaign. • In 2023 ,the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) in Bangladesh , provided 59 female members of Community Land Rights Groups with livelihood support and 20 youth female members of CLRG with training. These communities were affected by large scale infrastructure development projects and have been advocating for support at the IOM. (g) • In 2023, the Ugandan parliament voted for the adoption of the Land Amendment Bill that included recommendations from FGG as part of the Land Actors platform focusing on better management for the land tenure record systems to address the rampart illegal evictions related to large scale corporate investments. The next step needed before enactment of the law is for the president to formally assent to the amendment . • In 2023, the local government of a county in Southern Kenya supported the setting up of the first country wide Widows Association to enable widows to defend their rights. The association will facilitate the widows coming together, organize awareness raising sessions on rights to land and inheritance. This is important as in the Kenyan context, widows are a group often marginalized: as a result of patriarchal culture, they often face disinheritance and even expulsion from their homes . FGG and partners in Uganda campaigned over the past years for women’s land rights including the rights of widows. (g) • In 2023, a county government in Western Kenya formed a taskforce to resolve the Yala Swamp land grab case, by organizing public hearings with community members, state agencies (Kenya Wildlife Service, Kenya Forestry Services, Kenya Fisheries, Ministry of Land, National Land Commission) and CSOs which was a result of FGG’s support to engagement between the community leaders and the government. (x) • In 2023, the Ministry of land and physical planning and the judiciary in Kenya agreed to develop a joint workplan with FGG’s partner to set up a special widows’ court and awarded them with 2 slots in the environment and land court as court users committee which followed from a request by FGG partner for a meeting with state agencies on progress being made on women’s land rights. (g+x) • In 2023, a branch of the law society of Kenya ordered every lawyer in the county to take and support 2 cases of succession (specifically in relation to inheritance rights for women) per year. This happened during the launch of the Widows movement on Women’s day following years of campaigns supported by FGG. (g +x ) • In 2023, the County Executive Committee member in charge of land, the judiciary and the Ministry of Land and Physical Planning developed a joint work plan with FGG on awareness raising and sensitization for specific communities on the Community Land Act. FGG and partners advocated for sensitization on the Community Land Act during various campaigns and advocacy meetings. • In 2023, the Ministry of Mines and Mining Development in Zimbabwe established a roadmap and a database for supporting women’s participation in mining which was a proposal made by FGG together with a partner CSO. The roadmap and database were proposed by FGG in order to support the government in reaching women small scale and artisanal miners for government awareness raising and support programmes (g) • In 2023, The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and t he Ministry of Education, Culture and Science accepted AA as the NGO representative at the CSW68 in the official Dutch government delegation to represent Dutch Civil society and promote better gendered tax and debt policies at UN member states. Which was the result of a selection process coordinated by Atria and WO=MEN who asked AA for the role. (g) • In 2023, the UN member states agreed through voting to develop a UN tax convention after the OECD and NL voted in favour for this in 2022. This is a step towards more democratic decision making on international tax legislation and an alternative to the OECD BEPS process. FGG lobbied for several years and has supported activities of Eurodad who is leading the fight for a global tax body. • The upazila level administrator of Kalapara in Bangladesh included a community affected by a naval base construction project in the list of communities eligible for rehabilitation. FGG supported the community with joint strategising and networking. • In 2023, MPs of ruling parties, special envoy of climate change and the environment to the Prime Minister, Bangladesh Parliamentarians' Caucus on Migration and Development) promoted the inclusion of migrant workers’ rights in the UN Legally Binding Instrument on Transnational Corporations and Human Rights (UNLBI) at the Regional Consultation on the UNLBI at Jakarta and at Regional Climate Summit 2023 at Dhaka. The special envoy on climate change and environment to the Prime Minister also advocated for taking migrant workers’ rights into account in relation to the global climate crisis at the COP28. migrant workers’ rights, UN binding treaty on business and human rights. Migrant workers’ rights in relation to the global climate crisis. AA had advocated for addressing migrant workers’ rights in relation to the global climate crisis during policy advocacy meetings • In 2023, the Ministry of Gender, labour and social development in Uganda incorporated FGG and partners’ recommendations on strengthening Social Protection Mechanisms, strengthening Coordination Frameworks, Free, Prior and Informed Consent, enhancing corporate social responsibility and accountability, and preservation of commons into the draft Social Impact Assessment (SIA) bill. The SIA Bill will be an important new law to hold corporations accountable for adverse social and human rights impacts of their operations. The drafting of the bill is still ongoing.. (x) • In 2023, the Inter American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) informed the Guatemalan government about communities official complaints on HR and WR violations related to a mining case based on a 2022 report by the HR ombudsman and asks them to respond to the allegations presented. FGG and partners lobbied towards the Ombudsman and invited them for a visit to the communities and filed an official complaint at IACHR. (g + x) • In 2023, the Parliamentary Standing Committee of the Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resources of Bangladesh formed a dedicated sub-committee for renewable energy (RE) expansion to achieve energy prosperity by 2041. This happened after the high-level international conference in Bangladesh on energy “Bangladesh Energy Prosperity 2050” that was jointly organized by FGG, partners, and the GoB. The conference was a culmination of sustained advocacy and campaigning by FGG and partners to promote a shift to renewable energy in Bangladesh, since 2021. • In 2023, the Director of Mines in Kenya awarded 4 concession mining areas to women and young artisanal miners as a result of the negotiations led by an FGG partner with the artisanal miners and the mining department. (g) • In 2023, local Upazila formally committed to building 2 training centres in Matarbari and setting up 01 entrepreneur centre for women’s economic empowerment. The communities, with the support of FGG, have advocated for the need for such centres as part of their campaigns to address the marginalization of the communities in the area. (g) • In 2023, the Policy and Operations Evaluation Department (IOB) adopted FGG’s recommendations in their evaluation report towards the Dutch government to improve the policy coherence and focus in Dutch international policies. In the IOB report FGG member ActionAid is recognized as an organization that utilizes the policy coherence process to bring about change. IOB interviewed FGG member AA twice on Tax Justice and on the application of a feminist lens on policy coherence. (g) • In 2023, the governor of a county in coastal Kenya held preparatory meetings with an FGG partner to jointly develop an Ocean Water Policy in 2024 together, which is a result of direct lobby talks the partner held with the governor about the need to develop such a policy. in order to regulate the extraction of salt from the ocean • In July 2023, the European Commission launched a proposal for a coordinated withdrawal of the EU and all EU Members States from the ECT . The Commission argued that it was not in line with EU policies and regulations on climate and investment issues. This proposal is in line with what FGG and our partner CSOs have been campaigning for since 2019 and marks the first time in history that the Commission prioritizes climate issues over commercial issues in a trade agreement. • In February 2023, a section of the Dutch House of Representatives (Lower House) tabled a motion calling on the country’s government to block the EU/Mercosur trade agreement as long as it includes the agricultural sector. Parliamentarians fear unfair competition from outside for Dutch farmers and believe that the negotiated agreement will lead to further deforestation in the Amazon, despite the pledges of the new Brazilian President. FGG is campaigning against the EU/Mercosur agreement since 2020. • In June 2023, French MPs have opposed the EU Mercosur trade agreement, in an adopted resolution . The French National Assembly is asking its government to inform the European Commission and the EU Council of France’s opposition to the agreement “in the absence of access to the European market conditional on compliance with European production standards and sustainability and traceability.” FGG has been campaigning against the EU/Mercosur agreement since 20202. • In 2023 the EU-Mercosur trade deal was stalled thanks to key European and Latin American governments who refused to sign the deal in its current form. The early 2023 by the EU Commission launched an additional declaration/statement to the EU-Mercosur trade agreement, that was supposed to address the environmental, climate concerns of EU member states and the European Parliament, was rejected both by Mercosur countries and critical countries in the EU (France, Belgium, Austria) FGG partners in Europe and in the Mercosur countries published an academic briefing, organised a speakers tour to Brussels and a conference with media and decision makers with 20 representatives from Mercosur countries. • The NCIP National Office in the Philippines invited community leaders to discuss issues related to tenure, CADT processes and illegal private sector activities . The NCIP also provided a certified true copy of the delineation map to the leaders. FGG supported these community leaders to have their voices heard and lobby for their tenure rights. (x) • The Department of Public Works and Highways National Office in the Philippines issued a memorandum to its Provincial and Regional Offices for validating the FPIC violations in the identified areas and were given a 15-day deadline to validate said FPIC issues. FGG partner lobbies specifically on government projects that did not undergo an FPIC process and this result is important as it reflects the various concerns raised by their communities in recent years. • In 2023, the Regional Director of DENR Region 10 in the Philippines sent out a letter to the regional Director of the Department of Health in reference to the complaint filed by the Sezukadang community regarding the aerial spraying which has resulted in health issues among the neighbouring communities. This is in relation to the communities ongoing struggle against a banana plantation company which operates in their domain without proper FPIC. • In 2023, during a parliamentary debate the Minister of agriculture, nature and food quality emphasized/confirming the need to take the international impact on farmers and food security in the global South into account when developing the Dutch oriented agricultural policy. This was reconfirmed in a separate meeting with a delegation of the manifesto. Recommendations and narrative in the manifesto – which was signed by more than 70 Dutch and international civil society organisations, agricultural organisations and companies, environmental organisations and scientist. The manifesto included the role of women farmers and how to change gendered power relations (g). • In 2023, the Netherlands Food Partnership organised a special meeting with their network where FGG could present the manifesto ‘The Dutch Agriculture Agreement reaches further than the Netherlands: offer prospects for sustainable farmers and consumers worldwide’, and have a discussion with their network. During the meeting the NFP emphasized the importance of the manifesto. • The Dutch political party CDA co-proposed a parliamentary motion on mapping where Dutch food exports interfere with food production and associated local market forces of small scale farmers in third counties. Omtzigt voted in favour of the motion. For both Omtzigt and CDA they supported these kinds of motions for the first time. It builds upon the parliamentary debate earlier that year in which CDA for the first time put forward the argument that trade should work for farmers worldwide (in line with the message of the manifesto). This did not occur before. • The Dutch political parties CDA and NSC participated in the FGG Election Debate ‘Nederland in de wereld’ herewith acknowledging their engagement on the topic and emphasizing in their contributions that trade should be of more benefit for people in the global South. This is a new line of thinking for CDA and for NSC as a new political party. FGG co-organised the election debate, trade and climate were discussed. • During the UNCCD conference the EU delegation ensured that the omission of a key recommendation made by FGG partners from Drynet- to stop public support to land degrading agriculture, infrastructure, extractives and mining- was corrected and added to the final report. The partners of the Drynet network noted that the recommendation was not added but only the EU delegation could speak during the conference session and it showed their willingness to include recommendations of Civil Society. • EU members requested input directly from FGG and Drynet on agenda items on papers for the UNCCD (land tenure and gender), in preparation for the EU position statement. Which was then shared in the EU group (a working party in international environmental issues) prior to the meeting. They included many FGG recommendations on land tenure, land degradation neutrality, gender, and CSO involvement in decision making into their position statements. (g + x) • In 2023, the final review of the RSPO Standard was postponed for adjustment in order to address unresolved matters regarding FPIC and labour (decent living wage). Partners, with counsel and advocacy support from BE, have specifically lobbied towards RSPO members to honour FPIC and workers rights, specifically focused on gender in the palm oil production sector. (g) • In 2023, results from consultations with CSOs were incorporated in the RSPO Complaints and Appeal Procedure. FGG together with partners have been lobbying for the CSOs to be included in the process of drafting the procedure over the passed years. (x) • In 2023, RSPO formulated a plan for implementation and allocation of a 5 million USD to roll out a 2nd phase RSPO outreach to Intermediary organisations. BE and CSOs designed the plan and lobbied for approval of the budget by the RSPO board. • During the UN water conference in March 2023, the Colombian Ministry of Environment co-hosted a session with 3 FGG partners on the transformative water pact (TWP). During this session a spokesperson from the ministry expressed their support for the TWP. Afterwards a press release on the website of the Ministry was posted confirming this support. • In 2023, the G77 agreed to push for the removal of the contentious term ‘multistakeholderism’ from the zero draft of Pact for the Future to be prepared by the co-facilitators of the Summit for the Future (Namibia and Germany). Multistakeholderism is a threat to multilateral governance impacting negatively on the participation and interests of developing countries and civil society. FGG partners, with allies, took part in advocacy to raise awareness on the concerns regarding multistakeholderism. [x] • In March, Colombian policymakers discussed establishing an audit commission on Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs) and ISDS clauses, and more than 50 representatives of congress signed onto a declaration highlighting their support for Colombia’s withdrawal from ISDS and a renegotiation of treaties. FGG worked with Colombian CSOs, trade unions and social movements to push for an audit commission on BITs and ISDS to be established by the Colombian government. • In May, the Colombian Minister of Trade announced that Colombia was going to renegotiate their trade agreements, following numerous advocacy meetings with different ministries to highlight the impact of ISDS in Latin America. Renegotiate BITs and FTAs including opposition to ISDS. FGG members and partners organized an international mission to Colombia to meet with different government ministries, civil society organizations and communities on the issue of trade and investment policies and ISDS, including the Ministry of Trade.

In 2024, FGG aims for 56 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Brazil, Mexico, Thailand), international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved government policies (result area C). FGG’s aim for 2024 is to improve government policies on among other things, the following: EU member states continue to raise concerns about the EU Mercosur free trade agreement;Support from national governments in Asia for an ambitious global plastic treaty that seeks to reduce plastic production, consumption and trade; Support from national actors in Bangladesh, such as the Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resource, the Standing Committee of MoPEMR, Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC), Sustainable and Renewable Energy Development Authority (SREDA), to address, promote and discuss the recommendations from the CSO-proposed National Energy Transition Pllicy (NETP), a document developed by Bangladeshi civil society to inspire policy change;Indonesia, Mexico, Thailand and/or India, which currently negotiate a free trade agreement with the EU, will resist including UPOV19 obligations in the agreement;At least two national governments support CSO demands on sufficient policy space for governments to regulate in support of sustainable development, e.g. on agriculture and e-commerce, during the WTO negotiations.

In 2024, 63 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Brazil, Mexico, Thailand), international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations supported and/or promoted FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved government policies (result area C). • In 2024, the Bangladesh government published a revised version of the CSO-proposed National Energy Transition Policy (NETP). The revised policy was requested by the energy advisor and includes CSOs’ proposals for public participation, transparency, accountability, and good governance in the energy sector, addressing current deficiencies. FGG and partner CSOs led the revision process through consultations with CSOs and the energy sector. (x) • In 2024, the District Commissioner of Cox’s Bazar ordered CPGCBL (Coal Power Generation Company Bangladesh Limited) to select land for the long-delayed technical institute for the Moheshkhali community and submit a progress report. FGG and partners advocated and raised the issue through local CSOs and community leaders. The local authority reopened the file and informed the District Commissioner. FGG advocated and raised the issue through local CSOs and community leaders. • In 2024, the Payra Port Authority in Bangladesh halted the displacement of 136 families and secured a verbal commitment on relocation from government authorities. These families have secured government-owned lands for resettlement and will receive compensation to rebuild their homes. FGG and partners undertook strategic media mobilization and actively engaged the community with sub-district administrators. • In 2024, the Trade and Investment Committee of the National Assembly in Kenya decided to undertake an analysis of all Kenya’s existing international investment agreements and requested FGG partners to build their capacity on the subject. This analysis is critical for raising awareness of the harmful aspects of Kenya’s current international investment agreements. This is a result of a conference organised by FGG partners in collaboration with the Law Society of Kenya. • In 2024, the National Land Commission in Kenya adjusted its process for communities submitting claims to community land that had been grabbed, scrapping submission deadlines. Community members can now submit claims to community land at any time. This is a result of a conference on Historical Land Injustices, organized by FGG partner and the Non State Actors on Land (a platform of Kenyan CSOs working on land rights). • In 2024, the Taita Taveta County Government formally registered 6 Community Land Management Committees (CLMCs). CLMCs, provided for by the Community Land Act 2016, empower community members to manage community land independently and protect it from land grabbing. FGG supported the partner who advocated for the CLMCs over the past years. • In 2024, the delegation of Finland at the CSW and the Women’s Rights Caucus supported recommendations on gender responsiveness in the CSW68 draft agreed conclusions, particularly regarding gender-responsive public services to improve the position of women and girls worldwide. FGG actively lobbied prior and during the CSW as part of the Dutch Gender Platform. (g) • In 2024, the Dutch delegation at the COP supported FGG’s call to embed gender equality in the New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) for Climate Finance. The delegation expressed commitment to pushing these recommendations in the NCQG negotiations. However, gender language was not included in the final COP negotiations text. The delegation asked FGG and a few other allied organisations working on gender just climate policies for input and textual suggestions to strengthen gender equality in the NCQG text. This was a result of continued collaborative engagement with the delegation, including a specific conversation about gender during the Bonn climate negotiations.(g) • In 2024, the EU Commission demonstrated support for FGG’s recommendations on Gender Action Plan III during regular meetings and exchanges. They evaluated their implementation of GAPIII in external policies and programmes over the past years. FGG has been part of the Gender Equality Group of Concord. • In 2024, the Mutoko Rural District Council in Zimbabwe supported an FGG partner in conducting three trainings: 1) Capacity of communities and stakeholders on the National Action Plan on Business and Human Rights (BHR) and African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), 2) Capacity of newly elected councillors on NRM laws, and 3) Multi-stakeholder engagement with companies to adopt grievance mechanisms. These efforts highlight the importance of government-supported platforms to increase human and environmental rights protections. (x) • In 2024, a Rural District Council in Zimbabwe supported an FGG partner in conducting trainings to capacitate women, communities, and stakeholders on the National Action Plan on BHR and AfCFTA. (x) • In 2024, the Water Development Board (WDB) of Cox's Bazar (Bangladesh) committed to request budget allocation for a permanent embankment from the Ministry of Water Resources (MoWR). This commitment demonstrates support for recommendations made by an FGG partner. • In 2024, the Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB) of an area in southern Bangladesh committed to building an embankment at Londa village near the Tiakhali River to protect 250 families from tidal flooding. They issued a letter to higher authorities requesting and demanding a budget for the project. The community, with support of FGG and partners had lobbied with government officials on this matter. • In 2024, the Upazila (sub-district) administrator of a coal-fired power plant-affected area in south-west Bangladesh verbally committed to providing housing to 79 families in the second phase of a rehabilitation project for landless and power plant-affected households. In the first phase of this project in 2024, 38 families received housing and land. Since 2017 FGG and partner have been directly advocating with sub-district authorities of the area for the well-being and compensation of families for their loss of homes and livelihoods. • In 2024, the Upazila (sub-district) administrator of a coal-fired power plant-affected area in south-east Bangladesh verbally committed to rebuilding a destroyed road and pledged to forward the community’s funding request for a cyclone centre to the Ministry. The community lives in a government rehabilitation project for people displaced by a major coal power plant project. • In 2024, the sub-district and district authorities of a coal-fired power plant-affected area in south-east Bangladesh committed to dredging a river in the area, with the government allocating a budget for the project. This dredging aims to improve water flow and protect the river’s biodiversity. The river was previously a direct source of livelihood for over 1,000 fishing families but has filled with sediment due to the coal power plant's construction and adjacent road, severely impacting the local fishing community. FGG has supported partners who have been campaigning for the dredging of the river. • the Indonesian court Pending a case brought by FGG partners, the state court of East Kalimantan ruled that Indonesian Ministry of Public Works and Housing was legally required to publicly disclose the social and environmental impacts assessments of the Sepaku Dam, which is part of the New Capital City development. • In 2024, the appointment of a CSO members, Secretary as the Gender Coordinator for Bomi County marked a significant elevation of women’s roles in governance. The achievement is being celebrated by women in the region, although they continue to strive for greater representation of women in national leadership positions. (g) • In 2024, UNCTAD supported proposals addressing inequalities in the digital economy between the North and the South, the capture of global data and digital value chains, and the need for global data governance. This support emerged during an experts meeting on inclusive digital economies. FGG had actively lobbied for these proposals through inputs at critical strategy meetings, as well as knowledge-sharing and capacity-building activities. • In spring 2024, the European Parliament agreed on a position for the EU to leave the Energy Charter Treaty (ECT). In summer 2024, the Council also approved a proposal from the European Commission to leave the ECT. This marked a major policy outcome on trade issues, as it led the EU, along with Poland, Lithuania, Slovenia, Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Ireland, France, Spain, and Portugal, to announce their decision to withdraw from the ECT. These decisions were largely driven by CSO pressure, with FGG as the initiator of the ECT campaign and a core member of the coalition for the past four years. • In December 2024, the EU and Mercosur countries finalised a trade agreement, but several member states, including France, Poland, Lithuania, Ireland, the Netherlands, and Belgium (or their parliaments), announced their intention not to support the deal. France pledged to form a blocking minority. Concerns were raised over unfair competition for farmers and the likelihood of continued deforestation in the Amazon despite pledges from Brazil's new president. FGG has campaigned against the EU-Mercosur deal since 2020. • In 2024, the Human Rights Commission of Tariquia and the National Ombudsman denounced attacks on human rights defenders by YPFB and called on the national government to provide adequate protection for these individuals. FGG provided financial and strategic support to its partner advocating for this protection. (x) • In 2024, the Bishop of Cachoeiro de Itapemirim publicly opposed the construction of Porto Central, providing significant support to the resistance against the port due to his wide reach as a public figure. This opposition resulted in a petition against the port signed by over 25,000 people, which was formally presented to Governor Renato Casagrande during an event in Vitória. FGG provided financial and strategic support to the CSO leading the campaign “Nem um poco a mais.” Additionally, two State Delegates and one Councillor voiced their public support for the campaign. • In 2024, Congress member Esmeralda Hernández proposed a new law to prohibit fracking and exploration of unconventional areas, including offshore oil and gas fields. Members of Commission V in the Colombian House of Representatives referred to arguments from FGG’s partner during discussions on draft law 328/24c, which designates gas as a transition energy. The Ministry of Mining and Energy incorporated two documents prepared by the partner into its roadmap for a just energy transition, with implementation pending by the end of the year. FGG provided financial and strategic support to its partner lobbying on this issue. • In 2024, several members of the Commission for the Environment in Honduras adopted a stance promoting the phasing out of fossil fuels. FGG provided financial and strategic support to the partners lobbying for this shift. • In 2024, members of the Dutch Parliament asked the Minister during a parliamentary debate to take tangible steps toward phasing out fossil fuel subsidies. FGG contributed input for this debate. • In 2024, two members of Dutch Parliament proposed a motion urging the government to develop a concrete path to phase out fossil fuel subsidies in collaboration with international partners within the International Coalition to Phase Out Fossil Subsidies (COFFIS) before COP30 (2025). Though the motion was not accepted, FGG provided strategic and technical input and initiated lobbying meetings with parliamentarians. • In 2024, over 400 key actors, including numerous civil society organizations and around 60 companies in the Netherlands, backed FGG’s call for large polluting companies to halve their CO2 emissions by 2030 at the latest. This statement emphasized the importance of this step in maintaining the goals of the Paris Climate Agreement. FGG initiated the action by mobilizing support from companies and CSOs. • In 2024, contributions were made to the latest Cambodian Land Law draft, ensuring two rounds of recommendations were finalised and changes urged by IPs were incorporated. These efforts marked a significant shift toward greater visibility for Indigenous land rights and strengthened collaboration between IPs and government officials. FGG supported the CSO who led the consultations to gather Indigenous peoples’ input on the new land law draft.(x) • In 2024, the Municipal IPMR was appointed to chair two committees at the local government unit: the Indigenous Peoples Committee and the Environmental Protection, Technology, and Urban Planning Committee. This appointment highlights the increasing role of Indigenous leadership in governance and decision-making processes. FGG has supported the IPMR increasing knowledge on his role in the legislative council. • In 2024, a resolution was issued to support an initiative proposed by a youth-led Indigenous Peoples Organisation (IPO) partner. This initiative focuses on establishing a community-based museum dedicated to preserving and showcasing the rich cultural heritage and traditions of their community in a specific municipality. FGG supported the community through small grants during their community visit when they tried to re-organise their community-based youth organisations. • In 2024, the Ministry of Environment and Rural Development in Cambodia set an agenda by inviting two communities three times to share their experiences in land and forest management. They awarded one community with an award of excellence for its active efforts in forest protection, fishery management, and community mobilisation. Additionally, key actors requested the CSO partner to assist with the land registration process for six Indigenous communities. (x) • During the 13th WTO ministerial conference in February, 5 additional countries (Namibia, Swaziland, Egypt, Pakistan and Brazil) alongside India, Indonesia and South Africa expressed their opposition to renewing the WTO e-commerce moratorium. The WTO e-commerce moratorium is a global commitment to continue the current practice of not applying customs duties (i.e. tariffs) on electronic transmissions. What is determined as electronic transmissions has not been clearly defined. In the age of digitalization, the moratorium has allowed for the monopolization of global tech firms, while also limiting the generation of potential customs revenue from electronic transmissions and sovereignty over data for Global South states. FGG and partners have been advocating opposition to the moratorium, including by working with partners in Indonesia and South Africa. • In 2024, Argentinian senators rejected parts of the Regimen de Incentivos para Grandes Inversiones (RIGI, Regime of Incentives for Big Investments) law in line with the positions of Argentinian civil society. FGG and partners created a group to analyse the law and its implications, drafted a joint letter, signed by 20 organisations, to the Senate asking the Senate to reject RIGI in light of the threats it represents. (x) • In 2024. the government of Colombia announced it will renegotiate the UK-Colombia BIT on account of ISDS. FGG and partners published a report on ISDS in Colombia in 2023. • During the 176th Session of the FAO Council, from 2-6 December 2024, the Council formally welcomed the proposal to hold a second International Conference on Agrarian Reform and Rural Development (ICARRD+20) to be held in Colombia in 2026. FGG has supported advocacy on this issue since 2022. FGG In March, FGG and partners co-organised the Land Deal Politics Initiative conference in Colombia. • In 2024, during the LDPI Conference in Bogota Colombian Minister of Agriculture Jhenifer Mojica publicly announced Colombia’s intention to host, together with the FAO, a new international conference on agrarian reform (ICCARD+20) in 2026. The commitment was subsequently celebrated by Brazil’s president Lula in his visit to Colombia. This has been a key policy demand of FGG and partners since 2022. FGG and partners co-organised the Land Deal Politics Initiative conference in Colombia. • In 2024, the Honduran Attorney General and Minister of Economy discussed the problem with ISDS during the CELAC Social Meeting in Tegucigalpa in June. FGG and partners prepared a report on ISDS in Honduras which was shared with policymakers.

In 2025, FGG aims for 57 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Kenya, Mexico, Thailand) international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved government policies (result area C). FGG’s aim for 2025 is to improve government policies on among other things, the following: • In Bangladesh, key authorities, such as ministries and the energy authority support our recommendations to sign and implement technological exchange agreements to ensure the availability of green and renewable technologies at fair prices. • The EU-Mercosur trade agreement is not signed and key actors continue to voice serious concerns or outright opposition to the trade deal. • In the 11th round of negotiations for the UN Binding Treaty FGG aims to maintain the support of the 12 governments that have defended FGG recommendations and aims for the support of an additional 5 governments. • EU politicians support the ask that the EU does not make new trade contracts with Morocco about Western Saharan territories. • Government bodies in India support FGG recommendations on cross-border data flows with data rights, AI auditability and algorithmic transparency and provisions on data localisation. • Local government actors in the upper watershed of the Athi river use the insights on water quality and quantity, provided by the Athi River Community Network through citizen science and remote sensing, to discuss and promote equitable water governance and agroecology. • Key actors from the forestry department in Thailand will facilitate spaces for dialogue between community leaders and forestry officials towards sustainable land management practices to ensure equitable access to land resources and address environmental concerns. • Key actors in Cambodia will recognise communal land titles to resolve claims over the lands that have been contested by a land concession company. • Key government actors in the Philippines will support and/or promote the inclusion of IPOs in Local Special Bodies.
