For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)

In 2023, FGG contributed to 25 policy and/or practice changes that are aimed at corporate regulation by governmental institutions in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: • In 2023, two leading committees from the European parliament (International Market and International Trade Committees) voted for a significant improvement in the previously presented proposal on an EU-wide ban on forced labour products. They consist of: 1) proof or remediation for workers as a condition for lifting a product ban, 2) a reversal of the burden of proof system whereby companies would need to prove the absence of forced labour in cases concerning areas and sectors identified by the EU commission as high risk of "state-imposed forced labour", and 3) a centralised complaint mechanism to facilitate action by victims. The two committees also voted to start immediate negotiations with the EU Council in order to agree and adopt legislation as soon as possible. FGG, as part of a wide civil society coalition, had actively lobbied EU lawmakers, among others by briefing on essential elements to make the proposed regulation efficient, implementable and above all, impactful to address forced labour meaningfully. (x) • In 2023, the government of Rajasthan passed a Platform Based Gig Workers (registration and welfare) Bill. This is a landmark legislation in the Indian landscape aimed at bridging the legislative gap with reads to protections for gig workers. The bill aims to create a fund for guaranteeing social security benefits platform-based gig workers. FGG contributed to the consultation process around the bill and put forward a vision for decent work at platform negotiated workplaces including a taxation levy and a participatory board that has worker participation. • In 2023, the OECD implemented a very inclusive process for the revision of the OECD guidelines. FGG, through OECD Watch urged the OECD Working Party on Responsible Business Conduct (WPRBC) to hold the first two public consultations ever held by the WPRBC during the stocktaking. The consultations sought input from diverse stakeholders, ensuring civil society from all regions of the world. (x) • In June 2023, FGG, through its support of the OECD Watch network successfully advocated for a progressive revision of the newly renamed OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct (guidelines) that extensively reflects priorities of civil society. The updated Guidelines include very strong recommendations on climate change, on reprisals and protection of human rights defenders and civic space, and on respecting the rights of workers in supply chains (rather than just employees). The Guidelines address two topics that were completely missing from the text previously: the text includes new and progressive language on respecting animal welfare; it also guides enterprises to avoid forced displacement and respect legitimate tenure rights and the explicit recognition for an inter sectional approach (gender and human rights due diligence and reference to land rights including the VGGTs). FGG, through OECD Watch, contributed by participating in public consultations and actively engaging with the Dutch Ministry. (g) • In 2023, the OECD guidelines on defending civic space also improved to ensure that the update standards are significantly better in terms of outlining expectations for corporate respect for human rights defenders and civic space. At OECD Watch's request the UN Rapporteur for Defenders wrote a statement to the WPRBC about the need to strengthen the text, which resulted in some of our final sticking points being resolved – of note, getting the controversial (for one state) term “human rights defender” in there, on top of the stronger language on standards for companies. (x) • In 2023, the OECD’s Declaration on promoting and enabling responsible business conduct in the global economy has been strengthened. OECD Watch participated and made sure the declaration became stronger on key elements of focus for civil society, such as the importance of its roe in the achievement of the SDGs. For CSOs the document is a great source to cite for government commitment to next steps on many rights on corporate harm issues. • In 2023, the Dutch Ministry of Finance conducted and published a research on structurally loss-making companies. FGG, through Tax Justice NL, has been pushing for this type of investigation for a long time and worked together with members of parliament to make sure the research would be conducted. From an economic perspective it is strange that a company makes losses for a long time but continues to exist. Since there is no profit tax to pay if there is no profit, this raises suspicion for a tax avoidance strategy. The findings of the report give insight in how the Netherlands is used as a conduit tax haven. • In December 2023, the EU Parliament and Council adopted amendments to the Critical Raw Materials Act to ensure more meaningful engagement of communities, including indigenous people and women in the Global South when sourcing and processing raw materials. FGG and the Raw Materials Coalition contributed to this amendment through providing oral and written input to the Dutch government representative. (g) • In 2023, the Dutch government adopted a feminist foreign policy which reflects the representation of women, marginalized communities, power relations and policy coherence, FGG in collaboration with the Dutch Gender Platform successfully pushed for the inclusion of these elements during the consultation process. (g) • In 2023, a major port authority in Bangladesh started constructing an alternative road, following protests against the potential damage to their roads from heavy construction traffic. This change avoided using the existing roads in Eatbaria which faced the risk of accidents and accelerated damage due to heavy vehicle use. This followed from protests from the community supported by partner CSOs. • In 2023, the Chief Administration Officer form a local government in a district of Western Uganda followed up with the Ministry of Finance during the budgeting of the financial year 2024/2025 and ensured that the compensations worth UGX. 100 million for 2 communities who were evicted from their land for investment purposes will be released and paid to them. FGG partners supported the communities to advocate for compensation and remedy for land grabs.(x) • In 2023, the County Commissioner in a a county in Southern Kenya established a Community Development Agreement Committee together with a mining company. FGG has been advocating for implementation of the Community Land Law which prescribes that such CDACs need to be established as part of responsible mining. (x) • In 2023, the Land Board in a county in Southern Kenya has stopped three land grabs in which women’s land was sold without their consent. The women advocating for were supported with training through FGG partners on their land rights. (g) • In 2023, the Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate adopted recommendations from Human Rights in Wind Turbine Supply chains in their policies and invited FGG to co-design the implementation plan of this tender process to include human rights and safeguards in wind energy tenders. • In 2023, the local government in a district of Western Uganda made resolutions including profiling all the stakeholders in Kiryandongo and requesting them to present their investment plans to help the district to monitor the plans of the corporates, conduct quarterly engagement meetings with the investors to ensure respect, protection and promotion of human rights of the communities, to put in place community benefit sharing mechanisms, and for the companies to adopt Corporate Social Responsibility measures to help them respond to the needs of the communities. FGG and partners documented various human rights abuses and met with the local government and the companies to address these and called for an end to impunity for the corporates involved. • In 2023, a local government official in a village in the Pathuakali district in Bangladesh , successfully intervened to stop a Power Plant from encroaching upon a major canal which is a crucial irrigation source for the community. This prevented environmental damage and preserved the villagers’ livelihood and food security. FGG supported CSOs and communities to advocate for their rights at the local government authority. • In 2023, officials from the Ministry of Labour in Kenya , instructed a mining company to allow the employees to be part of a union and to stop the arbitrary revocation of contracts. This happened after an FGG partner held a meeting with the community and workers on worker’s rights and assisted the community to write a petition. (x) • In 2023, the Ministry of Finance and Investments in Zimbabwe introduced a 1% Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) tax on granite and lithium in the 2024 National Budget which will be used to benefit communities where minerals are being extracted. FGG and partners have pushed for community benefit from national resources during meetings with policy makers. • In 2023, the President of Indonesia supported a document that served as a legal intervention process in the administrative court , supporting the Ministry of Environment and Forestry against private interest where he issued 1,541 social forestry and 107 Agrarian reform tenure certificates to ensure tenure security of IPLCs. (x) • As per 1 January 2023, the Dutch government does not allow any applications for Export Credit support for new oil and gas projects and with this ending ECA support for fossil fuels. FGG supported partners in the Global South to advocate against ECA support and generated media attention in the Netherlands through the ECA-watch network. • The governments of Norway and Australia joined the Clean Energy Transition Partnership (CETP, Glasgow statement) at COP28, aiming to end ECA support for fossil fuels. FGG co-leads the ECA-watch network to engage with these governments. • The UNFCCC adopted recommendations of the Kick Big Polluters Out coalition to require COP28 to disclose their affiliation with industry . FGG is an active member of the Kick Big Polluters Out coalition, which has been campaigning against the fossil fuel industry and corporate capture of the climate negotiations. This is an important step towards defending civic space, specifically the UN climate negotiations, from undue corporate influence. (x) • On 18 April 2023, the senate of Colombia adopted a bill to ban fracking and the exploitation of unconventional deposits . Following the approval by the Senate, the bill is currently being debated in the House of Representatives. FGG provided financial support to support mobilizing civil society, organizing campaigns and generating media attention to ban fracking.

In 2024, FGG aims to contribute to 30 policy changes that are aimed at corporate regulation by governmental institutions in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: The EU will adopt a strong corporate sustainability due diligence directive (CSDDD) including provisions on liability and access to court for victims, and climate obligations for companies;The EU and member states will withdraw from the Energy Charter Treaty (on top of the countries that already announced to take steps to withdraw from the treaty);Adoption of a feminist lens to address gender equality concerns with and corporate violations by the Kenyan Ministry of labour;The County Government of Siaya (Kenya) will establish a joint team to work on Yala Swamp and will take up AAK and partner’s recommendation for safeguarding community land rights and providing compensation and other forms of remedy in the area;The Dutch parliament adopts a due diligence law that reflects the perspectives of and input from SOMO and the MVO Platform and provides better protection of human rights in global value chains;The EU will adopt stricter or improved due diligence requirements along battery supply chains;The RSPO board will adopt revamped complaint mechanisms and a revised planning and control standard on human rights, land rights, civil society participation and women’s rights;The new Dutch government will end all support for fossil fuel projects via ADSB;The Dutch government will decide to stop supporting the Mozambique LNG project and address human rights violations that already took place in this project;FMO will implement the Land Rights Plan (LRP) in Malawi to the satisfaction of the Salima communities and take responsibility for outstanding issues by adopting a policy or practice that addresses these issues;FMO will recognise its responsibility in the human rights violations that took place and will remedy the harm done in the Barro Blanco project.

In 2024, FGG contributed to 16 policy and/or practice changes that are aimed at corporate regulation by governmental institutions in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: • In 2024, the Bagerhat subdistrict administrators established a strict monitoring process to ensure land access for 40 landless families included in the Sreeghat rehabilitation project in Bagerhat. They conducted a site visit to ensure these families could access the land assigned to them. • In May 2024, the EU adopted the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD). The directive incorporates strong elements aligned with FGG’s recommendations, particularly on meaningful stakeholder engagement, the due diligence process, and access to justice. • In 2024, the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Trade and Development improved practice by organising a specific consultation meeting (SDG gender impacts toets) to assess the impacts of human rights due diligence legislation on gender equality. This consultation fed into the national implementation law of the CSDDD. While a gender impact assessment is legally required for any legislative proposal, this was the first time the Ministry carried out a thorough assessment in consultation with CSOs. The consultation and its conclusions, resulted from FGG’s continued advocacy on the need for gender-responsive legislation including a strong gender impact assessment, the publication of the ActionAid briefing “Towards a gender-responsive transposition of the CSDDD” and the joint written contributions developed together with WO=MEN. (g) • In 2024, the Ministry of Mines and Mining Development in Zimbabwe incorporated key policy recommendations into the draft Value Addition and Beneficiation Strategy. These recommendations related to the definitions of benefaction and value addition and ensuring value addition leads to the production of a full product. FGG’s partner pushed for the government to define beneficiation and ensure value addition towards a full product. • In 2024, the National Land Commission (NLC) and the County Government of Siaya (Kenya) reduced the size of land allocated to Lake Agro (company) from 6,764 ha to 2,446.1 ha in the lease agreement drafted and shared with the public. This happened after campaigns and advocacy meetings organized by the community, supported by FGG. • In May 2024, EU Member States gave their final approval to the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (EU CSDDD). The adopted legislation requires larger companies to ensure human rights and environmental protection throughout their supply chains. Notably, the final text explicitly includes the term "living wages," emphasizes a more central role for trade unions and freedom of association, addresses the impact of companies' procurement policies on human rights violations, and applies to the entire supply chain rather than just a company's closest business partner. From the moment the law passed the European Parliament until the Member States gave their final approval, FGG lobbied intensively as part of a broad civil society coalition to influence the legislation positively. FGG collaborated closely with Dutch and European stakeholders, created communication materials, issued public statements, and conducted media outreach. It also lobbied EU and national policymakers, engaged European brands, and supported its European network in advocating for an ambitious transposition of the directive into EU Member State laws. This included providing written input for the consultation on the Dutch implementation law and amplifying ambitions for the textile and garment industry at the Dutch governmental level. • In April 2024, the European Parliament approved the Forced Labour Law. FGG, as part of a broader NGO coalition led by Anti-Slavery International, lobbied for the EU Forced Labour Regulation proposal. This proposal aims to hold companies accountable by obliging them to provide remediation for victims of forced labour and ensuring that products linked to forced labour are banned from the market. • In 2024, the Constitutional Court in Colombia addressed a legal case supported by a campaign alliance advocating for the Afrowilches community's right to be consulted prior to implementing fracking pilot projects. The Court issued Ruling 514, which mandates prior consultation with the Afrowilches Community Council before such projects commence. This ruling is a significant precedent, reinforcing the right of territorial inhabitants to participation in decisions affecting their lands. FGG contributed to this impactful achievement by providing financial support to the Latin America CSO involved in the campaign alliance. (x) • In 2024, 6 conservative Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) voted in favour of the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD). This achievement was the result of years of research, advocacy, and movement-building by the MVO Platform and FGG. • In 2024, EU member states and the European Parliament officially adopted the CSDDD, marking a historic milestone for corporate accountability. It included a.o. recommendations on issues such as responsible disengagement, stakeholder engagement, and due diligence steps. This success also stems from long-term advocacy and efforts by the MVO Platform, OECD Watch and FGG. • In 2024, the Dutch government adopted several recommendations from the MVO Platform in revising responsible business conduct conditions for public procurement contracts (Internationale Sociale Voorwaarden, ISV). The MVO Platform, hosted by an FGG member, had advocated for these changes for years through research and engagement. • In 2024, the Ministry of Finance and the CPB adopted FGG’s method for calculating lost revenue from abolishing the tax on share buybacks. Initial estimates suggested a cost of €800 million annually, but FGG calculated it at approximately €2 billion. Following discussions, a revised estimate of €1.5 billion was agreed upon, increasing parliamentary pressure to reconsider the tax due to higher expected revenue. • In 2024, the European Commission’s department for competition improved transparency and disclosure requirements for participants in public Digital Markets Act (DMA) workshops. FGG’s analysis of the DMA implementation revealed strategies Big Tech companies used to avoid compliance. FGG then advocated for additional resources for the DMA team and stricter transparency rules. • In 2024, the European Commission’s department for competition opposed Amazon’s proposed takeover of iRobot, contributing to the companies abandoning the deal. FGG’s analysis highlighted risks to data protection and market concentration posed by the merger. • In 2024, five governments—Austria, Belgium, Chile, Croatia, and Germany—established robust policies addressing retaliation risks against complainants in NCP cases. OECD Watch had long advocated for zero-tolerance policies against retaliation through initiatives like its 2024 (re)Evaluation of NCPs. • In June 2024, the Kenyan government rendered its Bilateral Investment Treaty (BIT) with the Netherlands inoperative following Kenya’s earlier unilateral cancellation of the treaty. This outcome was supported by FGG’s ongoing awareness-raising and knowledge-sharing on BITs. • In 2024, the EU Commission included recommendations in its draft guidelines for due diligence implementation under the EU Batteries Regulation. FGG, in collaboration with civil society allies, actively participated in several consultations to inform these guidelines. This achievement was the result of years of research, advocacy, and movement-building by the MVO Platform and FGG. • In September 2024, the UN Summit of the Future (SOTF) took place in New York, where multistakeholderism was excluded from the scope of the Pact of the Future. FGG and partners had been advocating for the SOTF for two years and successfully ensured multistakeholderism was not considered in the framework of the summit itself. Once drafts of the Pact were released, FGG and partners provided inputs on text revisions, which were shared with states to aid their negotiations on the Pact.

In 2025, FGG aims to contribute to 47 policy changes that are aimed at corporate regulation by governmental institutions in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: • The EU adopts a negotiation mandate for the 11th session of the UN Treaty on Business and Human Rights negotiations. • More EU member states leave the Energy Charter Treaty. • EU member states transpose CSDDD into national legislation. • Development of DPIs should be done with public consultation, secured through participatory governance frameworks, and include robust accountability mechanisms to prevent rights’ violations, all grounded in democratic principles. • Adoption of a public AI model or technology-enhanced learning within school systems in India. • Governments use the OECD Guidelines (where higher than national law) as a justification and basis for strengthening existing and passing new law and regulation promoting RBC. • EU merger review rules have been revised and include FGG recommendations. Additionally, at least one big tech merger or partnership was stopped based on revised EU merger review rules.

description.narrative: governments regulating the private sector
# key actors who support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations

comment.narrative: In 2021, FGG aims for 82 key actors to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments act to regulate private sector actors (especially corporations and including financiers/banks) to respect human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)

In 2021, 57 key actors supported and/or promoted FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments act to regulate private sector actors (especially corporations and including financiers/banks) to respect human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability.

In 2022, FGG aims for 66 key actors to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments act to regulate private sector actors (especially corporations and including financiers/banks) to respect human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)

In 2022, 73 key actors supported and/or promoted FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments act to regulate private sector actors (especially corporations and including financiers/banks) to respect human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability.

In 2023, FGG aims for 57 key actors to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that governments act to regulate private sector actors (especially corporations and including financiers/banks) to respect human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)

In 2023, 73 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments, international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations supported and/or promoted FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved corporate regulation by governmental institutions (result area D): • In 2023, the Dutch Minister of Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation promised during a debate before the House Committee that the Netherlands will continue to put pressure on the European Commission to come up with an EU-wide IMVO directive and in the meantime it will be fully committed to prepare its own legislation on the theme. FGG strongly campaigned with other organisations and willing companies -including a petition that was presenter to the minister and members of parliament, signed by over 40,000 people. • In 2023, 4 Dutch political parties (PvDD, D66, GL/PvdA and Volt) added a climate duty for corporations in their election manifesto. Meaning, these parties support FGG recommendations that companies should only be eligible for financial support by the government if they have a concrete climate plan which is in line with the goals of the Paris Agreement. FGG send a letter to Dutch political parties with input for their election manifesto including a key point for a climate duty for corporations. • In 2023, 7 Dutch political parties (PvDD, GL/PvdA, VOLT, ChristenUnie, D66, SP, CDA) included FGG recommendations on a binding mandatory human rights due diligence legislation in line with the international OECD guidelines in their party program in the run up to the national elections in November. • In 2023, 1 member of the European Parliament , committed to vote in favour of the CSDDD. FGG, in collaboration with CNV International organised a Human Rights Due Diligence conference for CDA, advocating for strong legislation at the EU level. • In 2023, 1 Dutch parliamentarian , successfully submitted two motions requesting the government 1) to address the NCP concerns regarding CSDDD not being compliant with OECD guidelines and in EU negotiations make sure it will align and 2) to carry out a test ton the impact of the CSDDD on developing countries with specific attention to human rights and environment, plus to align with the OECD guidelines when transposing the EU directive into Dutch legislation. • In 2023, The UN Commission of Status of Women 67 (UNCSW 67) Co-Chair noted and appreciated FGG’s perspectives on gender-inclusive public digital innovation and penalization of corporate impunity for women’s human rights violations in the digital age. FGG pushed for this outcomes through advocating with the Women’s Rights Caucus, a global, intersectional and inclusive coalition of more than 200 feminist organizations, networks, and collectives that advocates for gender equality within the UN Commission on the Status of Women (CSW).(g) • In 2023, the Dutch government has continued to emphasize the importance of aligning many elements of the future Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) with the international normative framework on responsible business conduct. This position was further supported by the analysis of the different CSDDD proposals, which was published by the Dutch National Contact Point (NCP) for the OECD Guidelines in the summer of 2023. The report was written upon request of the Dutch parliament, following continued advocacy from the MVO Platform, hosted by FGG, that called for alignment of the Directive with the OECD Guidelines. This advocacy was targeted at both Dutch Parliament and the Dutch government, which ultimately resulted in the Parliament request for this analysis. • In June 2023, the European Parliament's report on Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) was approved by a broad cross-political majority. And in December, the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union reached an agreement on the CSDDD, which presented a unique opportunity to tackle systemic human rights and environmental abuses in global value chains. FGG partnered with a broad coalition of CSOs to advocate for a strong law through public statements, media outreach, lobbying at EU and national level, supporting the Justice is Everybody’s Business campaign by being a member and disseminating a digital email petition calling EU citizens to put pressure on policy makers. • In November 2023, a resolution was adopted in the UN calling for a UN tax framework reform, a result that for decades was considered impossible to achieve and could eventually move decision-making on global tax rules from the OECD, a small club of rich countries where this has sat for over 60 years, to the UN. This follows substantial advocacy efforts, public awareness raising, and international cooperation by Tax Justice amongst others. • In January 2023, the International Labour Organization (ILO) conducted a High-Level Tripartite Mission in the Philippines and endorsed FGG, through the GoodElectronics’ network, recommendations. The GoodElectronics Regional Coordinator contributed several cases and an analysis of the electronics sector to a report submitted in January 2023 by labour groups to the International Labour Organization High Level Tripartite Mission. The endorsement by the ILO Mission of key reforms, including the creation of a Presidential Commission for Freedom of Association and the ratification of ILO Convention 190, was crucial for advancing lobar rights in the Philippines. (x) • In 2023, the governments of Cameroon and Ghana supported FGG recommendations by hosting the Africa LBI State forum – a regional consultation with States participated by diplomatic missions, Geneva missions and stats officials from various African countries. FGG connected the states of Cameroon and Ghana and influenced the agenda of the forum with perspectives from different affected groups in Africa, including women workers, indigenous and affected communities. (g+x) • In 2023, the government of Ghana organized a ministerial stakeholder consultation on the content of the UNBT, BHR to define their position on the treaty text for future engagement in the treaty process (led by the MOFa and the Ministry of Justice). FGG engaged with the government in preparation for the Africa forum and advocated to the government of Ghana to have a leading role and show political commitment. • In 2023, state representatives from Cameroon and France actively expressed their support for the negotiations for a UNBT during two side events specifically for FGG’s recommendations on gender and a just transition for the first time. Two side events were organized by FGG and partners and the attendance of these state representatives was a result of joint advocacy efforts. (g) • In 2023, the Geneva Mission of Mozambique supported FGG’s recommendation to set the agenda of their to discuss the UNBT and its position. The mission produced a report with recommendations on the future engagements of Mozambique in the treaty process. FGG organized several bilateral advocacy meetings with the Geneva mission to advocate for this support. • In 2023, 6 UN Member States from Africa (Cameroon, Nigeria, Ghana, Mozambique, Ethiopia and Malawi) increased their active participations in the UNBT BHR negotiations. This was a result of the regional African forum in Ghana, holding multi-stakeholder consultations with actors from African States. FGG lobbied for their active participation. • In 2023. 1 Dutch political party (PvDD) included our recommendation on UN Binding Treaty on Business and Human Rights and the recognition that women are often disproportionally affected by corporate abuse in their party program in the run up to the national election sin November. FGG provided written inputs which were fully integrated in their party program. (g) • In 2023, the EU Parliament adopted the JURi-report with amendments to the CSDDD. The amendments bring the CSDDD moire closely in line with the existing OECD guidelines for MNEs and include gender-responsive amendments. FGG took part in joint advocacy for a gender-responsive CSDDD through meetings, public events in the EP, open letters. (g) • In 2023, the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Trade and Development actively pushed the EU to analyse the UNBT BHR and adopt a negotiations mandate for the 9th session. FGG lobbied to keep the UN Treaty BHR on the agenda and call for the Netherlands to push the EU for a mandate. (g) • In 2023, 8 UN member states (UK, Uruguay, Mexico, Ecuador, Colombia, Chile, Bolivia, Argentina) supported FGG recommendations to include a gender perspective in the UNBT for the first time during the 9th session of the OEIWG in their oral interventions during the negotiations. FGG has been lobbying for a feminist binding treaty through advocacy meetings with national delegations, dissemination of key recommendations, several oral statements, raising awareness with social media kit. (g) • In 2023, during the BHR negotiations it was proposed to prepare a new UN resolution on the process for a UNBT, which would put the current UN mandate in jeopardy. Many UN member states -especially from the Africa and Latin American region defended the process and prevented this from happening. • In 2023, the national delegation of Honduras expressed a strong and close position to FGG’s stance during the UNBT negotiations in Geneva on the need for a binding treaty with a feminist perspective. (g) • In 2023, the Decentralization and Development Commission of the Congress (DDCC) of the republic of Guatemala organized a working meeting with key actors responsible for following up on BHR in Guatemala. This is a significant step because all 12 deputies, forming the DDCC, supported the meeting to discuss BHR in Guatemala. Their position is to align the binding treaty with the guiding principles on BHR. FGG collaborated with the commission and to push for Guatemala to take a position in the UNBT process. • In 2023, 1 Guatemalan representative participated in the UNBT negotiations and recommended to focus the treaty on transnational companies and WRs. She also proposed a bill on BHR to follow-up on in 2024. Her recommendations are focused on women's rights and indigenous rights (related to palm oil and mining companies), and to expand civic space by organizing meetings with key actors and CSOs based on FGG recommendations. • In 2023 ,the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs committed to further develop a strategy to consult affected women and communities by the mining industry. High level policy makers reached out to FGG to participate in a round table for further support with the Dutch extractive strategy. (g) • In 2023, a district commissioner from Zambia supported FGG’s recommendations by starting human rights and environmental impact assessment to advance the community's relocation and remediation process. These communities have been affected by the mining industry and FGG supported them to lobby for a good relocation process. • In 2023, the District Police in Mufulira Zambia named Green and Justice as GBV focal point to improve the handling of complaints of GBV in mining affected communities. There is a mediating role for the unit with community paralegals and victim support for GBV complaints and improving access to justice. FGG and partners researched these issues and held sessions with these communities resulting in recognition of their expertise. (g) • In 2023, the Ministry of Home Affairs of Zambia supported FGG recommendations by drafting a new policy (awaiting adoption in parliament) on independent monitoring of air pollution by mines, instead of mines managing their own pollution detection. • In August 2023, 4 deputies of the URNG in Guatemala summoned officials from the Ministry of the Environment, Ministry of Health, Human Rights Ombudsman's Office, Ministry of Agriculture and COPADEH, to comply with the recommendations in a report published by the Human Rights Ombudsman. in collaboration with FGG and partners. containing the human and rights situation of the communities affected by the palm oil plantations, especially focused on gendered impacts. (g) • In 2023, a local Upazila Nirbahi Officer in Bangladesh , issued a directive to a major powerplant company to immediately begin distributing houses to people that had been displaced by the power plant project. As a result, within a week, all 249 affected families received houses in the larger rehabilitation project, following the earlier settlement of 40 families in the smaller project. After a series of awareness raising and capacity building, FGG and partners organized and facilitated an advocacy dialogue among upazila level local government representatives, community representatives and local CSO leaders. • In 2023, a local government representative from Bangladesh instructed a major power plant authority to keep their promise to establish a technical training institute for the community. The also pledged to regularly follow up on the institute's development regularly. FGG facilitated advocacy dialogue between the communities affected by the coal fired powerplant and the government. • In 2023, the government of Zimbabwe finally agreed on auditing responsible mining. The government launched and convened the Responsible Mining Audit which can be attributed to campaigns for responsible mining done by FGG and partners. • In 2023, the Dutch Minister of Climate and Energy launched an ‘international coalition to phase out fossil fuel subsidies’. In this coalition he calls upon other countries to be transparent on the amount of fossil fuel subsidies of their country to be able to address international barriers to phase out fossil fuel subsidies together, and to implement national action. FGG, together with other NGOs, had a conversation with the minister in preparation for COP28 and included phasing out fossil subsidies in the demands towards the NL delegation at COP28. • In October 2023, the Dutch parliament adopted a motion that calls on the Dutch government to draw up scenarios for phasing out fossil subsidies. FGG co-authored a report that quantified the size of fossil fuel subsidies in the Netherlands, which received a lot of media attention and was cited in questions to the Dutch parliament. • In October 2023, the Dutch Parliament voted in favour of a motion to come up with scenarios for the phase out of fossil fuel subsidies for corporations. published a report in which was calculated that the amount of Dutch fossil fuel subsidies was at least 37.5 billion euros each year. Phasing out these subsidies, and reinvesting the saved expenses in renewable energy and energy efficiency, social protection measures, and increased international climate finance for developing countries would reduce Dutch emissions between 13.1 and 19.8 percent by 2030. • In October 2023, Dutch parliament passed a widely supported motion on postponing the decision to continue to provide export credit insurance (ECI) to TotalEnergies for the LNG project in Mozambique. The motion explicitly states that the decision should be based on a re-assessment of this ECA support and parliament should be informed about and involved in the decision-making process in regards to a possible continuation of the ECA support for this project. • In 2023, the Municipal IPMR from the Philippines prevented a pineapple plantation company from expanding its business to the communities in CADT 206. The IPMR also played a key role in acting on the complaint of the Sezukadang community on aerial spraying where he facilitated meetings of community leaders to anticipate provincial inquiry on aerial spraying. The Municipal IPMR, as the voice of Indigenous Peoples in the local legislative body has asserted for the recognition of rights of indigenous people. FGG provided technical support during the IPMR reflection sessions. (x) • In 2023, the NCIP National Office in the Philippines directed the regional Compliance to Ancestral Domains Office with a memorandum order with the subject to follow-up on the compliance which was given to the Regional Director of the NCIP Regional Office for the issuance of Cease and Desist Order to Kennemer Food International (KMFI) and Green Arrow Agri Ventures (GAAVI) for their banana plantation project for violation of the FPIC process. This is a result of continuous lobby efforts made by the Sezukadang community. Not all government agencies respond to community resolutions filed by IP communities so having this memorandum is important prove of support that the government is following up. (x) • In 2023, the EU commission proposed an end to ECA support for oil and gas projects during the OECD meetings in 2023. FGG co-coordinated the ECA watch network, generating lots of media attention and global south partners putting pressures and fighting projects. • NHPC (client of the World Bank, EdF, AfDb and FMO), through ongoing mediation facilitated by the CAO between affected communities of a project in Cameroon and NHPC has led to some first commitments towards livelihood restoration, fisheries access, jobs and representation of women in affected communities. FGG has continued to provide support to organize affected women for participation in the mediation process. (x) • The AfDB, Is participating in a mediation process and partly compensating communities in Senegal through cash compensation. The communities faced the loss of land and housing as a result of the Malicounda power plant. FGG and partners have been addressing compensation issues continuously. • The FMO and DEG established a fund for livelihood restoration – a unique after-closure impact mitigation arrangement for Indigenous communities affected by the Barro Blanco project. FGG contributed by joint advocacy with local partners towards FMO and setting up an assignment procedure to attract a fund manager. The communities were able to represent themselves directly in discussions with FMO and DEG. (x) • In 2023, members of the congress at a public hearing in Colombia and the country’s representatives at the 9th session of UN negotiations on a Binding Treaty on Business and Human Rights in Geneva expressed their support for the treaty. FGG supported CSOs lobbying the government by sharing information on the proposed legislation as well as with financial support in previous years for knowledge building and developing regional campaign materials. (x + g) • In 2023, 2 national deputies from Argentina presented a draft law in the National Congress on the regulations of transnational corporations in support of the UN Binding Treaty. They also put the Binding Treaty in the policy plans of their political parties. This was a result of campaigning by a national and regional CSO in Latin America and the Caribbean. FGG provided strategic and financial support. (x + g) • In 2023, the minister of human rights and citizenship and 2 government representatives in Brazil publicly expressed their support and commitment for the UN Binding Treaty and national legislation on Human Rights and Business. The Human Rights and Business agenda is now a strategic objective for the ministry and an inter-ministerial working group will develop the policy including CSO representation. This is a result of ongoing campaigning by one national and one regional CSO. FGG supported these financially and strategically • In 2023, the global campaign for a UN Binding Treaty contained efforts to derail and breakdown the UNBT process . The Chair of the process, Ecuador, presented a new proposal of the text that highlighted significant changes from the Third Revised Draft, being less protective of rights-holders, which opened criticism against the non-democratic and non-transparent methodology of the Chair. The proposed text came as a shock to states and civil society engaged in the global campaign, as these changes did not come out of the standard procedure of the negotiation process. The African group, representing all 54 African states, highlighted that they did not agree with the text nor the proposed agenda, defended by other states. FGG continues to advocate and push through the UN Binding Treaty as part of the Global Campaign. • In November 2023, two lawmakers from Malaysia raised concerns on the possible adverse impacts of carbon markets on forests and indigenous customary territories in the country and the possible environmental and public safety and health impacts of an offshore CCS project. This was done through the submission of 3 questions and the speeches in the state legislature, indicating their willingness to critically respond and re-examine false climate solutions that have been planned by the state executive authorities. This is a result of ongoing lobbying by a CSO supported by FGG. • In 2023, the Standing Committee on Democratization, Governance and Human Rights (DGHR of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) Parliamentary Forum recommended to the 53rd plenary that the SADCPF “Urge SADC Parliamentarians to raise awareness among stakeholders in their respective countries, including the among relevant government ministries, regarding the UN Binding Treaty on Business and Human Rights and encourage robust participation in the process to ensure that the final outcome would be inclusive, covering all human rights in order to curb corporate impunity of TNCs” Importance of the Binding Treaty to regulate transnational corporations. FGG funds a partner in the region to facilitate the southern campaign. • The Global Inter parliamentary Network expanded its membership including MPs from Guatemala, Brazil, and Bangladesh. The GIN is an important component of the international and national advocacy efforts that take place around the UN Binding Treaty process and national efforts to strengthen legislation to protect human rights. Guatemala, Brazil, Bangladesh. FGG supports the GIN. • The government of Bolivia and Colombia called upon the WHO to review the current place of coca in the UN Drug Control System, which if reclassified can vindicate the rights of indigenous peoples and open legal international markets for natural and traditional coca products, fortifying Andean economies. This relates to recognition of cultural and indigenous rights for coca growers, who are put at risk because of drug prohibition policies. (x) • In 2023, the Paraguayan government is pushing for legislative reform of the regulation of cannabis production in line with public health needs while allowing for small scale traditional farmers to access the market. FGG worked with partners in Paraguay in the past and linked them to partners in the region. • In Brazil, two politicians promoted remunicipalisation in the context of ongoing privatization efforts in Brazil, particularly around water. A PT state deputy and president of the Education, Culture, Sports and Technology Committee of the Legislative Assembly, published an Op Ed in May 2023 promoting re-nationalisation for the future of water policy. In October in the context of widespread (metro, rail and sanitation workers’) strikes against planned privatization in São Paulo state, state deputy of the Legislative Assembly of Sao Paulo filed a bill to carry out a popular consultation for each privatization process, also citing remunicipalisation cases. FGG and partners contributed to this outcome through our work on Reclaiming Public Services and the Public Futures Database, which were utilized as resources by advocates for public ownership of services.

In 2024, FGG aims for 58 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Brazil, Mexico, Thailand), international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved corporate regulation by governmental institutions (result area D). FGG’s aim for 2024 is to improve government policies on among other things, the following: Political actors in two Latin American countries will support or promote recommendations for a process of national legislation on binding rules for transnational corporations;Political actors in Brazil will increasingly support a draft law on binding rules for transnational corporations;Engagement on UN Binding Treaty on Business and Human Rights in the context of migrant worker’s rights to ensure safeguard of the migrant workers in Bangladesh, e.g. with the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare & Overseas Employment (MoEWOE) and the Climate Parliament of Bangladesh;Key actors from local government units recognise Ancestral Domain Sustainable Development and Protection Plans (ADSDPP) of Indigenous People in the Philippines, as basis for resource development within ancestral domains. ADSDPPs document the IPs' vision and plans for development, as well as their framework for natural resources management in accordance with their traditions and customary laws, including the regulation of development projects within the Ancestral Domain by both government and private sector;The new Dutch coalition will commit, in its coalition agreement, to ambitious Human Rights Due Diligence legislation (HRDD/IMVO law);Political actors at EU and national level will adopt our priorities in the legislative processes on due diligence, and in the development of guidance and accompanying measures;The EU parliament calls on the EU commission to replace the EU ECA regulation 1233/2011 with new EU legislation that is fully informed by just transition principles and human rights and environmental due diligence frameworks and standards including gender analyses and participation of civil society organisations in decision making processes around ECA supported projects and based on the commitments adopted at COP26;Dutch policymakers advocate for a review of the ECA policy in line with Just Transition principles;Progressive EU parliamentary groups mention an end to government support for the fossil fuel sector in their elections programs;At the OECD meeting in Q4 of 2024 a coalition of countries, including the UK and Canada advocate for stopping ECA support for oil and gas by the end of 2025;EU member states advocate for review of the OECD ECA arrangement in regards to fossil phase out.Non-judicial ruling in an ICSID (International Center for settlement of Investment Disputes) case filed by fossil fuel companies against Columbia that takes into account community perspectives on a responsible exit;Governmental actors in Nigeria or Colombia call for companies to remediate environmental and social damage before divesting from fossil fuels.

In 2024, 53 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Brazil, Mexico, Thailand), international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations supported and/or promoted FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved corporate regulation by governmental institutions (result area D): • In 2024, the Deputy from the SEMILLA political party in Guatemala supported the gender recommendations outlined in the report on the situation of human rights and women (Ombudsman’s Office, 2022). The Deputy followed up by planning a dialogue table with state entities mandated to intervene in the problems identified in the project region. This was requested and advocated for by FGG partners. • In 2024, 4 deputies from the SEMILLA political party in Guatemala brought together communities, organisations, and the Presidential Commission for Peace and Human Rights (COPADEH) to mediate the analysis and search for solutions to problems caused by the palm oil agro-industry in various regions of the country. This effort demonstrated their commitment to addressing these issues. FGG together with partners advocated for this to raise awareness of the situation in the project region. • In 2024, a representative in Guatemala summoned the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to discuss the need to support the construction of the Binding Treaty on Business and Human Rights, taking into account feminist, indigenous peoples', and environmental perspectives. FGG and partners have provided information to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to discuss the core articles of the Binding Treaty. (g) • In 2024, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) analysed evidence based on investigations into nickel mine impacts and threats to communities to make progress on a petition. They agreed to a follow-up process and meetings with the communities, organisations, and State to resolve the case, which is significant for the affected communities. (g+x) • In 2024, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and COPADEH in Guatemala participated in the Binding Treaty negotiations for the first time. This marked a significant milestone as Guatemala's government had never engaged in this way before. The institutions recognised the expertise of an FGG partner by reaching out. • In 2024, the Environmental Department in Bagerhat, Bangladesh, halted the purchase of land for a new cement factory adjacent to an existing plywood factory that has caused environmental and health issues. Regulatory barriers and accountability for private companies were introduced following direct recommendations from local CSOs and affected community leaders. FGG and its partners have actively supported the community’s protests against the factory, highlighting issues like abrupt land purchases and pollution. (x) • In 2024, the county government of Kitui in Kenya drafted its first-ever county-level Investment Policy, which includes a chapter on mining. Mining companies are now required to demonstrate compliance with ESG safeguard policies, sustainable mining guidelines, and land acquisition processes that respect individual and community land rights. • In 2024, the county government of Taita Taveta in Kenya drafted its first-ever Mining Policy. Mining companies are obliged to demonstrate compliance with ESG safeguard policies. Additionally, the county government appointed Mining Inspectors tasked with checking compliance. This initiative followed a peer-learning visit to Kwale County, where the community around the Base Titanium Mine demonstrated collaborative approaches with the company. This was a direct ask by FGG’s partner who provided inputs to the draft. • In 2024, the county government of Kilifi (Kenya) announced that salt firms must begin paying for ocean water used in salt extraction. This directive is part of the new Kilifi County Ocean Water Policy, still under development. The policy will address pollution caused by salt companies, benefit-sharing, and loss and damage affecting the local community. • In 2024, the Kole District Local Government in Uganda monitored Gulshan Construction Co. to evaluate whether the company fulfilled its commitments. These included compensating affected community members, constructing a church, digging boreholes, renovating cracked houses, and refilling the quarry ground. Progress was reported as agreed. FGG and partner were requested to assist in the evaluation. • In 2024, the President of Uganda ordered the State Minister of Ministry of Lands, Housing & Urban Development (MHLUD) to convene a meeting to address issues raised by the community in a petition. These issues included human rights violations by investors. The meeting was held in the Kiryandongo district and involved community members, investors, district leaders, and political leaders. FGG facilitated the participation of the HRDs to attend the meeting. • In 2024, the EU Commission conducted a legal analysis of the UN Binding Treaty on Business and Human Rights (BHR) in terms of EU and member state competencies. This marked a significant step toward securing an EU mandate for the negotiations, driven by growing support among member states, including the Netherlands. FGG continues advocacy (last 5 years) towards the Dutch government and coordination among European allies together with the informal coalition NL4Treaty. • In 2024, the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Trade and Development published its proposal for a national human rights due diligence legislation transposing the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) for public consultation. The proposed legislation explicitly recognised the need for gender-responsive approaches to due diligence to address gender-specific impacts of corporate harms, introducing specific guidelines in its explanatory guidance (MvT). FGG continued advocacy on the need for gender-responsive legislation, the publication of the FGG briefing “Towards a gender-responsive transposition of the CSDDD” and joint advocacy collaboration with WO=MEN. (g) • In 2024, the Permanent Mission of the Netherlands in Geneva delivered its first-ever general opening statement during the 10th session of UN Binding Treaty negotiations. They expressed readiness to engage constructively and stressed the need to consult CSOs in the process. This statement reflects a clear push for an EU negotiation mandate and support for civil society's role in the treaty process. FGG members lobbied for a pro-active and constructive role in the treaty negotiations. • In 2024, the European External Action Services defended the importance of a gender-responsive UN Binding Treaty on BHR during the 10th negotiation sessions on two occasions, following pushback on gender language by Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Russia. • In 2024, the German government supported safeguarding women's rights in mineral supply chains both nationally and internationally. They invited an FGG partner to contribute to a roundtable discussion at the OECD Minerals Forum. The discussion focused on strategies to address and mitigate women’s rights abuses in mineral supply chains. The German and Dutch governments remain the only two governments supporting this work on women's rights in mineral supply chains. • In 2024, the Dutch Ministries of Economic Affairs, Infrastructure and Water Management, and Foreign Affairs recognised an FGG members’ expertise on women and human rights in the extractive sector. They invited FGG to contribute to an expert session on implementing the Dutch National Raw Materials Strategy on 8 July 2024. • In 2024, the Ministry of Mines and Mining Development in Zimbabwe convened a second responsible mining audit. For the first time, this process included district government departments as stakeholders, reflecting a step towards broader stakeholder involvement. FGG advocated for the audit and an inclusive process, pushing for a 3rd responsible Mining Audit. • In 2024, the Zimbabwe Human Rights Commission, an independent constitutional body, formalised its relationship with FGG through an MoU. This engagement involves convening mobile legal aid clinics, establishing a compliance mechanism, and supporting work on the National Action Plan on BHR. FGG had many engagements to inform ZHRC and work together. • In 2024, the missions of Ghana, Cameroon, and South Africa in Geneva made several textual proposals to articles 5, 7, and 8 during the UN Binding Treaty negotiations on BHR in line with FGG recommendations. These proposals emphasised a gender-responsive approach, victim protection, access to remedy, and a strong liability regime. (g) • In 2024, the management of AfDB declined to finance phase 2 of the TER project in Dakar until compliance with AfDB policies was ensured. FGG supported CSOs and communities by facilitating complaints through AfDB’s complaint mechanisms and organizing visits to headquarters for advocacy purposes. • In 2024, the Dutch Parliament passed a motion based on FGG’s recommendations concerning the Mozambique LNG project. The motion supported independent investigations into alleged atrocities linked to the project, marking a significant step toward protecting civic space and aiding those speaking out against human rights violations. FGG worked closely with CSOs in Mozambique and the Netherlands to share insights on these issues and bring them to the attention of Parliament members. (x) • In 2024, AfDB ensured continued payments for compensation and resettlements related to the TER and Malicounda projects in Senegal, with 80% of affected individuals receiving compensation. FGG provided ongoing support to complainants and continued advocacy efforts with the AfDB board. • In July 2024, the EU Commission proposed ending ECA support for oil and gas at the OECD level. Advocacy efforts included generating media attention, network-building activities, and co-coordinating the ECA-watch network. • In 2024, the RSPO Board endorsed the second phase of its outreach initiative to Intermediary Organisations (IMOs), including CSOs, unions, women’s and Indigenous organisations, and smallholders. FGG, as a member of the RSPO Board of Governors, successfully lobbied for the adoption of this phase, ensuring broader engagement with key stakeholders in the palm oil supply chain. (x, + g) • In 2024, the Dutch Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management (IenW) responded to questions raised in the Dutch Parliament and a joint NGO letter concerning Malaysian timber entering the Dutch market under the Dutch Timber Procurement Policy. In their response, the Ministry agreed to field a mission to Malaysia by its advisory committee, TPAC, to further investigate the issue. FGG partner and member facilitated dialogue between Indigenous representatives, Dutch parliamentarians, government officials, and the media, supporting advocacy efforts to address the concerns raised by Save Rivers CS. (x) • In 2024, an MoU was signed between two communities and an agro-company, with the involvement of administrative authorities. This agreement safeguards the environment, protects community rights, and ensures increased economic benefits for the communities. The MoU was developed through a participatory process, with active engagement from both community leaders and the agro-company. Smallholder farmers were promoted, and the company committed to maintaining over 10 hectares of community farms. Furthermore, community members will have the opportunity to generate income by selling palm nuts to various buyers, not just to the company, with the initiative primarily benefiting women and youth through income-generation activities. (g) • In 2024, the European Parliament adopted an urgency resolution titled "The Shrinking Space for Civil Society in Cambodia," highlighting the case of a labour rights organisation, an FGG partner. The resolution echoed FGG's stance, underscoring the concerning repression of civil society in Cambodia and the unfair targeting of the organisation. This development reinforced FGG's advocacy efforts regarding civil society protection in the region. (x) • In 2024, the report "Governing AI for Humanity," drafted by the UN AI Advisory Board, reflected FGG’s push for a human rights-based approach to AI governance. The report incorporated FGG’s recommendation to adopt a ‘common but differentiated responsibilities’ approach, inspired by the IPCC, in establishing obligations for the global north and south. FGG advocated for inclusive and equitable digital innovation, focusing on challenging Big Tech’s excesses through knowledge sharing and capacity building. • In 2024, the Brazil T20 Communique and Implementation Roadmap made recommendations on participatory governance, balancing innovation with the rights of vulnerable communities, and building regulation and technological design that promotes information integrity. These themes were detailed in FGG’s policy briefs under the ‘Inclusive Digital Transformation’ task force. FGG supported these efforts by advocating for inclusive and equitable digital transformation across the digital value chain through knowledge sharing, perspective building, and capacity building. (x) • In 2024, key recommendations from FGG’s response to India’s draft Digital Competition Bill, regarding greater transparency in advertisement data collected by Big Tech, were reflected in an antitrust directive banning Meta from using WhatsApp data for advertising purposes. FGG advocated for ethical digital innovation practices, emphasizing the need to challenge Big Tech’s predatory practices through knowledge and awareness building. • In 2024, the Future of European Competitiveness Report called for better enforcement of the Digital Markets Act and Foreign Subsidies Regulation to enhance competition and prevent gatekeeping. This recommendation reflects FGG’s advocacy for breaking up Big Tech, an effort supported by FGG through knowledge sharing and capacity building. • In 2024, the UN Global Digital Compact action commitments recognized the critical role of digital infrastructure development in advancing Agenda 2030. This included not only connectivity infrastructure but also the creation of digital public goods, public digital infrastructure, data exchanges, open training data, and compute resources for inclusive digital economies. These commitments reflected FGG’s advocacy for centering public value in digital innovation. FGG supported inclusive and equitable digital innovation through knowledge sharing, awareness campaigns, and capacity building. • In 2024, the OECD Draft Recommendations on Information Integrity highlighted the importance of transparency, accountability, open government practices, and holding technology and government platforms accountable to promote information integrity. These recommendations reflected FGG’s advocacy for meaningful communication based on democratic principles in a platformized public sphere. FGG also supported regulating social media platforms to counter digital threats to democracy through knowledge sharing, awareness campaigns, and capacity building. • In 2024, the OECD Watch developed due diligence guidance for responsible AI by engaging the OECD Watch Expert Working Group to frame key aspects of due diligence, provide use cases to implement the guidelines, and expand the list of potentially impacted rights and uses. FGG, as a member of this expert working group, contributed to this process, building on its advocacy for challenging Big Tech’s excesses and fostering inclusive and equitable innovation practices. • In 2024, the Karnataka state government published the draft "Karnataka Platform-Based Gig Workers (Social Security and Welfare) Bill," which included provisions on algorithmic transparency, among other protections for platform workers such as social protection and income security. FGG advocated for the right to decent work and algorithmic transparency for platform workers through knowledge sharing, awareness campaigns, and capacity building. • In 2024, the Colombian government, through the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development, publicly expressed its support for a bill against fracking and the exploitation of unconventional deposits. This bill, filed by an alliance of CSOs, was signed by 80 congressmen, including senators and representatives. FGG provided financial support to the alliance. • In 2024, a state lawmaker in Asia raised critical questions about Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) and the dangers of false climate solutions during a legislative assembly speech in November. The Asian CSO, supported by FGG through financial and strategic assistance, engaged with two state lawmakers to deepen their understanding of false climate solutions, including hydrogen and CCS. The CSO continued advocating against the adverse impacts of these solutions, particularly on forest carbon offsetting projects and energy transition issues. • In 2024, the Nigerian government further delayed the sale of Shell Petroleum Development Company (SPDC) and slowed the process of its disengagement. FGG and partner had previously published substantial research on this matter, which was followed by community protests and activist demonstrations supported by FGG. • In 2024, the Dutch government aligned with MVO Platform recommendations on the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) during the final stages of trialogue negotiations. FGG contributed to this achievement through years of research and movement building efforts. • In 2024, during a parliamentary hearing, policymakers and economists supported FGG’s argument that subsidising heavy industry companies for sustainable production is highly cost-inefficient. A publication from an FGG member in the economics journal ESB, focusing on a Dutch company, argued that renewable energy for heavy industry in the Netherlands is expected to remain structurally more expensive compared to other European countries, and scarce resources are used inefficiently. The article’s calculations were frequently cited during the hearing. • In 2024, members of the European Parliament expressed support for the Rebalance Europe and Beyond Big Tech manifestos developed by CSOs. These manifestos advocate for the bold application of competition and industrial policy to limit Big Tech’s market power. Several recommendations from these initiatives were reflected in the European Parliament’s annual competition report, signalling growing political support for reforming competition rules to deliver a fair and plural digital economy. • In 2024, the OECD included OECD Watch’s recommendations in several drafts of forthcoming due diligence guidance for responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI) (g, x). These recommendations emerged from two CSO consultations hosted by OECD Watch, which resulted in three submissions and several oral interventions. • In 2024, the UN Secretary-General’s Panel on Critical Energy Transition Minerals joined OECD Watch in drafting a joint statement calling for stronger performance of National Contact Points (NCPs) in promoting OECD Guidelines and handling complaints. OECD Watch led its business and union counterparts, including Business at OECD and the Trade Union Advisory Committee, in submitting the statement to the OECD Secretary-General and Ministerial Counsel, outlining shared priorities for NCP performance. • In 2024, the UNHRC adopted decision 56/116, enhancing the support capacities of the open-ended working group on transnational corporations and other business enterprises. During the 9th session of the UN Intergovernmental Working Group on the Binding Treaty in October 2023, a technical decision was made to extend the intercessional meeting days. Ahead of the UNHRC’s 56th session, a proposal including the demands of the Global Campaign was submitted. The Global Campaign advocated for intercontinental consultations instead of regional consultations. The decision specifies that from 2025, for a period of three years, up to 10 intercessional thematic consultations will be held annually in Geneva. It also requests the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights to provide enhanced human, technical, and financial support for these consultations. FGG and partners, having supported the Global Campaign for a Binding Treaty over the past decade, engaged with state representatives ahead of the consultations to discuss the campaign’s positions and processes. • In 2024, two provisions of the Binding Treaty text were adopted in alignment with the positions of the Global Campaign during the 10th session. FGG and partners played a key role in achieving this outcome through advocacy efforts as part of the Global Campaign. • In 2024, eight states—Cameroon, Indonesia, Ghana, Brazil, Mexico, Cabo Verde, Djibouti, and Guatemala—supported progressive positions close to those of the Global Campaign during negotiations on the Binding Treaty. FGG and partners contributed to this success through their advocacy work as part of the Global Campaign.

In 2025, FGG aims for 92 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Ghana, India and Bangladesh), international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved corporate regulation by governmental institutions (result area D). FGG’s aim for 2025 is to improve government policies on among other things, the following: • The OECD supports FGG’s recommendations by publishing a comprehensive Just Transition due diligence tool that incorporates gender considerations, supporting companies in their due diligence processes during the energy transition. • In Bangladesh, ministries of relevant departments support our recommendations to hold value chain actors, corporations, private sector actors, and other stakeholders responsible for community suffering and environmental degradation. • The EU Delegated Act and Guidance developed on industry initiatives integrate some of our key advocacy points (binding and enforceable nature, equal representation of workers, focus on remediation, financial contribution). • Influential policymakers, academics, or media endorse a key civil society recommendation for establishing reduction related targets for critical minerals or resources, within the EU or other EU national or international fora. • A more ambitious COP position from the Dutch government on phasing out fossil fuel and international climate duty for businesses. • Platform accountability measures that curtail data extractivism and other practices that entrench market dominance. • Data governance measures that support redistribution of data value by promoting people’s rights and ownership over data as a resource. • Ethical use and development of AI in workplaces and in the public sector. • Breaking up and breaking open big tech monopolies through anti-monopoly action and collaborative advocacy.
