In 2023, FGG contributed to 5 policy and/or practice changes that are aimed at policy space and funding for transformative practices by governmental institutions in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: • In 2023, the department of environmental and climate change in a county in coastal Kenya validated the Climate Change Policy and the (climate change) Risk Assessment which provide space for community members to share their views to be captured into the documents. FGG has advocated for the validation and adoption of this document and mobilized community leaders to share the community aspirations and ideas on adaptation and mitigation measures. (x) • In 2023, a district Commissioner from Zambia ensured improved access for women to new Constituence Development Fund by lowering the barriers for access to the fund and providing guidance on the application. FGG organised various sessions on sustainable livelihood and climate solutions for women and an advocacy meeting with Parliamentarians and District Commission asking for access to this new fund. (g) • In 2023, the agriculture office of a local government in Bangladesh provided new salt-tolerant and climate-tolerant crop seeds, fertilizers and saplings to 70 farmers, improving their economic situation considerably and promoting FGG practice recommendations. FGG supported the local partner with joint strategising on promoting agroecology practices. • In 2023, a local government department in Bangladesh registered 20 youth farmers as a farmer group which is working with the agricultural department to support small and marginal farmers with sustainable climate-tolerant and salt tolerant farming practices. The increased awareness of the government is a result of lobby and advocacy done by FGG partners. • On 12 April 2023, the provincial law declaring “Camino de las flores” located in Buenos Aires Metropolitan Area, to be a protected landscape was approved and adopted by the municipal government of Buenos Aires, in Argentina . FGG has financially supported a CSO to advocate for this bill, including writing the bill. They will also be part of the management committee that will be set up together with the government to devise a management plan for the 200 ha of grassland that make up the “Camino de las Flores”.

In 2024, FGG aims to contribute to 7 policy changes that are aimed at policy space and funding for transformative practices by governmental institutions in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: Key actors such as energy sector stakeholders, universities and local government institutes will implement FGG recommendations on renewable energy-based model communities, renewable energy-based innovation, livelihood solutions and renewable energy-based capacity strengthening of community women entrepreneurs;Key government actors (local, regional or national units) will adopt resolutions supporting agroecology in local communities in Indonesia and the Philippines; Adoption of a public AI model for technology-enhanced learning within school systems in Southern India.

In 2024, FGG contributed to 9 policy and/or practice changes that are aimed at policy space and funding for transformative practices by governmental institutions in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: • In 2024, the Advisory Council of Government Bangladesh gave final approval to permanently repeal the Quick Enhancement of Electricity and Energy (Special Provisions) Act (QEEES Act), also known as the indemnity act for the energy sector. The QEEES Act had enabled energy contracts without public procurement, bypassing transparency and accountability, and leading to corruption. FGG and partners campaigned for the repeal of the QEEES Act, highlighting its violations of citizens' rights and facilitation of corruption. FGG supported CSOs, collaborated with experts, and organized twelve lobbying meetings with key stakeholders. (x) • In 2024, the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs in Bangladesh abolished Section 34ka of the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission Act 2003 (BERC Act 2003). The amended law now requires government entities to submit proposals for power or gas price increases to BERC, which will hold public hearings and decide within 90 days. This abolishes autocratic decision-making, ensures public participation, and expands civic space, giving citizens the opportunity to voice concerns and hold the government accountable which is a result of ongoing lobbying by FGG partners. (x) • In 2024, the county government of Kitui, Kenya, included an allocation for community-designed climate actions in the county budget for 2026/27. This demonstrates commitment to advancing locally-developed initiatives addressing climate challenges and results from advocacy meetings by FGG’s partners with the county government. (x) • In 2024, Voi Law Court (Kenya) adopted and implemented local panels for Alternative Justice Systems (AJS) which was a recommendation by FGG partner and a CSO network, thereby enhancing access to remedy. These panels primarily address land-related issues, such as land grabs and land use, especially in contexts where large tracts of land are earmarked as private wildlife reserves. • In 2024, the Kitui County Government, Kenya, formally established dozens of ward climate change committees across the county. They organised training sessions for committee members, primarily consisting of community members, to make the committees operational and effective in addressing local climate needs. • In 2024, the Ministry of Forestry of Indonesia recognised three Indigenous Peoples (IP) forests by accepting and approving the management plans crafted that year. This marked a milestone in the recognition of IP forests, which integrate sustainable forest management practices with agroecological farming methods and Indigenous knowledge. These forests are among the first in Indonesia to adopt such a management plan following their formal recognition. The achievement is particularly notable given the challenges of persuading traditional foresters of the value of Indigenous practices, such as shifting cultivation, hunting, and gathering within their forest territories. FGG supported the CSO by providing grants and supported the communities prepare their management plans.

In 2025, FGG aims to contribute to 20 policy changes that are aimed at policy space and funding for transformative practices by governmental institutions in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: • The Dutch Fund for Climate and Development (DFCD) consortium will adopt FGG recommendations in their evaluation criteria, including ensuring climate finance is gender-responsive. • In Bangladesh, the government will adopt recommendations on the CSO proposed “National Energy Transition Policy” or formulation ofe a comprehensive “National Energy Transition Policy” and address inconsistencies in existing power and energy policies in coordination with all stakeholders. • Inclusive policies in the Philippines recognise the rights of Indigenous peoples and local communities integrate knowledge and practices in local and national agroecology strategies as well as give priority to IP communities and women led groups to access programmes and services to agroecology (food production, livelihood and enterprise development).

In 2023, 37 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments, international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations supported and/or promoted FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved policy space and funding for transformative practices. • In 2023, ASN Bank and Laudes Foundation signed up as key partners of the Good Clothes, Fair Pay campaign. FGG was one of the driving forces behind the campaign as part of the European Citizen Initiative. • In 2023, 18 investors of a garment brand signed a public letter to pay more than 4,000 garment workers that produced for Nike in two factories in Thailand and Cambodia $2.2 million in unpaid wages and benefits owed since 2002. Some of the investors also called for other investors to sign during the company’s AGM. This is a result of one of the Urgent Appeal cases made possible through FGG. • In November 2023, FGG co-organised the Roots of Resilience Conference in collaboration with the New School and the government of Kerala on cooperatives. A crucial outcome of the conference was the unveiling of the Thiruvananthapuram Declaration – a New innovation Ecosystem for Our Collective Digital Futures, which outlines a vision and commitment to shaping the future landscape of digital innovation . FGG supported the Kerala Development and Innovation Strategic Council (KDISC) and the Platform Cooperativism Consortium (PCC) with establishing a robust framework, actively integrating a feminist vision, for alternative platform cooperatives and fostering a global digital commons. The Declaration which has been open to endorsements and has been translated into several Indian and non-Indian languages, was launched in the presence of government representatives and a member of the state legislature. (g) • In 2023, Niti Aayog (a public agency think tank) responded to FGG’s recommendations and requested FGG for consultancy on its knowledge portal, which is a live repository of policies, acts and best practices. • In 2023, the Gender Park’s initiative of the Government of Kerala to work towards gender equality and empowerment sought FGG’s advisory inputs for shaping policies and practices to correspond to data ethics in the digital area. Building on One of FGG’s members long standing consultative relationship with the Government of Kerala, One of FGG’s members was approached to provide advisory inputs to the process. (g) • In 2023, the G20 New Delhi Leaders’ Declaration prominently emphasized the importance of "safe, secure, trusted, accountable, and inclusive digital public infrastructure". This recognition highlights the crucial role such governance plays in driving technological transformation globally and reflective of our impact. FGG co-produced a T20 brief, focusing on robust digital public infrastructure governance, which fed into the G20 declaration. • In 2023, The UN CSW Outcome document focused on building alternate visions of new feminist institutional structures and rejecting the outdated idea of techno-solutionism. FGG, was able to make a strong impact at the 67th session of the UN Commission on the Status of Women (CSW67) through multiple engagements, advocacy with ministries and delegations, CSOs including contributions to the draft text that were reflected in the CSW outcome document. (g) • In 2023, the municipality of Raxruhá in Guatemala publicly supported the proposal and actively worked with local CSOs in review and exchange sessions on inclusive water management. This proposal publicly and legally recognizes the human right to water, the role of municipal authorities to guarantee this right to all, focused on access for women and indigenous communities, incorporates the guiding principles of companies and human rights. FGG coordinated the proposal development process. (x+g) • In 2023, the Parliamentary Standing Committee of the Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resources in Bangladesh made recommendations to the parliament for the exemption of imports tariffs of renewable energy-based technologies. This happened after the high-level international conference in Bangladesh on energy “Bangladesh Energy Prosperity 2050” took place that was jointly organized by FGG and partners. • In 2023, Bangladesh’s ruling political party included a commitment in their manifesto to ensuring at least 20% of Bangladesh’s energy consumption should be from green and clean energy which was a result from the Energy Prosperity 2050 forum co-organized by FGG. • In 2023, several motions were submitted by policymakers to the Dutch parliament in line with the Just Transition perspective advocated by FGG together with the Critical Raw Materials coalition aiming at responsible-just- renewable alternatives being developed that protect environmental and human rights of affected communities in the Global South. • In 2023, the Campus Coordinator of a state university in the Philippines provided support to the formulation of a memorandum of agreement that goes beyond sustainable agriculture encompassing the overall development of families within the peasant and fisherfolk communities. This was after ongoing lobby efforts of a CSO supported by FGG through a capacity development grant. • The GEF in their Global Biodiversity Frame Fund included FGG recommendations such as a 20% aspirational share of the fund to Indigenous People and Local Communities. GEF council members from countries such as the Netherlands and Belgium have asked for CSO input on the Global Biodiversity Frame Fund that the GEF is managing for better implementation of the Convention Biological Diversity (CBD). (g) • The Global EbA Fund provided project support to develop a plan on inclusive water governance after FGG introduced the concept of a People’s plan for Community-based Tidal River Management. This concept was developed together with local CSOs in Bangladesh. • In 2023, the House Committee on Climate Change Chair Congressman and Congressional Representatives filed the Climate Accountability (CLIMA) bill in the House of Representatives in the Philippines. If approved, the bill will require businesses to proactively prevent and address potential climate-related harms resulting from their operations and decrease their emissions of greenhouse gasses. With the financial support of FGG, a partner CSO worked to draft the bill and engage with congressional representatives to ensure it would get their support to submit to the House of Representatives.

In 2024, FGG aims for 21 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Brazil, Mexico, Thailand), international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved policy space and funding for transformative practices. FGG’s aim for 2024 is to improve government policies on among other things, the following: Promote renewable energy (RE) in Bangladesh; including the CSO led proposed National Energy Transition Policy (NETP), RE-based model communities, RE-based innovation labs, RE-based alternative livelihood solutions, and RE-based capacity strengthening of community women entrepreneurs; De-privatisation of energy and public services on the agenda of government officials at the municipal levels and national levels in Asia, America and Africa;Digital goods in key sectors of development, such as agriculture and health, promoted by Indian government, e.g. ministry of Agriculture, Health, Informations and electronics; More financial and (trade) policy space for land-related Transformative Practices supported by key actors within the new Dutch government and parliament;Key government actors (local, regional or national) gives priority to IPLC women and youth to access programmes and services related to agroecology in Indonesia and the Philippines.

In 2024, 21 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Brazil, Mexico, Thailand), international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations supported and/or promoted FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved policy space and funding for transformative practices. • In 2024, the Ministry of Mines and Mining Development in Zimbabwe sponsored the training of women at the Zimbabwe School of Mines for a short course on cutting and polishing. They also invited 2 members of the Women in Gemstones Association of Zimbabwe (WIGAZ) to exhibit their products free of charge. This initiative is significant as it created a platform for women miners and actively provided them with business networking opportunities. (g) • In 2024, the Zimbabwe School of Mines supported women miners by offering courses through a recognised institution of higher learning. These courses provided accredited certification, improving the viability of women miners' businesses. Women are now engaging in value addition, enhancing their businesses' growth and sustainability. (g) • In 2024, the Ministry of Agriculture in Zimbabwe developed an Agroecology Strategy for the country. This strategy is pivotal as it aims to foster a transition towards resilient and sustainable agriculture and food systems through agroecological approaches, promoting the sustainable consumption of healthy food for all, something FGG and partners have been promoting for years throu8gh several meetings with the ministry. • In 2024, an FGG petition calling out Nike and supporting the Violet Apparel and Hong Seng workers Major Nike investors. fighting for $2.2 million in stolen severance and wages gathered over 140,000 signatures. At the annual shareholder meeting, two major investors backed a proposal that urged Nike to pay the workers and suggested the company commit to worker-driven initiatives such as the Accord. Unfortunately the resolution did not pass. • In 2024, the GEF Secretariat engaged with FGG on its recommendations and incorporated suggestions for a publication. FGG was informally requested to advise the GEF on improving CSO involvement in the GEF funding for the ninth replenishment (2026–2030). (x + g) • In 2024, an FGG partner received a small grant from the Embassy of the Netherlands to Kenya, supporting their tree-planting efforts. This demonstrated the Embassy’s recognition of the CBO’s role in conserving the Thogoto Forest. FGG supported the partner with strengthening their lobbying and advocacy practices. • In 2024, RVO and the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs supported a session at the CBA18 conference on “LLA and landscapes,” organised by a Kenyan FGG partner. The Athi River Community Network was featured as a case study in a role-play that involved practitioners, donors, and policy-makers. This initiative highlighted the value of a locally-led approach and echoed FGG’s recommendation to connect communities across river basins to foster inclusive water governance. The FGG partner later replicated the role-play for RVO’s Valuing Water Initiative through an online session. • In 2024, the Embassy of the Netherlands to Bangladesh prepared a session for the 10th International Conference on Water and Flood Management titled “Water Governance and Youth Aspiration.” The session showcased the Transformative Water Pact—developed in 2023 with FGG members and partners—as an example of inclusive water governance. Youth participants were encouraged to reference this Pact when developing their session proposals. • In 2024, a research consortium consisting of Dutch and Bangladeshi research and knowledge institutes submitted a proposal to NWO, building on a concept paper developed by an FGG member in collaboration with Deltares. The proposal focused on climate adaptation and governance through knowledge exchange between the two countries. Community-based Tidal River Management (TRM) in the Betna-Marichap area—initiated by an FGG member and partner since 2023—was selected as the case study. • In 2024, FGG partner Uttaran was included as the civil society representative in a consortium for action research on “Polder 31” in Bangladesh. Supported by Partners for Water (RVO), the initiative aimed to generate actionable solutions for inclusive in-polder water management. • In June 2024, the Global Learning and Strategic Convening on the Political Economy of AI, Data, and Digital Technologies was held in Mexico City. The panel discussions emphasized the skewed political economy of AI and digital technologies and advocated for the establishment of an alternative institutional order. FGG actively lobbied for AI regulation that considers the implications for the Global South and challenges Big Tech's excesses through knowledge sharing and capacity building. • In 2024, UNESCO, in collaboration with the Government of Kerala and the Government of Finland, published a report highlighting the impact of FGG’s “Little KITEs” program, implemented by Kerala Infrastructure and Technology for Education (KITE), across 2,174 high schools in Kerala. FGG participated in the report's launch event, which led to the Finnish government expressing interest in partnering with Kerala. FGG contributed to this initiative by developing and publishing an impact study that underscored the success of this model in equipping students with skills beyond technological literacy. • In 2024, Parques Nacionales Naturales influenced governmental bodies through its research and report on the effects and impacts of offshore oil exploration on certain species. FGG provided financial and strategic support to the CSO engaged in lobbying on this issue. • In 2024, advocacy on EU-Mercosur and environmental and social justice gained visibility through the elected senator Constanza Moreira from Frente Amplio, Uruguay. FGG’s arguments were publicly discussed across media platforms, including TV, newspapers, and radio, following an advocacy meeting held by FGG and partners (g). • In 2024, a joint statement was issued by the Korean Parliamentary National Assembly Forum on Climate Change and the Global Plastics Treaty (GPT). This resulted from lobbying efforts by FGG and CSOs to advance ambitious positions for the treaty (x). • In 2024, the governmental delegation of Bangladesh actively supported ambitious measures during GPT negotiations. They voted for production reduction, a supply cap, and included strong language advocating reuse targets in the treaty text. FGG and CSOs lobbied for these ambitious positions (x). • In 2024, the Social Forestry and Environmental Partnership Center, a unit under the Ministry of Forestry assigned for social forestry development, continued to work with several farmers groups in the downstream sector, this has improved state owned timber company’s business performance and addressed community pressure on Java’s forests, and were able to address 46% of the critical land in Java. (x) FGG supported the CSO partner who worked on the facilitation of youth cohort in their Social Forestry Heir program. • In 2024, water defenders faced increasing repression during the Peoples’ Water Forum (PWF) in Indonesia. The Indonesian government cancelled the event venue multiple times, confiscated materials, and paramilitary groups, disrupted a PWF press conference. Police also shut down the forum. Additionally, PGN members reportedly broke into the hotel where Indonesian social movements were staying and blockaded the premises. The UN Special Rapporteur on the Human Rights to Safe Drinking Water and Sanitation visited the hotel alongside PWF activists to witness the situation firsthand and speak with those locked inside. A group of academics signed a public letter in support of the activists. The PWF remains a critical space for opposing corporate-led water privatisation, with this repression setting a concerning precedent. FGG and partners supported the organisation of the PWF in Bali. (x) • In 2024, the South African Minister of Labour Affairs highlighted the myths surrounding energy transitions, citing FGG’s research in an op-ed. FGG and partners published a report on myth busting the energy transition in the same year. • In 2024, REN21 underscored the importance of energy justice in its report, emphasizing citizen participation and ownership as key elements. FGG and partners have been working for several years on remunicipalisation to challenge narratives around the privatisation of public services.

In 2025, FGG aims for 35 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Bangladesh, India, Zimbabwe), international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved policy space and funding for transformative practices. FGG’s aim for 2025 is to improve government policies on among other things, the following: • The drafting of a national Water Law in Guatamala that includes key aspects proposed by social and community organizations, such as FPIC, women's right to water, participation and representation of peoples and communities in decisions about water. • To stop the acquisition of agricultural and ecologically sensitive lands for power plants and mega development projects in Bangladesh. • Ministries in Government of India (eg. Ministry of Agriculture, Health, Electronics and Information Technology) support FGG recommendations on development of digital public goods and infrastructure in agriculture, healthcare, finance and education with public consultation, participatory governance frameworks, robust accountability mechanisms to prevent rights’ violations, all grounded in democratic principles. • Representatives of local, regional or national governments or policymakers in Latin America promote FGG recommendations around public energy, universal public services and/or gender-just water provision. • The Philippine Department of Agriculture will bridge connections between IPLCs at the national and local levels so that practitioners are better positioned to engage to gather better support for agroecology practice; • The Philippine Department of Trade and Industry and Department of Science and Technology - assisting women groups in their business plan development in terms of registration and product development.

# of laws, policies and norms/attitudes, blocked, adopted, improved for sustainable and inclusive development

comment.narrative: Of the targets for FGG’s policy and practice change indicators (6E, 6D, 6E and 6F), 71 concern laws, policies and norms/attitudes, blocked, adopted, improved for sustainable and inclusive development.

Of the results for FGG’s policy and practice change indicators (6E, 6D, 6E and 6F), 43 concern laws, policies and norms/attitudes, blocked, adopted, improved for sustainable and inclusive development.

Of the results for FGG’s policy and practice change indicators (6E, 6D, 6E and 6F), 87 concern laws, policies and norms/attitudes, blocked, adopted, improved for sustainable and inclusive development.

Of the targets for FGG’s policy and practice change indicators (6E, 6D, 6E and 6F), 24 concern laws, policies and norms/attitudes, blocked, adopted, improved for sustainable and inclusive development. For more information on our concrete targets, we refer to the target narratives on FGG's indicator 6.

Through its SCS indicator 2, the Ministry counts the number of laws and policies that are blocked, adopted, improved as a result of CSO engagement. FGG counts this through its ‘6SCS2’ indicator, for which it counts the ‘policy change part’ of its generic indicator 6 in which policy and practice change results are combined. More specifically, FGG counts the number of laws, policies and norms/attitudes, blocked, adopted, improved for sustainable and inclusive development. In 2023, FGG contributed to 24 changes in policy.Examples of such successful policy change include:For stand 1 – Trade and investment agreements – Result area C: In November 2023, the Dutch government adopted a Feminist Foreign Policy which reflects the representation of women, marginalised communities, power relations and policy coherence. FGG, in collaboration with the Dutch Gender Platform, successfully pushed for the inclusion of these elements during the consultation process. During the ‘Shaping Feminist Foreign Policy’ conference FGG partners from the Global South shared their visions on what is needed for an inclusive Feminist Foreign Policy based on their experiences with the negative social and environmental impacts of mining and other large-scale investments. For strand 2 – Climate and environmental policies – Result area C: In December 2023, at the Annual UN climate Conference (COP28), the Dutch Minister of Climate and Energy launched an international coalition of 12 countries to phase out fossil fuel subsidies. In this coalition the minister calls upon other countries to be transparent about the amount of fossil fuel subsidies, to address international barriers to phasing-out fossil fuels together, and to implement national action. Fossil fuel subsidies gained a lot of attention in the media and Dutch Parliament after FGG members co-published a report that quantified the size of fossil fuel subsidies in the Netherlands. For strand 3 – Policies on tenure – Result area C:In Indonesia, FGG supported a court intervention case by KPH Jawa, a consortium of CSOs working on the Java Forest, which resulted in a positive court decision in support of the Ministry of Environment and Forestry (MoEF) to reduce the State Forestry Company (PERHUTANI) and accelerate the Social Forestry and Agrarian Reform for the Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities. As a result the president issued 1,541 Social Forestry and 107 Agrarian Reform tenure certificates to ensure the tenure security of IPLCs, primarily from Java Island and former PERHUTANI areas.For strand 5 – Rules for business and corporate conduct, cross-sectoral – Result areas D & E: In June 2023, the updated OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct, were released, which is a major win for civil society. The updated Guidelines improve standards for access to remedy on all of the 13 overarching topics, and many sub-topics, raised by FGG as part of the OECD Watch network. The new guidelines include explicit recognition of an intersectional approach, including gender and human rights due diligence, and references to land rights, including the VGGTs. The revised version also includes greatly improved climate provisions, which now stipulate that companies must implement transition plans in line with the 1.5 degrees of the Paris Agreement, including short, medium and long-term goals. In addition, the risks of damage to biodiversity, deforestation, pollution and the importance of a just energy transition have also been added to what will be expected from companies. FGG members contributed to this result by participating in public consultations and engaging with the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Ambitious OECD guidelines can have a global impact since they will set a standard for the current and future European and Dutch policy processes regarding corporate sustainable due diligence legislation. For strand 6 – Rules for business and corporate conduct, extractives sector – Result areas D & E: In December 2023, the European Parliament adopted the Critical Raw Materials Act, which included several of FGG’s recommendations. This was a result of multiple advocacy meetings and communication with policymakers, including dissemination of a position paper1 on the draft Critical Raw Materials Regulation in May 2023, which included ten key concerns and recommendations related to the European Commission’s Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing a framework for ensuring a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials. For strand 7 – Rules for business and corporate conduct, garment sector – Result areas D & E: Two leading committees from the European parliament (International Market and International Trade Committees) voted for a significant improvement in the previously presented proposal on an EU-wide ban on forced labour products. They consist of: 1) proof or remediation for workers as a condition for lifting a product ban, 2) a reversal of the burden of proof system whereby companies would need to prove the absence of forced labour in cases concerning areas and sectors identified by the EU commission as high risk of "state-imposed forced labour", and 3) a centralised complaint mechanism to facilitate action by victims. The two committees also voted to start immediate negotiations with the EU Council in order to agree and adopt legislation as soon as possible. FGG, as part of a wide civil society coalition, had actively lobbied EU lawmakers, among others by briefing on essential elements to make the proposed regulation efficient, implementable and above all, impactful to address forced labour meaningfully. For strand 8 – Rules for business and corporate conduct, tech sector – Result areas D & E: The government of Rajasthan passed a Platform Based Gig Workers (registration and welfare) Bill. This is a landmark legislation in the Indian landscape aimed at bridging the legislative gap with regard to protections for gig workers. The bill aims to create a fund for guaranteeing social security benefits platform-based gig workers. FGG contributed to the consultation process around the bill and put forward a vision for decent work at platform negotiated workplaces including a taxation levy and a participatory board that has worker participation. For strand 9 – Fair and green systems: agroecology – Result Area F: The Committee on World Food Security - which serves as a forum in the United Nations System for review and follow up on food security policies - included a coordinating role (platform) in its Multi Year Program of Work 2024-2027 to leverage its convening power as the foremost inclusive international and intergovernmental platform to discuss food security and nutrition situation and coordinate collective action at all levels. This is significant in relation to defending civic space, as global food system governance is at risk of corporate capture. This outcome is the result of years of civil society advocacy for the CFS to take a leading role in coordinating global policy responses to the food crisis. Specifically, pressure from the Civil Society and Indigenous Peoples Mechanism (CSIPM) through on-the-ground mobilisation, in the form of two consultation processes in 2020 and 2022 and the “You do politics, We go Hungry” campaign. Since 2019, FGG has been an active member of the CSIPM working group on global food governance and the task team on global policy coordination on food crises, supporting the team by contributing to the strategy and drafting documents for submission to governments. 1https://www.somo.nl/somo-position-paper-on-critical-raw-materials-regulation/

In 2023, FGG contributed to 144 policy and/or practice changes that are aimed at corporate conduct by governmental institutions in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: • In 2023, 26 garment brands signed the TransparencyPledge and started fully disclosing where their products are produced. For the first time there were also brands from the luxury sector that have signed the pledge. To put pressure on these garment brands toe enhance transparency, FGG collaborated closely with organisations such as WikiRate, Opdesh OpenCorporates, MappedInBangladesh and GLEIF to increase the availability of data on supply chains. • In 2023, 101 garment brands from Bangladesh and Pakistan signed the International Accord on Health and Safety in the Textile and garment industry. The Accord has country programmes in Bangladesh and Pakistan, and signatories of the International Accord have to sign at least one of these country programmes. The almost 200 brands that had signed the previous Accord agreement had to re-confirm their commitment. The 2023 Accord will run for three years, with an automatic extension of three more years, and will expand its important work to more countries where workers continue to work in unsafe factories. By the end of 2023, 89 brands from Bangladesh and 93 from Pakistan signed the Accord and reconfirmed their commitment which is of great importance in reducing the amounts of factory incidents in these countries. Additionally, the accord includes a gender-based violence complaints mechanism (g). • In 2023, 2 garment brands and 1 supplier provided remedy to 4 cases of labour rights violations in their supply chain in from Indonesia, Guatemala, Myanmar and Cambodia as a result of CCC’s Urgent Appeal cases. As a result of these urgent appeals there was severance and back-pay to workers who had been illegally fired, reinstatement of workers who had been fired after a strike demanding improved working conditions and a wage increase, severance to workers who have lost their jobs after a factory went bankrupt and a full back pay and rehire opportunities to union leaders and activist. (x) • In 2023, the government of Croatia, which owned a factory that went bankrupt during the pandemic paid severance to the 237 workers who had lost their jobs after the factory went bankrupt which was a result of an Urgent Appeal case. • In 2023, both RWE and Uniper withdrew their ISDS cases against the Netherlands in relation to the decision to phase out coal-fired power generation by 2023. This way, the Netherlands avoids the scenario of having to pay huge compensations for sound and legitimate climate policy. FGG has raised awareness on the risks of these cases through research and media attention and prepared a legal intervention for the RWE case. • In 2023, a Turkish road construction company in Uganda opened a complaints register for persons affected by the project in a district in Northern Uganda, registered their complaints, and put a community social liaison officer to handle them. FGG and community representatives met with the company and local government, undertaken a fact finding mission and shared the results with the company in order to receive grievance and remedy. (x) • In 2023, a mining company in Kenya adopted a comprehensive resettlement program for the community affected by their mining operations and have established and trained their community development agreement committee (CDAC) on their roles, including in relation to gender justice. This was done in response to community advocacy for such measures supported by FGG and partner CSOs. • In 2023, a sugar company in Kenya took a large number of measures to improve working conditions in their sugarcane plantation and factory in Homabay county in Kenya. The measures included reduction of working hours, improved safety measures for workers, gender responsive measures, increasing pay of farmers, hiring of workers from within the community, operational processes to reduce negative environmental impacts of the sugarcane processing (removing of sugarcane waste products, channelling of wastewater). This happened after FGG and partner CSOs shared a report from a corporate audit with the National Environment Management Authority, the local government department of social services, labour office and the company itself. • In 2023, 2 Salt firms operating in coastal Kenya finally opened up roads which they had earlier blocked. This followed a campaign by the community, supported by FGG, for the salt firms to open up all blocked roads to the beach and grazing fields that have been privatized by the salt firms. • In 2023, a mining company in Kenya awarded the Community Development Agreement Committee 63.802 euros as proceeds from the mining in the area. Partner CSOs of FGG have supported the community to advocate for adherence to the Mining Act 2016 provisions on this regard. • In 2023, a granite mining company in Zimbabwean fenced their mining area in response to community, recruited workers from the local community, supported community schools with transportation of children and provided materials to repair houses after community led advocacy talks. FGG supported the community to set up meetings with the company resulting in the company taking their responsibilities. • In 2023, a mining company in Zimbabwe implemented CSR projects in the form of borehole drilling for potable water provision and educational assistance through payment of school fees for children. This happened in response to advocacy by the Women’s Forums in Mutoko. FGG supported the forum through trainings and joint strategising with CSOs. • In 2023, Zimbabwe Miners Federation established a gender desk to make the mining sector in Zimbabwe more inclusive and gender sensitive. The desk was a recommendation which FGG and partners lobbied for. (g) • In 2023, Zimbabwe Miners Federation developed a database to better serve artisanal gemstone miners with access to markets which was a recommendation from FGG and partners. • In 2023, 3 private insuring and banking companies from England and Japan publicly declared their refusal to support the EACOP project and any other related oil initiatives in Uganda. Through their statements they provided pressure on other companies to also withdraw from the EACOP project. FGG provided financial support and jointly strategised with the partners in Uganda that are part of the StopEACOP campaign.

In 2024, FGG aims to contribute to 59 policy changes that are aimed at corporate conduct by governmental institutions in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: The OECD will develop an ambitious climate guidance on climate due diligence including a feminist just transition perspective;In the Dutch national regulation on corporate sustainability due diligence, the Dutch government will include strong wording on climate obligations and the financial sector, and increase possibilities for local communities and environmental and human rights defenders to hold companies accountable; Companies in the energy sector will compensate for community level human rights violations that people are currently facing, and take concrete measures to prevent such violations in the future;Palm oil companies will compensate communities for harm done to them;Mining companies (gypsum, iron, natural stones) will compensate communities affected by their operations and take concrete steps to prevent similar violations in the future;Additional garment brands producing in Bangladesh and Pakistan will sign the International Accord;Garment brands will improve the transparency of their supply chains beyond Tier 1 production, and include information such as sub-contractors and wage data; Garment brands will increase wages in their supply chains;At least two leading energy sector value chain actors will adopt and/or implement FGG policy and practice recommendations by compensating for and preventing community-level violations that people are currently experiencing.

n 2024, FGG contributed to 175 policy and/or practice changes that are aimed at corporate conduct by governmental institutions in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: • In 2024, German companies suspended commercial relations with palm oil companies Industrias Chiquibul and NaturAceites after learning about rights violations committed by these companies against the Q'eqchi' population in the Northern Lowlands of Guatemala. FGG and partners played a pivotal role in facilitating the process by mobilizing communities, building the capacity of local CSOs, engaging relevant stakeholders, and strategically leveraging media. • In 2024, the Ashuganj LNG-Based Power Plant Authority stopped filling the 100-year-old Hafiz Peda's Canal in Kolapara Upazila, a crucial water source for agriculture, irrigation, and household use. This decision averted severe water scarcity, water flow disruption in the Baroikola Canal, and negative impacts on the environment and biodiversity. FGG and partners actively supported the community’s protests against the factory, highlighting issues like abrupt land purchases and pollution. • In 2024, TK Group factory authority installed new machinery to reduce sound pollution and ensured transparency by displaying a citizen charter. Previously, the plywood factory in Bagerhat caused significant environmental and health issues, including high noise levels and uncontrolled wood debris leading to air pollution. • In 2024, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) incorporated CSOs recommendations into its Environmental and Social Framework. Key changes included enhanced transparency, strengthened policy language, a new climate standard, a prohibition on asbestos use, and recognition of informal workers’ rights. FGG and partners contributed to developing the recommendations as part of the CSOs platform led by the NGO Forum on ADB. • In 2024, a major sugar multinational, agreed to implement recommendations such as introducing a tracking system for tractors transporting sugarcane from farmers to the factory—improving post-harvest handling and revenue for small-scale farmers—and competitive employment of locals via localised advertisements. • In 2024, Datuama Artisanal and Small-scale Miners Association in Kenya consented to allow 2 women mining groups to undertake mining activities. This marked progress in advancing women’s economic and empowerment rights. (g) • In 2024, an agricultural company in Uganda made reasonable efforts towards fulfilling the SOPs issued. Families occupying land allocated for large-scale investment were compensated in preparation for relocation, and physical abuse of community members by company agents has ceased. • In 2024, a Kenyan Water Company, in collaboration with the county government, started investing in clean water provision for domestic use in Marereni. The initiative extended the water network to households and supplied free water meters to manage consumption, addressing contamination and compensating the community. This happened after advocacy meetings by community members supported by FGG’s partner. • In 2024, following hydrological and sediment mapping research conducted by FGG partners and local communities, community members took immediate action to rehabilitate the wetland. They implemented recommendations by removing siltation to ensure the free flow of water from the wetland into the Nyongara River. Members of the Friends of Ondiri Wetland Kenya (FOWK) contributed both labour and financial resources toward this community-led initiative. • In September 2024, after extensive advocacy by the Paani (water) committees and FGG partner, the Upazila administration and the Bangladesh Water Development Board provided support, including financial aid, to eradicate severe waterlogging in Tala Upazila. The Youth Paani Committee played a pivotal role by mobilizing local community members to clean four blocked canals. This initiative proved critical, as it addressed the needs of 29,754 households severely impacted by waterlogging. • In 2024, the Bangladesh Agricultural service department, following extensive advocacy by FGG members and partners as well as youth farmer group members for ‘fair pricing’, supported the small-scale farmers to reduce their production costs and mitigate the financial strain caused by the high prices of agricultural inputs. • In 2024, urgent appeals supported by FGG's Urgent Appeal system were successful against 7 garment brands and suppliers from Cambodia, Sri Lanka, India, and Bangladesh. • In 2024, 6 garment brands signed the Transparency Pledge and began fully disclosing their production sites. Notably, one brand extended its disclosed data up to Tier 4, covering the sourcing of raw materials. FGG continued to lead efforts to enhance transparency in supply chains by directly lobbying brands and collaborating with other key actors in the field of supply chain transparency. • In 2024, 140 additional garment brands signed the International Accord on Health and Safety in the Textile and Garment Industry, raising the total number of participating brands from 101 to 251. • In 2024, signatories to at least one of the two country programmes under the International Accord increased significantly. The Bangladesh programme saw an increase from 89 to 212 signatories, while the Pakistan programme grew from 93 to 129. The Accord complaints mechanism also extended its coverage to include all forms of gender-based violence, harassment, and discrimination (g). • In 2024, 6 garment factories in Bangladesh dropped charges against hundreds of workers and peaceful protesters who had faced charges following mass protests during the national wage-revision process. This outcome was a result of lobbying and campaigning efforts by FGG and its partners. • In 2024, two major oil companies decided not to proceed with oil exploration and exploitation in the Amazon region of Tariquia in Bolivia. This decision was made in response to requests from local communities and the broader network opposing these projects. FGG consistently provided strategic and financial support to local CSOs and the wider network advocating for this outcome. • In March 2024, the Indonesian Constitutional Court refused to lift the ban on mining in coastal areas and small islands requested by the nickel company operating in Wawonii Island, Southeast Sulawesi, PT Gema Kreasi Perdana. In late 2023, an FGG partner in Indonesia alerted FGG to this legal challenge and requested urgent support to establish a group of supportive lawyers, conduct press events and other public campaign activities, and prepare legal interventions highlighting the impacts of nickel mining on small-scale fishers and biodiversity.

In 2025, FGG aims to contribute to 70 policy changes that are aimed at corporate conduct by governmental institutions in line with FGG recommendations to advance fair and green value chains (i.e. laws, policies being blocked, adopted or improved) for sustainable and inclusive development. These include: • In Uganda, an investor will implement FGG recommendations on land resettlement to residents, on compensation for all residents affected by the project and on labour opportunities for residents. • Additional garment brands will sign the International Accord and brands will include a ‘non-RMG factories’ in the Accord programme. • Garment brands and/or factory owners will meet the demands of FGG and its partners on an urgent appeal case in providing remedy. • Garment brands will improve the transparency of their supply chain (including wage data). • Dutch companies and/or financial institutions have adopted a Climate Transition plan that is in line with the 1.5 degrees Paris Agreement.

comment.narrative: In 2021, FGG aims for 58 key actors to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that corporations and other private sector actors (including financiers/banks) act to respect human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability in their value chains. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)

In 2022, FGG aims for 33 key actors to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that corporations and other private sector actors (including financiers/banks) act to respect human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability in their value chains. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)

In 2022, 12 key actors supported and/or promoted FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that corporations and other private sector actors (including financiers/banks) act to respect human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability in their value chains.

In 2023, FGG aims for 32 key actors to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at assuring that corporations and other private sector actors (including financiers/banks) act to respect human rights, women’s rights and environmental sustainability in their value chains. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)

In 2023, 35 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments, international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations supported and/or promoted FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved corporate conduct. • In 2023, 2 garment brands made public statements on the demands of trade unions in Bangladesh for the revision of the national minimum wage for garment workers. FGG lobbied at these brands directly as well as through stakeholder meeting participation. • In 2023, the Asus group in Taiwan recognized the establishment of a Filipino migrant workers union, a member of GoodElectronics, hosted by FGG, played a crucial role in assisting a group of Filipino migrant workers and successfully negotiated the recognition of the union with the companies management. GoodElectronics intend to replicate this success in further organising efforts among other migrant worker groups. • In 2023, 10 Dutch companies signed the renewable energy agreement in which they specifically also commit to do gender responsible due diligence in their supply chains. FGG provided concrete recommendations to the agreement to make sure that it was gender responsive based on research done by FGG. (g) • In 2023, 19 high level representatives of 19 private companies and energy sector value chain actors (including solar energy companies and a major bank) in Bangladesh during various sessions at the Bangladesh energy Prosperity 2050 conference, made statements committing to increasing investment in renewable energy for a green transition, while urging the government departments to regulate the transition in a just manner. This was a result of continuous advocacy by FGG and partners over the past years at the companies in question. • In 2023, a Turkish road construction company in Uganda has committed to drawing a restoration plan to rehabilitate the land that has been affected by their road construction project at the project completion. FGG has supported the affected community to meet with the district government and the company to present and advocate for their asks. • In 2023, a major power plant authority in Bangladesh has initiated a scholarship program for 30 students of Matarbari and Dholghat as a form of community support. This happened as a result of sustained advocacy by the community supported by AA and partner over the past years. AA and partner have lobbied and advocated with the power plant authority for compensation to the affected families and compensation for loss of livelihood of the community members. In response the authority provided the scholarship while other demands remains unfulfilled. • In 2023, a granite mining company in Zimbabwe agreed to adopt the Grievance Redress Mechanism, which they are still harmonising with the internal operational procedures they have in place to deal with complaints. FGG, through a partner CSO developed a model GRM and shared it with various granite mining companies whilst advocating for adoption. (x)

In 2024, FGG aims for 11 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Brazil, Mexico, Thailand), international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved corporate conduct. FGG’s aim for 2024 is to improve government policies on among other things, the following: Garment brands and/or multi-stakeholder initiatives use their leverage in favour of the wage demands from independent local trade unions in Asian countries;Leading energy sector stakeholders will support recommendations on Renewable Energy (RE) expansion and RE based livelihood solutions for women’s equitable access to RE to ensure gender justice in Bangladesh; Private sector actors in the Philippines adhere to FPIC processes on their projects and investments. National market players in the granite and gemstones sector support fair and green trade, and decent work for women through supporting and promoting gemstone trade, export and marketing that enables locals to benefit from gemstone mining;Zimbabwe Miners Federation will work with Trade Unions to assist its members to promote decent work for women through responsible mining and sustainability, they will be part of the campaign on Gemstone export and marketing to encourage locals to benefit from gemstone mining.

In 2024, 7 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Brazil, Mexico, Thailand), international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations supported and/or promoted FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved corporate conduct. • In 2024, RSPO in Guatemala audited a palm oil company and suspended the certification for three plants producing palm oil. The audit revealed five major non-conformities related to land, water pollution, labour rights, and social conflict. While the exact findings were not disclosed transparently, this suspension is significant as it confirms violations, discrediting the companies’ claim of being the second most "green" company in the country. FGG contributed to the report which showcased the human right violations for the German due diligence law. Based on this information, RSPO investigated the case. • In 2024, a palm oil company in Guatemala donated land to the municipality of Sayaxché Petén, enabling community transit without restrictions. The community must secure financing to construct the road, and the agreement has yet to be implemented. This ‘donations’ is a result after years of advocacy by the community, supported by FGG, as the community was fully enclosed by the plantation and a large river. • In 2024, 2 mining companies in Kenya agreed to conduct capacity-building sessions for women and youth artisanal miners on value addition. This initiative aims to foster inclusive development by involving mining communities in sustainable resource extraction, economic growth, and livelihood enhancement for women (g). • In 2024, a major international bike and bike accessories manufacturer hosted a multi-stakeholder roundtable discussion on gender-responsive human rights due diligence implementation by companies in the e-bike industry. The discussion particularly focused on mineral supply chains in e-bike batteries, with big companies participating. The event, featuring speakers from FGG, IMVO-Steunpunt, and Fairphone, showcased the industry's support for addressing this issue (g). • In 2024, Defold Mine granted mining permits and lowered fees within the Exclusive Prospecting Orders. This adjustment has allowed most women miners in Hurungwe to apply for permits while affording lower fees for gemstone mining. FGG partners assisted in the negotiations and further advocated for reduction of fees which were a hinderance to most women miners. (g) • In 2024, a Business coalition at the OECD collaborated with OECD Watch to draft a joint statement advocating for stronger performance of NCPs in promoting the OECD Guidelines and handling complaints. OECD Watch led its business and union counterparts, including Business at OECD and the Trade Union Advisory Committee, in submitting the statement to the OECD Secretary-General and Ministerial Counsel. The joint submission outlined shared priorities for enhancing NCP performance and promoting effective due diligence practices.

In 2025, FGG aims for 9 key actors such as (policymakers within) national governments (e.g. Brazil, Colombia, Thailand), international and multilateral organisations (EU, UN, World Bank) and corporations to support and/or promote FGG policy/practice recommendations aimed at improved corporate conduct. FGG’s aim for 2025 is to improve government policies on among other things, the following: • Value chain actors in the power and energy sector will support our recommendations on capacity building and inclusion of women and youth in the development projects in Bangladesh. • Garment brands and/or multi-stakeholder Initiatives (MSIs) publicly support and use their leverage to promote the wage demands from independent local trade unions in Asian countries. • A Colombian fuel company endorses FGG’s vision on a Just Energy Transition.

In 2024, 533 CSO actors lobbied and advocated for improved policies and practices in trade and value chains and advance fair and green practices based on capacities mutually developed. Trade & investment agreements • In 2024, 2 CSOs from Uganda and Kenya, raised awareness about the harmful impacts of the Energy Charter Treaty and other IIAs during public events organised in both countries, in collaboration with FGG alliance and other partners. FGG supported these events through joint strategising and activity funding. • In 2024, through joint advocacy campaigns targeting insurers and brokers of Total Energies under the global-to-local and local-to-global campaign strategy, the number of publicly declared financial institutions and reinsurances rejecting the East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) rose from 27 to 34. • In August 2024, 1 CSO in Ghana launched a storytelling campaign to amplify the voices of local communities impacted by fossil fuel projects. The campaign used social media toolkits, infographics, and video testimonials to highlight the socio-economic and environmental effects of fossil fuel financing on local communities. • In 2024, a CSO led efforts to introduce the Green 2024 Political Manifesto, advocating for socially owned, climate-safe, and equitable energy systems. This initiative emphasized halting high-risk projects like the Keta Delta Oil Block and prioritizing renewable energy investments benefiting local populations. • In 2024, advocacy efforts in Togo focused on the adoption of environmental standards and regulations within export credit agencies (ECAs), pushing for mandatory CO2 emission reductions and environmental impact assessments as key financing criteria. • In November 2024, four CSOs in Indonesia, as part of the Indonesian Justice Coalition, lobbied government officials for greater transparency in trade agreements, demanded participation in the Indonesia-EU CEPA negotiations to ensure socio-economic impact assessments, and raised concerns about economic justice in the European Parliament. These efforts were amplified through public awareness campaigns, open letters, meetings with policymakers, and collaborations with international advocacy networks. • In November 2024, three CSOs, with FGG’s support, convened the Civil Society Forum on Aligning Investment Policy Frameworks to Climate and SDGs in Entebbe, Uganda. This forum challenged outdated Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs) that limit Africa’s sustainable development policy space. The conference resulted in the drafting of the Entebbe Declaration on Reclaiming Investment Frameworks for the people and the planet. • In October 2024, 1 CSO from Uganda led discussions at the 6th Annual Business and Human Rights Symposium, advocating for corporate sustainability due diligence and access to EU markets. This engagement influenced policymakers to integrate human rights due diligence standards into Uganda’s National Action Plan on Business and Human Rights (also for 5). • In 2024, a CSO from Uganda played a key role in influencing stakeholders to establish the Investment Core Group, a coalition of CSOs focused on ensuring investments contribute to sustainable development and local community benefits. This was achieved through meetings and public calls for policies aligned with human and environmental justice, including advocating for a review of the Uganda Investment Code Act (2019). • In 2024, 15 CSOs in Mexico campaigned against trade agreements and corporate impunity, engaging with Mexican and EU authorities on human rights clauses in trade agreements. They organized the International Seminar on Free Trade Impacts, with a focus on women’s resistance, and produced reports and materials on free trade’s effects on local communities. Public awareness was promoted through social media and publications (g). • In 2024, one CSO in Kenya disseminated knowledge at the 15th Association for Women’s Rights in Development (AWID) International Forum in Bangkok, Thailand. This initiative built the capacity of over 100 CSOs on trade and feminism, connecting trade to feminist issues such as post-conflict recovery, migration, and climate. • In 2024, Gender and Trade Coalition members facilitated the Financing for Development (FfD) Trade workstream at the Fourth International Conference on FfD (FfD4), leveraging their technical expertise and networking skills to advance advocacy efforts. • In 2024, 11 CSOs globally expanded alliances to resist harmful free trade and investment treaties. This included engaging grassroots organizations in Africa opposing clauses in the AfCFTA, strengthening ties with Latin American networks fighting the EU-Mercosur trade deal, and supporting European advocacy against the Energy Charter Treaty and FTAs. • In 2024, four CSOs in Brazil enhanced feminist political advocacy strategies and strengthened intersectional approaches to foreign policy. This was achieved through collaboration between civil society and government institutions during a panel organized at the FFP event in Mexico, where FGG presented their 2023 work on FFP. • In 2024, 26 CSOs denounced non-compliance with environmental and labour commitments under the EU-Andean Countries FTA. These efforts involved workshops, digital campaigns, and meetings with policymakers to address the issue. • In 2024, 29 members of the Tanzanian Trade and Investment Coalition used their knowledge of BITs to train government officials in identifying opportunities to stop or renegotiate Tanzanian BITs. This capacity-building process was facilitated through workshops, interviews, and meetings. • In 2024, 2 CSOs strengthened their lobby and advocacy towards WTO as part of the Our World is Not For Sale Network. FGG participated as a civil society representative at the 13th Ministerial Conference of the WTO. FGG and the OWINS network advocated against harmful international agreements on digitalisation in agriculture and e-commerce. • Throughout 2024, FGG continued its advocacy efforts at the European Commission, focusing on the environmental and social challenges linked to EU-Mercosur agreements. This advocacy work contributed to sustainability and human rights issues gaining a more prominent position in trade and investment negotiations. FGG supported these efforts by facilitating access to decision-makers and media outlets, presenting evidence and research on impacts, and developing coordinated messages and joint activities. • In 2024, FGG co-organized a speakers' tour with 2 representatives from an FGG partner in Mozambique and a journalist who documented the impacts of LNG projects in Mozambique. The tour included stops in Brussels, the Netherlands, France, and Germany, bringing concerns about LNG projects conducted by EU-based companies and the financial involvement of EU private and public financiers directly to EU stakeholders. These concerns encompassed human rights violations, forced resettlements, economic impacts, deforestation, climate change effects, lack of democracy, and unbalanced economic repercussions. • In 2024, 25 CSOs from Malaysia increased their knowledge about waste-to-energy (WtE) incineration during a symposium that provided situational analysis and capacity-building to debunk the Malaysian government’s proposal to construct 18 WtEs. FGG provided financial support for the symposium.
