It mobilized the indigenous food sovereignty movement to resist policies and laws harming indigenous rights and livelihoods. (g + x) • In 2024, a CSO partner in Indonesia organised a youth jamboree themed “GenZMile United for Identity and Local Food Sovereignty,” which enhanced young people’s capacities to actively protect the environment, preserve local culture, and promote food sovereignty. Participants deepened their understanding of cultural identity and learned their roles in building food security and supporting community-based economic independence. They also engaged in lobbying with government institutions and local organisations to foster collaboration across sectors. FGG supported this initiative through small grants. • In 2024, IP partners in the Philippines identified recommendations for promoting traditional and local food systems. They assessed local food production and supply, highlighted unique local produce, and identified challenges faced by farmers and IP communities. Key action points included capacity building for seed banking, establishing trial farms, food documentation, business planning, and strengthening local food systems. Advocacy focused on government support and integrating local cuisine into ecotourism. These recommendations were designed to become agenda points for discussions with the Department of Agriculture (DA). FGG facilitated networking and event organisation to support these initiatives. • In 2024, an academe partner in Indonesia, building on a youth food systems dialogue initiated in 2023, facilitated a national workshop on promoting Local Knowledge for Sustainable Food Systems. This effort expanded networks among CSOs, academies, and youth across cities and provinces, focusing on reviving sustainable food systems and passing traditional wisdom to younger generations. Key actors from the ministry were invited as resource speakers during the workshop. FGG supported this through small grants. • In 2024, 1 CSOs from Colombia strengthened their lobby and advocacy right to lobby for the recognition of indigenous and farmers rights of traditional medicinal plants in various UN drug policy declarations and resolutions. FGG provided support in co-organising lobby activities. • 7 international and regional food sovereignty organisations came together to support the international Planning Committee for Food Sovereignty (IPC) - an autonomous and self-organised global platform of small-scale food producers, rural workers organisations and grassroots/community-based social movements, representing 300 million small-scale food producers in every region of the world, organised into 6000 local and national organisations - under the facilitation committee to agree on the process for the Nyeleni Global Gathering. FGG provides critical analysis and technical expertise to support these organisations’ capacities in strategy development to prepare for the Nyeleni Global Gathering. In 2024 this included advocating through the FAO regional CSO consultation processes. • In 2024, one CSO from Uganda used its position paper on the inclusion of agroecology in the formulation of a food and agriculture policy as an engagement tool to work with both collaborators and policymakers. This led to policy recommendations on incorporating agroecology aspects into Uganda’s food and nutrition policy. Two high-level policy dialogues were held on the creation of a comprehensive food and nutrition policy that upholds agroecology and seed equity principles. • In 2024, one CSO conducted two high-level policy dialogues with policymakers regarding the development of a comprehensive food and agriculture policy, focusing on the integration of agroecology and seed equity aspects in the national framework. • In 2024, one CSO facilitated a two-day strategic planning training for an alliance of over fifty female led community based groups in Liberia, also helping to develop a five-year strategic plan for the women-led advocacy and campaign group. FGG supported this training session financially. • In 2024, one CSO documented the successes and strengths of farmer-managed seed systems in Kenya. This documentation serves as the foundation for lobbying and advocacy efforts directed at the Kenyan government and the Dutch Embassy in Kenya. FGG provided both expertise and financial support for this initiative. • In 2024, one CSO from Uganda developed a position paper on the inclusion of agroecology aspects in the formulation of Uganda’s food and agriculture policy. FGG supported the development of the paper through expertise and guidance. The finalised position paper was used as an engagement tool for both collaborators and policymakers, providing recommendations on integrating agroecology into Uganda’s food and nutrition policy. Fair and green systems; energy, water, other public goods and services • In 2024, 3 CSOs from Bangladesh, 2 large national-level CSO platforms, and the largest consumer association in the country presented a 14-point citizen demand advocating for a shift to renewable energy and publicly called for Bangladesh’s adoption of a CSO-proposed National Energy Transition Policy. FRR and its partner facilitated the formation and setup of the platforms and the drafting of the proposed policy in 2022. • In 2024, 1 CSO from Kenya advocated for the county government to allocate funding for the provision of clean drinking water in salt-mining-affected communities. FGG supported this initiative through funding. • In 2024, 3 CSOs from Guatemala lobbied municipal authorities for the approval of political agreements on inclusive water management, taking into account the needs of indigenous populations and women. FGG’s partner participated in discussions with local authorities and other partners. (g) • In 2024, 6 CSOs from Guatemala lobbied the new government during discussions about the proposed water law in Guatemala. FGG brought these partners together to strengthen their capacity and strategise collectively. • In 2024, five FGG partners from Brazil and Kenya advocated for transformative water governance, rooted in the principles of the Transformative Water Pact (TWP), during two public webinars attended by 140 participants. These webinars highlighted local struggles and their connection to the TWP, with a particular focus on the gendered dimensions of transformative water governance (g). • In 2024, one FGG partner in Colombia championed transformative water governance and the Transformative Water Pact (TWP) by coordinating and moderating two public webinars, which were attended by 140 participants. • In 2024, 7 CSOs from Myanmar strengthened their network and shared advocacy efforts by developing a strategic plan and initiating dialogues among members. This resulted in improved relationships, facilitated discussions on collaborations, and updates on ongoing projects. A first round of small grant support enabled member organisations to further strengthen their initiatives and create opportunities for young migrants affected by mandatory military service. FGG provided coordination and small grants to support these efforts. (x)

In 2025, 271 CSO actors will lobby and advocate for improved policies and practices in trade and value chains and advance fair and green practices based on capacities mutually developed. In 2025, FGG partners and members will advocate for among other things the following: Trade & investment agreements • For transparency and civil society participation in decision making, drafting and negotiation processes in relation to international trade and investment treaties • An ambitious UN Global Plastics Treaty and calling for a swift national level ratification of the Treaty. Tenure policies • Community land rights in the Ugandan context of forced displacement linked to large scale plantations (e.g. sugarcane, coffee) and a fair compensation and resettlement in cases of land grab and forced displacement as well as application of the Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) principle in large scale land acquisition processes • The restitution of ndigenous land rights affected by the operations of nickel mining corporations in Guatemala. • On the destructive effects of dredging projects supported by Dutch ECIs. • The recognition of indigenous land rights and indigenous natural resource management in Cambodia. Climate and environmental policies • A joint campaign towards the UNFCCC COP30 against false solutions to the climate crisis including carbon markets, net zero and NBS and an ambitious outcome of COP30 including an international climate duty for business. • To resist the inclusion of false solutions and corporate influence in national biodiversity policy laws in Latin America. Public financial institutions • Negotiate a responsible exit from Barro Blanco by FMO and monitor agreements already made. • CSOs use their strengthened lobby and advocacy skills to support communities in Senegal affected by mega IFI projects to achieve justice and remedy. Rules for business and corporate conduct, cross-sectoral • CSOs in countries such as Bangladesh, Guatemala, Kenya, Uganda and Zimbabwe engage in advocacy at country and global level to promote a feminist UN Binding Treaty on Transnational Corporations and human rights. • CSOs campaigning for corporate accountability legislation in non-EU countries are on course to get legislation passed in their jurisdictions. • Workers, trade unions, and/or communities are able to leverage corporate accountability laws to their advantage, e.g. by having access to relevant information that helps them to identify which companies will have to comply with the CSDDD. • For companies to take their responsibility for corporate-related human rights abuses through filing / pursuing an OECD Guidelines complaint, and/or have dialogues with the OECD, NCPs and governments regarding strong implementation of the OECD Guidelines. Rules for business and corporate conduct, extractives sector • Fair mining practices, safeguarding human rights in the operations of extractives companies, rights of (women) artisanal miners, support to miners' associations to safeguard rights of workers in the mining sector and artisanal miners in Zimbabwe. • Demand the State of Guatemala to respond to the consultation process with indigenous peoples regarding mining licenses for nickel mining companies operating in their territory and to end the criminalization of human rights defenders. • To advocate against the auction of ‘oil exploration blocks’ which will inter alia affect fishing territories in Brazil. Rules for business and corporate conduct, garment sector • Closely monitor the RMG Sustainability Council, the body implementing the Accord in Bangladesh, and push for compliance in any areas or instances where any parameters of the Accord programme (inspections, remediation etc.) are not fulfilled. • Lobby global unions on the governance of the RSC towards less employer influence over implementation mechanisms. • Lobby the Accord for the optimal implementation in Pakistan with regard to remediation, complaints mechanisms and governance and engage in media outreach and informing the general public about the importance of the Accord. • Through CCC’s Urgent Appeal structure and systems, actively lobby and negotiate with garment brands and factory owners, as well as campaign publicly, to remedy labour rights violations pertaining to employment relations, payment and compensation, labour practices, freedom of association, worker health and safety, gender-based violence and the protection of labour rights defenders. • Lobby national and EU policy makers on shrinking civic space in the garment sector. Rules for business and corporate conduct, tech sector • Fair and equitable digital trade rules regarding cross-border data flows, source code disclosure and tariffs on electronic transmissions, policy inputs and interventions into bilateral trade negotiations. Fair and green systems, agroecology • Lobby national governments for policies that support agroecology and food sovereignty. • Land rights advocacy and expanding youth leadership in agro-ecological practices with strong women’s rights angles and focus on youth leadership in Brazil. Fair and green systems; energy, water, other public goods and services • A comprehensive and equitable energy transition in Bangladesh. The focus will be on reforming the energy sector to ensure transparency, accountability, and sustainability, while prioritizing the protection of community rights and environmental preservation. • In Asia, CSOs will advocate for community owned renewable energy towards their government, on the basis of enhanced knowledge capacities, brought through engagement in a community-level solar energy pilot project.

description.narrative: strengthened capacities
# targeted civil society actors with strengthened capacities for lobbying and advocacy

comment.narrative: In 2021, FGG aims to support 659 targeted civil society actors to strengthen their capacities for lobbying and advocacy. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)
In 2021, FGG supported 591 targeted civil society actors to strengthen their capacities for lobbying and advocacy.

In 2022, FGG aims to support 445 targeted civil society actors to strengthen their capacities for lobbying and advocacy. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)
In 2022, FGG supported 926 targeted civil society actors to strengthen their capacities for lobbying and advocacy.

In 2023, FGG aims to support 514 targeted civil society actors to strengthen their capacities for lobbying and advocacy. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)

In 2023 the FGG programme has strengthened the lobby and advocacy capacity of 960 CSO actors. These actors are based in different places around the world, including but not limited to Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Costa Rica, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Liberia, Mozambique, Nigeria, the Philippines, South Africa and Uganda. Trade and investment agreements • In 2023, 20 CSOs from the Global South developed a clear vision, a set of principles and proposals for implementing a feminist lens across various aspects of foreign policy, including security, trade and investment, tax, diplomacy and international cooperation. FGG, in collaboration with global South partner organisations, went through a collective envisioning exercise of what a feminist future could look like. Collectively, FGG Alliance members shared their own grassroots’ and community experiences of the impact of trade and investment policies on their lives, and translated those experiences into a vision and a set of principles, as well as evidence-based proposals and recommendations for policy-making. FGG summarized this vision in the publication ‘Re-imagining Trade and Investment through a Feminist Lens’. In this publication FGG advocates for a more transformative approach. • In 2023, 1 CSO civil society platform comprising 18 organisations from Kenya increased their knowledge on the Energy Charter Treaty (ECT) and its impacts. FGG organized a training and awareness raising workshop on the risks of the ECT as a basis for future broader advocacy against Kenya’s accession to the ECT. • In 2023, 7 CSOs from Kenya increased their knowledge when attending an interactive webinar for Kenyan CSOs to inform them about the process around Dutch BITs. FGG organized a webinar on the topic as a response to a request of the Kenyan CSOs. • In 2023, 11 CSOs from South East Africa, Asia and Latin America strengthened their knowledge and advocacy skills for a Feminist Just Energy Transition during a jointly organized conference where they strategised, shared experiences, knowledge and developed a shared narrative for a Feminist Just Energy Transition. The goal of the conference was to come up with locally driven principles on what a feminist just transition is, why it is important and what it should entail. FGG funded the participation of the CSOs and networks to this conference. (g) • In 2023, 2 CSOs from Brazil and Uruguay strengthened their knowledge, research, lobby and advocacy skills on trade agreements, deforestation, climate change and human rights issues. FGG provided financial support as well as support with media and press releases and reports in relation to the EU/Mercosur. • Throughout 2023, a total of 12 partners in Tanzania strengthened their lobby and advocacy capacity in relation to Bilateral Investment Treaties and its harmful clauses to sustainable development, human rights and the environment. Through technical expertise and financial support from FGG, the partners also learned how to raise more awareness on the topic on their websites as well as generating media attention. • Throughout 2023, partners active in 9 different regional and international networks from Africa and Asia strengthened their knowledge on trade and the intersections of gender with the mineral economy, militarisation, corporate accountability, climate and agriculture by having internal discussion and find ways to collaborate in order to strengthen their lobby and advocacy activities. FGG supported the partners by linking the partners with the networks, sharing networking expertise and providing financial support. (g) • Throughout 2023, 5 partners from Uganda and Zimbabwe strengthened their lobby and advocacy capacity in relation to trade policy in land rights. Through research and disseminated learning materials the CSOs deepened their knowledge on their land rights and the accountability of investors. FGG supported these partners both financially as well as technically through webinars, meetings and content preparations. • In 2023, through their network 3 partners active in Thailand, Morocco, Brazil, Indonesia, Argentina, Uruguay, Uganda and Zimbabwe , build their knowledge on women’s rights and strengthened their lobby and advocacy skills on how to demand 1for women’s voices to be included in the processes of policy making on trade agreements. These partners organised strategic meetings and prepared articles and position papers on trade and investment and its consequences to women’s rights. FGG supported financially as well as providing technical support (g). • In 2023, 6 partners from Peru, Brazil, Uganda, Tanzania, Indonesia and Mexico, strengthened their lobby and advocacy skills in demanding a seat at the table and expressing their views on their national trade policy. Partners, with support of FGG, organised meetings, monitored governments trade and investment policies and demanded civil society participation in policy space at different national, regional and local levels. (x) • Throughout 2023, 4 partners from Ghana, Togo and Uganda strengthened their network by participating in 29 strategy and network-building meetings as well as joint actions during the Global Day of Action against Chinese investments on 20 November 2023. The partners organised two online dialogues for CSOs and local communities focusing on decarbonizing ECAs in Africa in which over 350 community members from oil and gas affected towns joined. FGG provided knowledge on ECAs and supported in developing advocacy strategies as well as financial support. • In 2023, 1 partner in Argentina strengthened its advocacy skills on ECA support for lithium projects in Argentina as well as their knowledge on a just energy transition. The civic space in Argentina is shrinking with the outcome of the recent elections, FGG is supporting the partner to find suitable routes to voice its message to a wider public as well as providing knowledge on ECAs and developing advocacy strategies. • In 2023, 14 CSOs from Indonesia increased their knowledge, advocacy and expanded their international network by taking part in the Indonesian Economic Justice coalition. FGG supports this coalition and works bilaterally with its members both through financial and technical support and with organizing campaigns and events such as the 2nd social forum on mining in Indonesia. • In 2023, 5 CSOs from Tanzania, Bangladesh, Nigeria and Kenya increased their knowledge on the Energy Charter Treaty expansion. FGG supported these CSOs with their campaigns around ECT expansion both nationally and regionally, and provided financial and technical support to partners. • In 2023, 17 CSOs from Latin America strengthened their lobby and advocacy skills and their networks on free trade agreements and ISDS in Latin America. FGG supported the CSOs financially, providing technical support and co-organising activities. Climate and environmental policies • Throughout 2023, 15 CSOs, of which 4 from the Global South strengthened their lobby and advocacy capacity through joining the Just Energy Transition Coalition, focusing on the litigation of the renewable energy sector and irresponsible disengagement by the fossil fuel companies. FGG mobilised the CSOs and is facilitating the conversations, building alliances and enhancing the advocacy capacity of the CSOs. • In October 2023, the ‘Transition Minerals’ network was established, in which 42 CSOs joined, during the 2nd Global TSF Mining and Extractive Economy conference in Indonesia. During the conference a workshop was organized by London Mining Network and FGG to discuss the potential for a global campaign on transition minerals. Participants identified the need for improved information-sharing among communities, increased research and documentation of impacts and continued advocacy through the ‘ Right to Say No’ campaign. Following the workshop, a network dedicated to transition minerals was formed with subsequent regular meetings focusing on further developing global campaign strategy. • In 2023, 2 networks of CSOs increased their knowledge on accessing climate financing and on inclusive development and leadership in a training session financially supported by FGG. • In 2023, 1 CSO from Togo , strengthened its capacity to do research on climate change, sea level rise as well as on their networking skills and advocacy skills. FGG supported them financially and through online capacity building meetings. • In 2023, 2 CSOs from the Philippines strengthened their knowledge and skills in sustaining and expanding forest restoration initiatives using indigenous tree species and built broader constituencies among the youth within their ancestral domains by initiating their own community gatherings (nokens). FGG supported and accompanied these youth groups with their organizational development and leadership formation as well as community organizing. • In 2023, 4 CSOs from the Philippines strengthened their lobby and advocacy capacity through participating in a National Consultation of Women Environmental Defenders (WEHRDs). This served as a platform for WEHRDs to present their environmental and human rights messages to government agencies, other CSOs and policymakers. FGG supported these CSOs technically by jointly formulating their messages which their communities are confronted with -like FPIC violations, conflicts caused by overlapping of tenurial instruments and are urging government agencies to have more genuine responses to their issues. It is an initiative to provide support to women defenders in advancing women’s empowerment and leadership capacities to be able to engage in meaningful and unique opportunities. (x) • In 2023, 1 CSO from Thailand supported the participation of four Indigenous People (IP) member organisations from Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Philippines, Vietnam and Thailand during the 2023 Asia Preparatory Meeting on UN Mechanisms and Procedures Relating to Indigenous Peoples, particularly the UNPFII, the EMRIP, SDGs, the WCIP and enhanced participation, treaty and charter based monitoring mechanisms and the Business and Human Rights Related Process. This is significant because this has resulted in producing concrete plans for engaging with the UN mechanisms and procedures. FGG contributed to this initiative through its small grants. (x) • In 2023, 9 CSOs from Africa, Asia and Latin America increased their knowledge and skills to engage in debates on the topic of carbon border tariffs and taxes. FGG organised a webinar on this topic in which the CSOs actively participated. • In 2023, 4 CSOs from Mozambique, Philippines, Georgia and Sri Lanka increased their knowledge on climate litigation through organized a webinar. FGG further supported this area of work through communications and facilitation of joint strategising. • In 2024, 1 network from Asia , strengthened their network and lobby and advocacy skills during a training for human and environmental activists. Two cases were highlighted in which they specifically focused on the gendered impact and emphasized amplifying the voices of women. FGG supported the network financially and with their organisational capacity.(g) • In 2023, 14 CSOs from Africa, Asia and Latin America , strengthened their lobby and advocacy skills in their preparation to participate at UNFCCC COP28. FGG supported the delegation with developing a COP28 strategy and a communication plan through a process that included consultation with representatives from all regions. FGG’s COP28 demands included civil society access demands and a feminist just transition (g and x). • In 2023, 32 CSOs from Africa and Asia strengthened their knowledge and advocacy skills on false climate solutions such as engineering, nature-based solutions and carbon markets. FGG conducted 3 training on false climate solutions and hosted a global online training as well as developed a toolkit for fighting false climate solutions, which includes a case that shows how women are affected more by false climate solutions. FGG also organized an information and skill share with FoEI member groups and allies during the FoEI Biennial General Meeting in November 2023 (g). • In 2023, 5 CSOs from Malaysia strengthened their knowledge and advocacy capacity to lobby against policies and legislation in Sarawak that promote false climate solutions, in particular on carbon markets and carbon capture and storage. FGG supported financially. • In 2023, 1 CSO from Malaysia , increased its knowledge on the intersection between false climate solutions and gender justice. FGG provided financial support to participate in a climate change and women stakeholder consultation arranged by a youth-led climate justice and feminist organisation in Malaysia. (g). • In 2023, 3 CSOs from Asia and Latin America increased their knowledge on a feminist and just energy transition by participating in a Feminist Just Energy Transition (JET) conference in which a core set of principles and demands for a feminist just energy transition was agreed upon by feminist activists from over 15 countries. FGG supported the CSOs financially to participate in the conference. (g) • In 2023, 6 CSOs from strengthened their lobby and advocacy skills as well as expansion of their networks by developing a joint plan to push for wetlands protection. FGG provided financial support to the CSOs to visit the wetland areas and convene discussions among the CSOs to raise awareness of the importance of these ecosystems and the need for a legal framework to protect them. • In 2023, 2 CSOs from Ecuador and the Philippines strengthened their lobby and advocacy capacity to put forward demands for climate justice, especially in relation to oil spills and land grabbing, and to demand justice for environmental human rights defenders at the international level by connecting with other CSOs in Europe that work with key institutions such as the European Parliament and justice court. FGG support this through its Internationalist Solidarity System by jointly strategised through online meetings, developing joint plans for 2024 and providing security training and recommendations for security measures. (x) • In September 2023, 7 CSOs from Asia Pacific, increased their knowledge and shared experiences on forest and biodiversity conservation, human rights and community rights in forest management. FGG organised a webinar on destruction of forest and biodiversity and human rights violations within the Asia-Pacific region. (x) • In October 2023, 6 CSOs from Latin America increased their knowledge on human rights and TNCs during a webinar, organized by FGG partner internationalist solidarity system team, entitled: How Transnational corporations act in violation of people’s rights and their human rights. Key cases and strategies were shared and discussed (x) • In November 2023, 23 CSOs from Asia-Pacific, Africa and Latin America strengthened their knowledge on how to respond to environmental human rights violations during face-to-face Biennial General Assembly in New Orleans in which over 40 FGG groups participated about the work of the International Solidarity System. FGG supported with organization, facilitation and financially.Policies on tenure • In 2023, 2 CSOs from Guatemala increased their knowledge on the gendered division of natural resources (such as land and water) and to identify the extent of access to water. During a training organized by FGG the CSOs were trained in participatory cartography as this shows the division of the natural resources. (g) • In 2023, 118 CSOs from Bangladesh strengthened their lobby and advocacy skills in order to lobby for a just energy transition. FGG organized national and international workshops and conferences, capacity building trainings and community issue-based courtyard meetings to increase the knowledge of these CSOs on topics such as Women’s Rights Fossil Fuels, Renewable Energy, Environmental Justice, gendered impact of mega developments projects but also skills to mobilize, demonstration and campaigning events. (x + g). • In 2023, 30 CSOs from Uganda increased their knowledge and advocacy skills on topics such as land and tenure rights, human rights frameworks, government obligations in relation to human rights, women’s land rights and freedom of expression as well as documentation, basic legal advisory skills and mobilizing and organizing. FGG supported through training, joint learning and exchanges between communities, activist groups and HRDs. (g + x) • In 2023, 5 CSOs in Kenya increased their knowledge and advocacy skills with tolls and frameworks to lobby for business and human rights and climate justice in order to address land grabs, environmental and health concerns, gender justice and workers rights in relation to mining operations, sugarcane plantations and sisal plantations. FGG organized the training and workshops. (g + x). • In 2023, 1 CSO from Kenya strengthened advocacy skills to discuss the grab of community land in the Yala Swamp by a sugarcane multinational with the governor and request this support. FGG supported with joint strategising. • In 2023, 7 CSOs from Kenya increased their knowledge on women and widows rights, land rights and matrimonial property rights. FGG organized multiple awareness raising and training sessions. (g) • In 2023, 3 CSOs from the Philippines increased their capacities in organizational development by developing a mission and vision and formulating strategic plans based on the needs of their communities around land ownership and self-determination through facilitation from FGG. Crafting these elements for an organization is important as these would be tenets with which they would be able to establish their identity, constituency, and collective action towards rights assertion. • In 2023, 1 CSO from the Philippines increased its lobby and advocacy skills by formulating their strategy and message to be able to influence the local government and pushing for their rights assertion from their unified ancestral domain. FGG supported the CSO by facilitating the learning sessions in which they developed their key lobby messages. • In 2023, 4 CSOs from the Philippines strengthened their knowledge on their rights as Indigenous People especially around the concept of their ancestral domains, lands and Indigenous Political Structure. During a number of sessions the CSOs reflected on the fact that despite many laws are in place to promote and protect IP rights, these laws are used to marginalize and discriminate against IPs . FGG facilitated these sessions (x). • In 2023, 28 CSOs from the Philippines strengthened their lobby and advocacy skills through participation of Indigenous Peoples Mandatory Representatives (IPMRs) and community leaders in reflection sessions where they learned to articulate their challenges and share experiences on what works in influencing the local government towards adopting resolutions and ordinances which they present. IPMRs are what links the indigenous communities to local legislative processes and agenda-setting as mandated by the IPRM law. FGG designed and facilitated these reflection sessions in response to the needs expressed by the community leaders. • 1 CSO form the Philippines reorganized their formation , policies and objectives to solidify their agenda and engage with government bodies that in many instances misunderstand and do not recognize their roles in policy making. FGG supported the reorganization by designing and facilitating the reflection session. (x) • 1 CSO from the Philippines , was formed to develop and strengthen the voice and movement of women beyond community level but also link the efforts of women at the ancestral domain level. FGG facilitated the organizational development and paralegal sessions with the women’s group. (g) • 1 CSO from the Philippines , strengthened their knowledge and strategy by reorganizing and initiating a leadership training session for its officers facilitated by FGG. In 2024 the FGG programme aims for 490 CSO actors with strengthened capacity for lobby and advocacy. These actors are based in different places around the world, including but not limited to Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Costa Rica, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Liberia, Mozambique, Nigeria, the Philippines, South Africa and Uganda. In 2024 the FGG programme engages in mutual capacity development through: Access: CSO actors, women in particular, will have better access to decision-making spaces;Constituency: CSO actors will strengthen their linkages with existing regional networks and movements that provide capacity building for IPLCs and EHRDs;Knowledge building: CSO actors will strengthen their knowledge through capacity development on specific topics based on the local contexts as well as skills such as community organising, joint strategising, human resources, knowledge production and dissemination, data and evidence-based analysis, information exchange, proposal development, basic project and financial management, fundraising, (women and youth) leadership, network building;Advocacy skills: CSO actors will strengthen their advocacy and lobby capacity through activities such as negotiation and communication skills development, peaceful advocacy tactics training, effective mobilisation strategies and knowledge building on fair and green practices;Leverage: CSO actors will strengthen their capacity to leverage on multiple (supra-national) pressure points;Enabling environment: CSO actors will strengthen their capacities to undertake action freely and safely, with a focus on feminist leadership. In 2024, FGG partners and members will increase their knowledge on and strengthen their capacity to lobby and advocate for among other things: Trade and investment agreements: Fair and green trade and investment agreements that enable governments to live up to their human rights obligations, with a particular focus on Feminist Foreign Policy, the Energy Charter Treaty and digital trade chapters in free trade agreements, e.g. EU Mercosur, EU-Indonesia, EU-India, EU-Mexico and EU-Thailand; Renegotiation and termination of International Investment Agreements and Bilateral Investment Treaties, e.g. with Argentina, Kenya, Nigeria, Tanzania, Turkey and Uganda;CSO participation in and influence on regional and international spaces of trade policy making (such as the WTO, UNCTAD, EU);The implications of trade treaties for specific countries, e.g. Uganda’s obligations under international trade treaties and conventions to protect workers and communities affected by the activities of palm oil companies.Climate and environmental policies: Environmental rights, such as climate justice, climate litigation and prevention of more pollution;Community forests as a means to measure carbon sequestration and counter deforestation;Fossil fuel company Total’s lack of due diligence measures in Mozambique, and the possibility of them using ISDS. FGG will engage in mutual capacity development to increase CSOs’ legal capacities to provide materials and evidence for the court cases,develop campaign materials to illustrate the impacts of the LNG projects, and to increase their access to media in the home countries of the gas companies involved.Policies on tenure:VGGTs, at national and UN level;Inclusion of women’s, indigenous and community land rights in national legal frameworks and internationally agreed guidelines, e.g. in Kenya, India and Uganda;Land grabbing, illegal logging on community land and land-related policies and issues of corruption;Inheritance rights and the use of alternative justice systems in resolving community land disputes;Indigenous communities regaining land tenure titles and rehabilitation of forest-based livelihoods in India. Public financial institutions: A full stop of ECA support of fossil fuels, need for a just energy transition and a ban on fossil exploration and extraction;Awareness raising on the importance of policy influencing towards IFIs/DFIs (WB, FMO);The policies and practices of international financial institutions and development finance institutions such as the World Bank and the Dutch Development Bank (FMO), the rights people have vis-a-vis the investments of these institutions, and the networks they need to influence these institutions’ policies and practices, in among other countries Malawi. Rules for business and corporate conduct, cross sectoralUN Binding Treaty on Business and Human Rights;European Union Corporate Social Due Diligence Directive.Rules for business & corporate conduct, extractivesExpansion of the fossil fuel industry in Latin American and African countries;Litigation against environmental pollution & corporate violations of human rights;Access to remedy including for community groups in Uganda; Engage companies and governments to prevent, mitigate, and remedy human rights abuses related to graphite mining in Mozambique;Socially responsible battery supply chains;Gender responsive service delivery for women miners in Zimbabwe.Rules for business & corporate conduct, garment sectorLabour and human rights such as living wages, workers health and safety, prevention and remedy of labour rights violations, freedom of association;Corporate regulation and supply chain transparency;Enforceable brand agreements.Rules for business and corporate conduct, tech sectorCSOs’ engagement in the reviews of mergers;Political economy of data, digital trade and e-commerce. Fair and green systems: agroecologyInclusive and gender-responsive natural resource governance that is supportive of agroecological practices in Kenya;Empowerment of Kenyan female leaders will advance Agroecology at (international) institutional/governmental level;Financial support at national and UN level for community-based transformative practices such as agroecology;Establishment of agroecological community farms, formation of community advocates/practitioners or Farmer Mentors for Ecology and Culture and the set-up of conversation hubs for continuing sharing of agroecology and cultural practices, in Indonesia and the Philippines;Mapping of traditional food conservation areas in the Philippines; Baseline assessment on food and agricultural food systems through collaboration with relevant networks in Indonesia.Fair and green systems: energy, water, other public goods and serviceA new water law in Guatemala that includes the rights of communities and indigenous people related to water and incorporates a gender justice lense; Seed systems development in Kenya;Rights and recognition of IPLCs in different contexts, including India, and Indonesia’s new capital city;Community-led water governance, increasing access to potable water, and protecting water sources in the Philippines and Indonesia; (Feminist) just energy transition; On digital justice, e.g. Just and sustainable/community led AI, digital public goods and infrastructures, digital commons.
