Their networks expanded by attending the AfDB annual meetings in Abidjan and gaining direct access to Board Members of the Bank (g). • In 2024, one CSO in Malawi strengthened its capacity by hiring a gender-based violence expert to address issues in the Salima case. FGG provided financial assistance. • In 2024, two CSOs in Mozambique improved their lobby and advocacy skills by increasing community mobilization capacities, enhancing access to decision-makers in the Netherlands, and engaging in joint strategising. FGG contributed by sharing information regularly and developing joint strategies targeting financial institutions involved in the Mozambique LNG project. • In 2024, five CSOs in Mozambique strengthened their networks and advocacy capacities by formalizing four natural resource management committees (GCRN) across different villages. This formalization enabled these committees to be recognized and actively participate in advocacy initiatives. FGG supported these efforts through joint strategician and financial assistance. • In 2024, one CSO in Cameroon organized a workshop for a network of Cameroonian CSOs monitoring IFIs on the financial structure of the IFI-financed Nachtigal dam. A CSO established an organizational structure to ensure the participation of women affected by the Nachtigal project in mediation efforts between the dam company and affected communities. FGG provided strategic support and contributed to the development of an action plan arising from the mediation process (g).Rules for business and corporate conduct, cross sectoral • In 2024, 4 CSOs from Uganda increased their knowledge and advocacy skills in relation to Business and Human Rights, defending civic space, and implementing the Ugandan National Action Plan (NAP) on Business and Human Rights and the Social Impact and Accountability Act (SIAA). FGG supported through training workshops and joint strategising. (x) • Throughout 2024, 5 CSOs from Kenya operating to address the rights of communities impacted by large-scale corporate investments strengthened their capacities on feminist project implementation approaches and HRD security, policy influencing, and campaigning (g+x). • Throughout 2024, 6 CSOs from Kenya strengthened their capacities on land rights, specifically the Kenyan Community Land Act and the theory around the tragedy of the commons. FGG supported through training workshops. • In 2024, 7 CSOs from Kenya strengthened their capacities on advocacy, particularly how to draft community demands in relation to corporate accountability. FGG supported through training workshops. • In 2024, 1 CSO from Kenya was trained on Alternative Justice Systems (AJS), their county model, and their roles and responsibilities. FGG supported through training workshops and joint strategising. • In 2024, 2 CSOs from Zimbabwe strengthened their knowledge on the Zimbabwe National Action Plan (NAP) on Business and Human Rights and the African Continental Free Trade Association (AfCFTA), as well as on strengthening women’s forums for improved community-led participation in the value chain and accountability. These activities promoted environmental justice, with FGG providing both financial and technical support. • In 2024, 32 CSOs across Africa, Latin America, and Asia learned about the UN Binding Treaty process and the need for a strong feminist UN Binding Treaty during multiple learning sessions organized by ActionAid International. Specific attention was given to the gender perspective in the treaty, rights of victims, access to remedy, human rights due diligence, and a strong liability regime. (g) • In 2024, 4 CSOs from Guatemala strengthened their capacities in reporting human rights violations in the palm oil sector in relation to the German due diligence law. This was achieved through collaboration, technical support, and joint strategising with FGG partners and members. • In 2024, 12 CSOs from Cambodia, Indonesia, India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, North Macedonia, Moldova, and Romania participated in a webinar titled "The EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive: One Step Forward on the Road to Corporate Justice." This webinar provided a comprehensive overview of the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (EU CSDDD), highlighting its scope and how the FGG network could utilize it to advance its priorities and protect labour rights. FGG organized the webinar to support knowledge sharing and strategic collaboration. • In 2024, 16 CSOs from South Asia and South East Asia participated in two online workshops. These workshops focused on the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (EU CSDDD) and the dynamics and impacts of Chinese investment in textile supply chains across regions. Organized by FGG, the workshops aimed to enhance understanding and promote strategic discussions on these crucial topics. • In 2024, participants in the campaign against Mekorot gained knowledge about Mekorot's activities in Africa and Latin America, focusing on how it organizes discriminatory access and water apartheid in Palestine, and its specific impacts on women and children. This knowledge was disseminated through two published reports and a subsequent webinar. These resources were utilized to organize an online campaign targeting The Federal Investment Council (CFI) and contracts initiated between Mekorot, provinces, companies, and local authorities involved in the Argentinian National Council. (g) • In 2024, 12 CSOs deepened their knowledge of the updated draft of the Binding Treaty on Business and Human Rights. The CSOs analysed key articles of the treaty with support of FGG.(x) • In 2024, during the 10th negotiating session of the open-ended intergovernmental working group on transnational corporations and other business enterprises concerning human rights, a meeting was held with the delegation of an FGG member. Together with the global campaign, FGG organized a training session on the legal-political positions to present at the negotiations. FGG attended the event with 16 participants from 8 countries, prepared statements on all articles, and advocated for increasing the treaty's effectiveness and ambition. FGG also participated in parallel events organized by the global campaign inside and outside the UN, including one held at a university, attended by students and local movements. (x) • In 2024, 89 CSOs strengthened their capacity to use the OECD Guidelines, due diligence guidance, and other responsible business conduct instruments. These skills empower them to file strategic complaints, advocate for progressive binding laws and policies on responsible business conduct, and push for positive national human rights and environmental reforms through the OECD accession process. FGG, through OECD Watch, facilitated this by conducting various capacity-building workshops on complaint strategy, legal advocacy, and accession advocacy (x, g). • In 2024, four global CSOs, networks, and institutions strengthened their understanding of corporate capture in multilateral decision-making through participating in multistakeholder forums in sectors such as health, education, debt, technology, environment, food, and agriculture. These organisations lobbied against multistakeholderism in relation to the UN Summit of the Future. FGG provided technical support, written reports, and co-organised dissemination activities to highlight the potential impacts of multistakeholderism on global south countries. • In 2024, 34 CSOs, social movements, and networks advocated for a UN Binding Treaty on Transnational Corporations and Human Rights. Their advocacy efforts included oral interventions during (online) Open-Ended Inter-Governmental Working Group (OEIGWG) sessions of the UNHRC, (online) meetings with national missions, publishing statements and analyses, media work, and organising public events at the Palais de Nations in Geneva as well as online. Two organisations specifically addressed the gender dimensions of the treaty. FGG co-organised strategy meetings, supported partners in preparing feedback on the revised draft of the treaty, and provided logistical and financial assistance to some CSOs.Rules for business & corporate conduct, extractives • In 2024, 3 CSOs (women’s mining groups) from Kenya (, were trained on livelihoods and business skills in the context of inclusive development in relation to the gemstones value chain. (g) • In 2024, 1 CSO from Zimbabwe strengthened their participation in the gemstone value chain by improving their skills in gemstone cutting and polishing. (g) • In 2024, 1 CSO from Zimbabwe was trained on mineral resource governance, the roles and responsibilities of councillors, and how they can exercise their role as policymakers. The training was provided by FGG and also focused on improving their relationship and collaboration with CSOs and communities. • In 2024, 22 CSOs focused on labour rights and environmental activism in Indonesia established the Morowali Clean Forum following a 2-day workshop. The Forum is dedicated to advocating for occupational safety, health, and environmental issues within the Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park. This workshop, titled “Challenges in Employment and Environment in Nickel Mining in Indonesia for International Advocacy,” was organised by FGG, GoodElectronics, and CNV. Its purpose was to foster collaboration among these organisations and identify joint advocacy goals. • In 2024, 10 CSOs from the Philippines, Indonesia, Brazil, Argentina, Uganda, Ghana, and DR Congo strengthened their capacity to understand and influence EU policies on critical raw materials (CRM). They engaged in research and developed joint strategies to address the impacts of CRM mining, just energy transition, climate change, and human rights issues. FGG organized a 3-day global learning and strategy meeting on critical raw materials to support these efforts. (x) • In 2024, 5 CSOs from Bolivia, Honduras, Brazil, Argentina, and Colombia strengthened their capacity in lobbying and advocacy, networking, knowledge sharing, and campaigning including through their involvement in the OilWatch Latin America network. FGG provided both financial and strategic support to the CSOs to enhance their efforts. (x +g) • In 2024, a Latin American CSO organized a strategy meeting with the coordination group of the campaign alliance, as well as a larger assembly involving all CSOs within the alliance. These meetings resulted in the development of a joint strategy and campaign against fracking and the exploitation of unconventional deposits. FGG provided financial support to the strategy meeting. (x) • In 2024, a Latin American CSO enhanced its knowledge of how the projection of the Caribbean as a "gas province" and the promotion of gas as a transition fuel perpetuate sacrifice zones and contradict climate action. The CSO also gained insights into the technical and political aspects of gas extraction and possible alternatives through organizing the first “Gas Congress of Caribbean Communities.” This event was attended by communities, CSOs and government representatives, FGG provided financial support. (x) • In 2024, a Latin American CSO conducted research to map transnational companies currently operating in or exploring lithium within the country. They developed an infographic map to serve as a tool for advocacy and campaigning efforts, FGG provided financial support. Rules for business & corporate conduct, garment sector • In 2024, 61 CSOs from South Asia, South East Asia, and Eastern Europe, including Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, and the Philippines, enhanced their capacities in campaigning, knowledge production and dissemination, information exchange, joint strategising and addressing critical issues in global garment supply chains, such as living wages, enforceable brand agreements, worker health and safety, prevention and remedy of labour rights violations, shrinking civic space and freedom of association, corporate regulation (including human rights due diligence), just transition, and supply chain transparency. FGG supported these activities by funding and organising annual regional meetings, where partners gathered to strategise, coordinate, support, and learn from each other. (g) • In 2024, 19 CSOs from South Asia and South East Asia, strengthened their capacities in coordination, campaign and lobby strategy, knowledge production, dissemination, and data-driven evidence analysis. These initiatives focused on urgent appeals, wages and freedom of association (centred on the Pay Your Workers/Respect Labour Rights campaign), worker safety (focused on the Accord), enforceable brand agreements, mandatory human rights and environmental due diligence, and just transition. FGG provided human and financial resources. (g) • In 2024, 9 Indonesian factory-level union leaders from 9 trade unions participated in a training workshop organised by FGG. This workshop developed their skills in campaign planning and execution to resolve labour rights violations and taught them to create campaign messages and materials around freedom of association and defending civic space. (x) • In 2024, 22 individuals from 12 CSOs in Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Indonesia, and the Philippines participated in a training held in Mae Sot, Thailand. The training focused on the Urgent Appeal System, evidence gathering, and access to information in opaque environments, such as informal work arrangements, subcontracting, and the dire conditions faced by migrant workers. These discussions also addressed contexts where freedom of speech and information is restricted, such as Myanmar. Participants planned next steps for research and case work during the training. (x) • In 2024, 19 CSOs from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka attended four national training sessions in South Asia. These sessions enhanced their knowledge of the Urgent Appeal System, enabling its effective use to safeguard labour rights in the supply chains of international garment brands. The trainings also focused on cultivating second-tier leadership within FGG partners in the region, empowering young activists to take on urgent appeal cases. This effort resulted in three new reports of potential cases from Bangladesh and one from Sri Lanka immediately following the trainings. (g) • In 2024, 12 CSOs from Turkey, Thailand, Sri Lanka, Romania, North Macedonia, Indonesia, India, Myanmar, Cambodia, and Bangladesh participated in an online peer-learning webinar with 19 CCC urgent appeal case coordinators. The webinar focused on the theme of remediation for garment workers’ unpaid severance and aimed to develop strategic approaches for investigating and lobbying brands on severance payment cases. (x) • In 2024, 7 global CSOs participated in two series of Disrupt the Fashion Industry workshop trainings tailored for Western and Eastern time zones. These workshops equipped participants with direct action methods to demand change in the global garment industry, focusing on themes like living wages, compensation, and severance. (g) • In 2024, 5 CSOs from Myanmar, strengthened their physical and operational safety through securing communication and joint strategising sessions. FGG supported the CSOs financially and through emergency support and partner coordination support as well as by reaching out to garment brands. (x) Rules for business and corporate conduct, tech sector • In 2024, thirteen CSOs from Asia, Africa, Europe, and Latin America expanded their networks, enhanced their expertise on digital topics, and strengthened their advocacy to promote civic space in multilateral and intergovernmental settings. Themes included global digital governance, global digital policy, digital justice in healthcare and agriculture, WSIS+20 Review, and the Global Digital Compact. FGG supported these efforts through strategy meetings, workshops, and collaborative advocacy. • In 2024, one global CSO advanced its understanding and advocacy capacity on the platformisation of work, the right to decent work, the digitalisation of traditional sectors, and the development of ILO Decent Work Standards in the Platform Economy. FGG provided workshops and research outputs to support their initiatives. • In 2024, 15 CSOs, part of the Break Open Big Tech Working Group, strengthened their knowledge and advocacy on topics such an anti-monopoly and antitrust action against Big Tech companies, enforcement of competition law, steps to break up tech monopolies and building alternative digital futures.. FGG co-chaired working groups and contributed through research outputs, strategy meetings, and workshops. • In 2024, one CSO from Fiji built its capacity and knowledge on the erosion of labour rights, the impact of platformisation on female workers, and advocacy in global internet governance processes. FGG provided training workshops, research outputs, and advocacy submissions to support their work. • In 2024, OECD Watch advanced its capacity, shared advocacy, and knowledge on themes such as responsible AI innovation, global data governance, and implementation frameworks. It also contributed to the OECD Draft AI Due Diligence Guideline. FGG supported their efforts through working groups, strategy meetings, and research outputs. • In 2024, one CSO from Indonesia enhanced its knowledge and capacity on digitalisation in agrarian and environmental systems, agriculture supply chains, and the role of digital technologies in farmer fields. FGG facilitated this through a targeted training workshop. • In 2024, 1 CSO strengthened a network of groups coordinating efforts to push for the enforcement of competition policy aimed at limiting excessive market power. FGG supported the development of this network both financially and with expertise, enhancing its capacity to advocate for fair market practices. • In 2024, FGG supported a global convening that brought together CSOs from the Digital Merger Watch. This initiative strengthened a network of groups capable of monitoring and intervening during merger review processes across different jurisdictions, aimed at restricting big technology companies from expanding their market power through mergers and acquisitions (M&A). • In 2024, a global network is strengthening its capacity by the creation of insights on digitalisation as a tool of capital and conservative/fascist forces (governments, political parties, churches, billionaires, etc.) and as a tool for the deepening of the system of oppression. Based on this increase in knowledge and exchanges, 4 webinars on the topic were elaborated, coordinated by FGG. Fair and green systems: agroecology • In 2024, a CSO from Argentina worked with women from a cooperative to enhance local communities' productive capacities in agroecology and food sovereignty. This improved the food self-sufficiency of a community kitchen, strengthening agroecological production and the distribution of healthy food. FGG provided financial support. (g) • In 2024, 10 CSOs from Latin America, Africa, and Asia enhanced their advocacy on agribusiness and false solutions at various levels, linking these issues to corporate power and strategies. This was supported by a report, a webinar on False Solutions, and the 56th Nyéléni Newsletter, which highlighted the corporate capture of agroecology. FGG financed the report’s publication and contributed articles to the newsletter. (x) • In 2024, 3 CSOs from Kenya, Nigeria, and Uganda improved collaboration between Climate Justice and Food Sovereignty movements through systematic online discussions on key issues, including False Solutions. FGG contributed to the proposal for a movement process. • In 2024, 5 CSOs from Argentina, El Salvador, Palestine, Nigeria, and Liberia prepared for participation in external movements such as the Nyéléni process by formulating common goals and strategies. They strengthened people’s movements and increased intersectional perspectives. FGG organized the internal process and contributed to the summit’s planning. (x) • In 2024, 3 CSOs from India, Togo, and Paraguay participated in the webinar “What kind of multilateralism and global governance do we want?” They gained insights into the evolving landscape of multilateralism and the Summit of the Future (SOTF) process. FGG, as a member of the People’s Working Group on Multistakeholderism, co-organized the webinar and fostered collective analysis. • In 2024, the Civil Society and Indigenous People Mechanism (CSIPM) for relations with the UN Committee on World Food Security (CFS) facilitated discussions on structural issues like trade and debt, boosting advocacy and consultations globally. This led to multilateral meetings on global food crisis policy coordination and advocacy on famine in Palestine. FGG participated in the FAO Committee on Food Security and contributed to CSIPM strategies for the CFS plenary. • A CSO from Argentina worked, especially with the women from a cooperative, on local communities’ productive capacities in agroecology and food sovereignty, which improved the food self-sufficiency of the community kitchen, strengthening their agroecological production and distribution of healthy and tasty food. FGG provided financial support. (g) • In 2024, two CSO partners from the Philippines increased their capacities in agroecology and continued their Agroecology and Culture (AgroEcCu) initiatives. They expanded their learning farms and adhered to agroecological principles, focusing on reviving traditional seeds. FGG provided technical support and mentoring for farmer mentors. • In 2024, two CSO partners in the Philippines expanded their learning farms to cover 2.3 hectares, replanting traditional seeds alongside other varieties and cultivating crops for household consumption. They initiated seed sharing programs and collected Indigenous plant varieties to address prolonged heat conditions. Traditional corn seeds were successfully shared with neighbouring communities. Some members participated in Training of Trainers programs for Agroecology Farmer Teachers. FGG offered technical assistance and mentoring for farmer mentors. • In 2024, one IP partner from the Philippines enhanced organisational management capabilities, reclaiming and replanting two hectares of mortgaged land. They established a coordination body of Agroecology Farmer Teachers, developed policies for ancestral land protection, and participated in the AgroEkulohista Conference to learn from other communities. FGG supported this initiative through technical assistance and mentoring. • A women-led IP partner from the Philippines established a ¼-hectare communal farm, practising agroecological and traditional vegetable farming methods. FGG supported the implementation through a small grant (g). • In 2024, A women-led IP partner in the Philippines gained skills in agroecology farming, herbal processing, and organic vegetable production. They developed AgroEcCu community farm plans, created an organisational vision, and started producing alternative medicines from traditional plants. They participated in learning exchanges, exploring strategies and continuing seed sharing. FGG accompanied them in small grant implementation (g). • In 2024, A CSO in the Philippines organised an Agroecology Camp that enhanced the capacities of 40 youth, engaging them in sustainable agricultural practices. Youth participants began supporting farm activities, documenting trial farms, and offering technical training for farmers. The CSO partner also advocated for youth representation in Provincial Consultative Bodies (PCBs). FGG provided grants and facilitation support (g). • In Indonesia, a CSO partner strengthened the capacities of 49 youth from West Java, sparking interest in local food issues and gardening. They facilitated training and mentoring for youth individuals and groups, fostering agents of change in environmental and food advocacy. FGG supported through small grants and technical assistance (g). • In 2024, One CSO from Indonesia established the Social Forestry Heir School education program, training youth in agricultural practices and environmental conservation. The program included legal aspects of transferring Social Forestry and Environmental Partnership (BPKSL) rights. FGG supported the program with grants and facilitation • In 2024, a women-led IP partner in the Philippines continued managing a small enterprise established in 2023 after multiple trainings, which resulted in developing their business plans. FGG provided grants and facilitation support (g). • An IP youth partner in the Philippines showcased their support for local enterprises through the One Barangay, One Product (OBOP) initiative. Their creative, locally produced items won recognition at the annual municipal festival. FGG supported the youth partner with capacity development assistance. • In 2024, 2 CSOs from Colombia and Morocco strengthened their lobby and advocacy efforts to promote the recognition of indigenous and farmers' rights to traditional medicinal plants in various UN drug policy declarations and resolutions. FGG supported these organisations by co-organising lobby activities. • In 2024, 7 international and regional food sovereignty organisations from Global, India, South Africa, and Latin America collaborated to support the International Planning Committee for Food Sovereignty (IPC)—an autonomous and self-organised global platform representing 300 million small-scale food producers through 6,000 local and national organisations. Under the facilitation committee, these organisations agreed on the process for the Nyeleni Global Gathering. FGG provided critical analysis and technical expertise to strengthen their capacity for strategy development in preparation for the Nyeleni Global Gathering. • In 2024, 6 CSOs from Africa, Latin America, and Asia enhanced their knowledge, networks, and advocacy skills on agroecology, food sovereignty, environmental justice, and people’s rights against corporate power. FGG co-organised activities and provided financial and technical support. • In 2024, four CSOs in Kenya, through their participation in the Kenya Landscape Actors Platform co-sponsored by CABI and One Thousand Landscapes, strengthened their capacity to lobby and advocate for landscape conservation via sustainable agricultural practices. • In 2024, with support from FGG partner Uttaran, a new youth Paani (water) Committee was established in the Betna basin, Bangladesh. The committee participated in capacity-building workshops and exchange visits with the youth Paani Committee from the Kapotakkho river basin to learn about water governance structures, Tidal River Management, and agroecological practices. Members from the Betna basin later disseminated this knowledge to their community members, especially those vulnerable to waterlogging, enhancing their awareness and capacity to advocate for sustainable water governance and agricultural practices. • In 2024, two CSOs in Bangladesh, through ‘people-centric Farmer Field Schools’ (FFS), empowered small-scale farmers to enhance their traditional and agroecological farming capacities. Peer-to-peer exchanges enabled farmers to learn about agricultural techniques, innovations, and strategies for successful advocacy for government support, including finance, market access, and technical assistance. • In 2024, one CSO in Kenya worked to maintain control of their community-led water project in the Matimbei community through capacity-building workshops on Kenyan water governance. Supported by a retired Water Resource Authority officer and the Bathi WRUA, the community documented their struggle to reclaim and maintain their water project with assistance from an FGG partner. • In 2024, six CSO partners in Kenya, through co-funding support from FGG for their collaboration with knowledge institutes in an IHE-Delft funded project, contributed to strengthening the Athi River Community Network. The network enhanced its understanding of water distribution and quality within the river basin and expanded its national and international connections to advocate for inclusive water governance.Fair and green systems: energy, water, other public goods and service • In 2024, 14 CSOs from Bangladesh increased their knowledge of the advantages of renewable energy as opposed to fossil fuels. FGG supported these efforts with training workshops and awareness-raising meetings. • Throughout 2024, 6 CSOs from Guatemala strengthened their capacities in lobbying on the new national water law proposed by the Guatemalan government. They also gained knowledge about the importance of including a gender perspective in the water law, treating water as a human right, and approaching water as a living being (g+x). • In 2024, a CSO partner in the Philippines organised an event reaching 205 participants from 21 organisations, including those in academe, church, civil society, and media networks. The event discussed Constitutional Frameworks, Jurisprudence, and the implications of Charter Change. The forum posed impactful questions regarding changes in economic provisions, including granting 100% ownership of land, businesses, agro-agri ventures, franchises, communication, education, advertising, and other facilities to foreign nationals. This sparked meaningful discussions on societal and economic implications. (x) • In 2024, a CSO in Cambodia strengthened the English language skills of Human Rights Defenders (HRDs), enabling more effective communication with non-Khmer-speaking stakeholders. This skill-building is significant as it broadens their networks within the donor community, increasing funding opportunities for their pro-democracy activism. (x) • In 2024, a CSO in the Philippines facilitated an Island-Wide Student Congress and hosted a Leadership and Press Workshop camp. The initiatives focused on prevailing demands in publication practices within local government units and student councils in academe. Participants gained skills to benchmark best practices and strengthen camaraderie across youth formations, enhancing their roles in social change movements. (x) • In 2024, 2 international CSOs and 2 CSOs from Brazil and India increased their knowledge, networking and lobby and advocacy capacity on public energy, specifically in building the right to public energy. FGG co-organised workshops with partners and provided technical support, particularly from a gender perspective.. How does public energy make contributions towards a feminist economy? (g) • In 2024, one Chilean university and one Colombian trade union enhanced their knowledge capacities on public energy by running a diploma course on public service provision. FGG supported this diploma programme. • In 2024, one global CSO and one African CSO were supported in organising a counter summit to the World Water Forum held in Indonesia. Water justice movements from across the globe convened at the People’s Water Forum (PWF) 2024 to challenge the corporate capture of global water governance at the World Water Forum, strengthen the global network of water justice movements, and advocate for public and community water alternatives to achieve true water justice for all. FGG provided financial and technical support. • In 2024, the Public Pathway Research Network was established, uniting seven research bodies and independent researchers to bolster South-based research, analysis, and action-oriented programmes for a pro-public energy transition. FGG supported the establishment of the network, became a member, and co-organised the strategy meeting that led to its formation.

In 2025, the FGG programme aims for 410 CSO actors with strengthened capacity for lobby and advocacy. These actors are based in different places around the world, including but not limited to Argentina, Bangladesh, Brazil, Cambodia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Kenya, Liberia, Mozambique, Mexico, Nigeria, the Philippines, South Africa, Thailand, Uganda and Zimbabwe. In 2025, the FGG programme engages in mutual capacity development through: • Access: CSO actors, women in particular, will have better access to decision-making spaces; • Constituency: CSO actors will strengthen their linkages with existing regional networks and movements that provide capacity building for IPLCs and EHRDs; • Knowledge building: CSO actors will strengthen their knowledge through capacity development on specific topics based on the local contexts as well as skills such as community organising, joint strategising, human resources, knowledge production and dissemination, data and evidence-based analysis, information exchange, proposal development, basic project and financial management, fundraising, (women and youth) leadership, network building; • Advocacy skills: CSO actors will strengthen their advocacy and lobby capacity through activities such as negotiation and communication skills development, peaceful advocacy tactics training, effective mobilisation strategies and knowledge building on fair and green practices; • Leverage: CSO actors will strengthen their capacity to leverage on multiple (supra-national) pressure points; • Enabling environment: CSO actors will strengthen their capacities to undertake action freely and safely, with a focus on feminist leadership. In 2025, FGG partners and members will increase their knowledge on and strengthen their capacity to lobby and advocate for among other things: Trade and investment agreements • The risks the Energy Charter Treaty poses for government's policy space to protect people's rights, the environment and the planet. • The relevance and risks of the Mercosur trade deal and the need to re-open the negotiations instead of signing an additional protocol. • Renegotiation and termination of International Investment Agreements and Bilateral Investment Treaties and the challenges international investment treaties pose for policy space to protect people's rights, the environment and the planet. Climate and environmental policies • To engage with the new Kenyan government programme on Community-Led climate action. • To raise awareness about threats posed by false solutions to the climate, food and biodiversity crises. Initiatives include biodiversity offsetting, carbon markets, carbon trading, nature-based solutions, GMOs and synthetic biology, geo-engineering, negative emissions technologies, bio-energy with carbon capture and storage, climate smart agriculture and sustainable intensification of agriculture; debt-for-nature-swaps and biodiversity inclusive spatial planning. • To raise awareness on environmental laws, biodiversity and climate change among local communities. Policies on tenure • To safeguard women’s and community rights and access to land in Kenya and Uganda; and to promote the strengthening of national legal frameworks for the protection of land rights. • To safeguard land rights of communities affected by land grab, loss of land, and forced displacement in the context of the building of large-scale fossil power plants and related infrastructure projects in Bangladesh. • To raise awareness on marine commons, land reclamation and sand-mining. • To document the creation and scaling up of the Special Culture Zone of the community on its customary land and forest management. • To mobilise communities for biocultural management of territories.Public financial institutions • To raise awareness on the importance of influencing towards International Financial Institutions and support community members to advocate towards the Malawi Human Rights Commission extension of influencing and visit the project site. • To support the communities affected by the Hydropower Achwa project in Uganda through monitoring developments and identifying a policy process to advocate for the community’s needs. Rules for business and corporate conduct, cross sectoral • To advocate for a UN Legally Binding Instrument on Transnational Corporations and Human Rights. • To use the data on companies covered by corporate accountability laws in their work. • To advocate for robust implementation of the revised OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises. • To increase expertise, strategic insight, and access to legal resources, for strategic litigation cases. Rules for business & corporate conduct, extractives • To engage companies and governments to prevent, mitigate, and remedy human rights abuses related to the extraction of e.g. black granite in Zimbabwe, limestone and gypsum in Kenya and nickel in Guatemala. • Due diligence in the extractives sector in Kenya including by jointly (together with a platform of CSO's working on extractives) developing a due diligence manual for the extractives and energy sector. • To provide specific research and to develop campaign materials to illustrate the impacts of the LNG projects and access to media in the home countries of the gas companies involved. • To expose the negative impacts of the fossil fuel industry in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia and Honduras and promote phasing out of fossil fuels in these countries.Rules for business & corporate conduct, garment sector • To advocate for worker health and safety and mandatory human rights due diligence such as living wage, enforceable brand agreements, just transition in the garment industry, shrinking civic space, freedom of association, supply chain transparency, prevention and remedy of labour rights violations. • On corporate regulation and supply chain transparency.Rules for business and corporate conduct, tech sector • To raise awareness on opportunities for coalition building within the tech sector. • To advocate for rules on digital justice, corporate governance, political economy of data, digital trade and e-commerce.Fair and green systems: agroecology • To deliver joint inputs to the Nyeleni Forum, the global food sovereignty movement. • To participate in the Transformative Water Pact which provides a platform for knowledge exchanges and networking on water justice. • On agroecology, food sovereignty and environmental justice and people’s rights against corporate power, including the rights of small-scale fisher folk and align with international human rights instruments like the Voluntary Guidelines on small-scale fisheries in Asia, Africa and Latin America, including India. • To build capacities of indigenous and small-holder farmers to integrate agroecological principles, and technical capacities in agroecology-based farming by providing trainings and developing AgroEcCu community farms. • For ‘Agroekulohista’ or farmer mentors to lead the integration of agroecological principles, by supporting their assessment and localised planning including regularising their organisational processes.Fair and green systems: energy, water, other public goods and service • A transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy in Bangladesh, while also defending civic space, and promoting the protection of rights of communities affected by energy related (fossil based) megaprojects such as power plants. • On public energy, universal public services and gender-just water provision in Latin America. • A (Feminist) just energy transition.

comment.narrative: Of the 659 CSOs FGG aims to support in 2021, 252 will strengthen their capacities relevant to advance gender justice. For more information, we refer to member IATI files (i.e. ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie, Friends of the Earth International, Samdhana, SOMO, Transnational Institute)
Of the 591 CSOs FGG supported in 2021, 239 strengthened their capacities relevant to advance gender justice.
